Legolas can be found somewhere near the road leading to Durthang in Lhingris.
Legolas has asked you to join him in his search for an old foe known to his father as the spider-queen, Ungwetári.

'I am glad you have come, ${PLAYER}....
'Be this the work of Ungwetári herself or that of her terrible children, the spiders of Lhingris are born of some terrible evil.'

'${PLAYER}, I have seen something terrible along the road to Durthang. A few spiders scuttled too near the ruins from Lhingris, and I was reminded at once of Mirkwood and the tales of my father, Thranduil!
'In an Age now past, he battled against a terrible spider -- itself only a child of one even greater. The great spider-queen: Ungwetári!
'It has been over three thousand years since my father heard her terrible name spoken by one of the Nazgûl, but I fear a creature so terrible and so near to the lands of the Enemy had strength enough to persist long beyond the years of Men!
'I must go into Lhingris and seek the source of the evil within the Ephel Dúath! If you wish to join me, I shall wait for a time near the road to Durthang -- but do not tarry overlong!'
In Search of the Spider-queen

At the urging of Captain Róglarg, you are to continue your search for the Elf-warrior at the gate to Imlad Morgul, Fennas Gost. Even if you do not intend to find the \qElf-warrior\q, you might still learn more of Gothmog's plans in Minas Morgul.

Beyond this gate lies Imlad Morgul, where Gothmog now hides in fear of King Elessar.
If the day comes to set siege to the Dead City of Minas Morgul, the bridge from Ithilien into the vale shall either have to be rebuilt or the gate of Fennas Gost must be thrown down.

'Next is... Fennas Gost....'
Róglarg appears disgusted at having to speak Sindarin.
'The gate to the Dead City has been sealed recently, but I doubt an Elf would have much trouble getting around it. Gothmog's plans in Gondor slipped, and now he's holed up in the Dead City. Some \qDread Terror\q he is!'
'If the Elf-warrior's been to the gate, he's either in Imlad Morgul or... he's made it to Ithilien and the High Up will have our heads.
'And lastly...'

Legolas fears that the tide of battle will soon turn in Shelob's favour, and only by drawing the attention of Ugrukhôr and Rûkhor to Cirith Ungol will the Tower survive her wrath and keep her confined to the Ephel Dúath.
You hastily scrawl a message warning that Cirith Ungol shall soon fall to Shelob and her brood!

Legolas can be found in the turret of the Tower of Cirith Ungol.
You have delivered the message of warning to Belzagar and written it as such in his book. You should now speak to Legolas.

Belzagar can be found in the turret of the Tower of Cirith Ungol.
Legolas has asked you to attempt to convey his message of warning to Belzagar to again reinforce the Tower of Cirith Ungol.

'It is all we can do, since the Gúrzyul would not dare treat with us. Nor would we with them!'
Legolas turns to Belzagar.
'Do you understand, Man of Mordor? Send word to your masters at once, or you and the rest of Mordor shall soon be devoured by Ungwetári... by Shelob!
'This is no great mercy, and this marks no alliance between our peoples. The spider-queen threatens the lands beyond equally as much as Mordor, and she must not be allowed to stray from the Ephel Dúath!
'My companion and I shall clear the way for your escape. I hope that your masters are wiser than you!'

You warn Belzagar that unless the Tower of Cirith Ungol is held by an even larger garrison, it will fall to Shelob's brood and she will begin to consume the lands of Mordor in her wrath. You tell him to send word to Ugrukhôr in Udûn as well as Rûkhor the Pale Herald begging for aid in containing Shelob to the Ephel Dúath.
Belzagar glares at you in silence.

'${PLAYER}, we must speak quickly. Is this the Man you met while you were disguised?'
You nod.
'Very well. He seems to ill-understand his own peril, and will not heed my words of warning to him.
'If he will not accept this warning, perhaps his masters will. The Captain of the Pit, Ugrukhôr, sent the last garrison to Cirith Ungol, and it seems this Man serves another known as Rûkhor the Pale Herald. They are of the Deathless, the Gúrzyul, and they may realize the ancient power that Shelob possesses.
'Speak to Belzagar and convince him of his folly. If he does not heed your words either, scrawl a warning in his book. I doubt you shall write over anything of greater import....'
A Message for the Pale Herald

'Some kind of trap? I don't like the sound of this at all!
'We're going to need more than you or I if Váskmun and the Firehorns went down there, and if you ask me, we shouldn't wait around for those Eye-mad cultists to find us either!
'Let us return to the ruins of Díngarth, and tell Legolas and the Stout-axes of what we have learned!'
'I think we've seen enough, ${PLAYER}!'

'It is quiet here, ${PLAYER}....
'If Váskmun and the Firehorns came to this place, they did so by another way. Knowing Váskmun, he probably marched his army right up to the gates of Barad-dûr!
'Hah! There will be no tales of proud dwarves this day, my friend. Váskmun's pride does his folk no good at all!
'Now, we must find some sign of him or his folk before we are discovered!
'Let us go!'

'What is all this?
'Váskmun and the Firehorns must have come through here... for the trail of dead has led us to this chamber. Hmm....
'Look, the passage descends even further! Oh no, ${PLAYER}, don't you dare think I've become jealous! Whatever this place might be, it is no Khazad-dûm!
'Ah, but something here leaves me uneasy, my friend. Does it seem to you that that statue is looking at us?
'Because it sure seems so to me!'

Purchase the Flame of Ancalamír from one of the High-enchanters.

'Did you feel the change in the wind upon crossing the Black Gate, ${PLAYER}? Everything in this accursed land is tainted. The earth, the water, even the air.
'Allow me to introduce myself. I am Narthavron, master smith of the Noldor. I was present when the Last Alliance broke into this valley and defeated Sauron's army. I was filled with sorrow and anger seeing the atrocities they had committed here, and have made it my life's work to find a way to purge the corruption. I now believe I have the right tool to achieve this.
'I have recovered one of the adamants of old, the Flame of Ancalamír. It will unravel many items throughout Middle-earth into different components that I have named \qEmbers of Enchantment\q, \qFigments of Splendour\q, and \qMotes of Enchantment\q. What do you think? I thought those names might help bring a little more light into this dark place. Anyway, after I break the objects down, I am then able to use some of those components to fashion extraordinary equipment. I have a feeling you will be instrumental in the Conquest of Gorgoroth, and as such will be encountering many of these special items in your travels. I have a proposition for you.
'I will allow you use of the Flame. My assistants, the High-enchanters, will help you. You need only touch one of these objects to the Flame and it will be reduced to one of these components. I believe that dwarf over there has been scavenging through the Orcs' forges. Perhaps he is willing to let go of something for this purpose. Find a piece of equipment, touch it to the Flame, and then return to me.'

'Aye, the Elf's right. I am seeking anything of value that might have been left behind. The Orcs were churning out thousands of blades and armour pieces from these forges, but most of them are foul Morgul-steel. Nothing I want anything to do with!
'Here, take this dagger I found. It's worthless to me! And tell that Elf he's better off leaving this sort of thing to the dwarves!'

'The Flame of Ancalamír has performed as expected, then? Excellent.
'In your travels, should you find equipment for which you have no use, I ask that you destroy it with the Flame and give the results to one of my assistants. They will reward you with powerful items of my own making, free from the foulness of this land.
'Good luck, and safe travels, friend.'
The Flame of Ancalamír

You should help Kurtil up off the ground.
'We will learn the reply to the first speaking. Seek it east and south, near the road that leads upward to Mornaur Forge.'

'Up here, you may look down on the Land of Making and Labour. Land of muddy marching. Land of swords made and swords raised. Look below and you will see. The shape is like a sword-gash, is it not? A tale is whispered among my kind: that Xayal Zangin, the Resplendant one, fought here, in this place, with the fire giant Zalim Atash, and their fighting broke the world. Many such tales are there among my kind.'
He laughs.
'Who can say what happened long ago? Not you or I? For who should remember. We have only tellings, and tellings tatter. Tatter and wear to dust. But now you must tell to me what flags it was you saw.'
You describe each symbol you saw, drawing in the barren dirt when necessary, and the Nurnhoth slave nods gravely.

'When two men speak, one talks and then the other. Back and forth. So it is when we speak with flags. Then only those with eyes can hear. The Captain of the Pit, our lord and taskmaster, he has no such eyes. Nor his enforcers. Nor his sorcerers. Nor even his spies! They hear not when the flags speak. Only we forge-workers do.'
Kurtil delves in his wandering patter into the meanings of the flags: how one describes the nature of the topic; another whether past, present, or future; a third whether a certainty, a possibility, a warning, or a wondering, and so forth. All in all, the flags are far more subtle and complex than Barathron took them to be.
'And now, let us seek out the second speech, the answering. We should look, I think, east of here and south, by the road up to Mornaur Forge. You will go and look. And when you have seen, there I will be upon the upward road.'

'Here, I will begin. Tell me, friend. When two men meet to speak, does one say a thing - and then both go off without another word? No, no, no.
'Ah, but first, this will not do. I must get up. Will you help me?'

Kurtil stands near the dwarves and corpse, behind a cart high up the path in northern Udûn, above Maudhúl Vôr.
Hear what Kurtil has to say.
You should search for Ushkbál the Overseer in the great foundry, on the northern side of Udûn, above Maudhúl Vôr.

The dwarves stand behind a cart high up the path in northern Udûn, above Maudhúl Vôr.
The trail of footprints led straight from signs of a bloody struggle to two dwarf-forgeworkers standing over a corpse. You should speak to them.

The corpse and dwarves are behind a cart high up the path in northern Udûn, above Maudhúl Vôr.
You should inspect the overseer's corpse to verify the dwarves' claim that he bears sword-wounds, while they hold only hammers.

The dwarves are behind a cart high up the path in northern Udûn, above Maudhúl Vôr.
You should talk to the dwarves, now that you have verified that the overseer's corpse bears sword and not blunt wounds.
You have not found Ushkbál the Overseer, but you have found signs of a bloody struggle. You should follow the footprints leading from the place and see where they lead.
'The great foundry lies north of the road below, above Maudhúl Vôr. You go and seek Ushkbál the Overseer on the good legs you have. I follow behind.'
'Stéthi, you explain. I'll botch it up, properly. Besides, I'm still catching my breath from dragging old Ushkbál all the ways up here.'
'You speak to them, yes? I think that best.'
'Look and you will see. No hammer felled Ushkbál.'
'If it is so, then it is so, yes? The dwarf speaks true.'

''Twas not us who did this thing. I know full well how it may look. We only dragged him here, out of the sight of prying eyes.
'Hoy, you there, Kurtil! I know you by face and by name. Whatever trouble you're up to this time, you must bow to plain truth: Who in the northern 'works would touch a hair on Ushkbál's ugly pate? None, that's who! No overseer we'd more gladly work for, neither.
'Besides, you see we carry only hammers and these wounds be swords' work, plain to see. Look yourself, ${RACE}.'

'Now then, that's settled, I hope! A smouldering shame about Ushkbál, though! We know not if it were one of the enforcers or some wild-frenzied soldier who stuck him through, but there you have it. He was our hope and he's gone.
'Well, and if you are here then you followed the signal flags, too, just as we. Let us work the iron together, we four, while it's got any heat left. Perhaps the work might be salvaged. If only we can think what to do now that we are on our own. What say you Kurtil? ${RACE}?'

'This is how I see it, and pardon my speaking thus, Stéthi. There are two impurities we've got in this slag. First-wise, there's no one to do the deed. Second, there's someone, somewhere, who knows the signal flags and maybe doesn't want the deed done.'

'Yes, yes, yes. The iron is hot now, but cooling, cooling...'
For a moment, Kurtil seems lost in thought.
'We need only someone to go. Who to fill the post? No, not I, Nurnhoth that I am. Who am I? No one. Will Gradrágh go? Ha ha. We know the answer to that, my friends. What of you, Slárnur? You will not. A shame!
'No Orc, nor dwarf, nor Nurnhoth here among us...'
Then a smile slowly spreads across Kurtil's face, lighting the twinkle back into his eyes, which fix on you.

'We must seek Ushkbál the Overseer, then. It is he who will accomplish what we seek.'
Paying no heed of any surprise on your face, Kurtil thinks for a long moment.
'He has agreed, agreed to talk to us at least, and there is hope for more. Surely, he is found at his post, north of here by the great foundry, which lies above Maudhúl Vôr.'

Having secured the pledge from the Easterling Lord Khôpol, you should return to Kurtil and the other forge-workers where they had been, on the height above Maudhúl Vôr.

'You are returned! And they have pledged their word? Strong as iron, an Easterling's pledge.
'See now who has also arrived. It is Gradrágh, another overseer. He wants only some persuading.'

'I see. So it is as you spoke.'
The Easterling Lord thinks for a moment.
'Yes, we will meet with these forge-workers and speak to them. You may carry them this pledge, ${CLASS}.'
'Go with Yordam to the Great Banner, Maudhúl Vôr, and the Black Gates. You will see. The war is not lost, even if it is not yet won.'
'So you are the ${CLASS}. Kurtil did not mention you were ${RACE}! If you ask me, we're in a hard place, all told. I don't know where to turn.'

'The Captain of the Pit and the Men of the West are like two stones, ${PLAYER}, and we the roots who will be ground between them. We must beg the Easterlings safe passage back to their lands, and we rely on you to go before them.
'Go then. Go to Rhûd Vorn and hail them as I showed you.'

You begin to explain the case of the forge-workers, but he quickly interrupts you.
'You speak as if the Eye was fallen. You speak as if the Cause was lost. This is not so and cannot be. How could it be, for the Black Gates still stand and the great banner still waves like a lone wing above the parade grounds. Why, only this morning I sent an Orc with a letter to the Black Word's commissary in Maudhúl Vôr. As sure as the ground I stand on, it has been delivered and needed provisions are on their way.'
When you do not back down, he stares hard at you.
'Folly! There is deceit afoot, if not by you, then by someone. I will send Yordam. He will go with you so that the truth may be known to me. Go.'
'I have seen the proofs, though I hardly believed my eyes. A ${RACE} from the West has spoken the truth! I return to Rhûd Vorn, as should you.'
'I will go with you, as my Lord commands. We will see what we will see.'

'Long is the tale to tell, but short is the time. Do you remember that the Captain of the Pit does not hear the signal flags' speech? He is the master of all Udûn, but many do not wish it so.
'When the ground shook and the gates fell and the Eagles crossed the skies, a light dawned upon our minds - that we might fly ourselves. Fly like the eagles and in Udûn dwell no more. But how? And then we remember the Easterlings camped in Rhûd Vorn. Perhaps, we thought, perhaps we might go back with them, to the lands far from Captains and cruel Gondorians and Elves.
'And so in flags was it written and in flags was it read by you and me and by others. Ushkbál the goodly overseer agreed to go before the Easterlings and plead our case. Now Ushkbál is gone and our hope rests on you, ${RACE}-${CLASS}. We ask you to go in Ushkbál's place and parley with the Easterlings. Only to meet! To speak awhile of what may be.
'Stand before Rhûd Vorn high on the height and hail them with the words that I will teach you.
Kurtil teaches you a formal military hail in the Easterling tongue.
'If fortune smiles upon us, they will agree.'

Then, everything abruptly changes. Gruesome scenes flash before you, furious slashing, dismembered limbs and blood, so much blood. You see the man through the eyes of the woman, lying on a cold, stone floor, completely ripped apart. You see her reaching out to him, but the light is fading from your shared vision. She is dying, and the weight of this is suffocating you.
Just in time, she releases you. You gasp for air as one more image comes to you. A face, beautiful, but dark. Not the same as the woman's, but similar, related. Hatred comes to you; the most intense hatred you've ever experienced. Hatred is this being's purpose now. And then, realization. This face must belong to Lhaereth the Stained.

Before you looms a grotesque stone figure. The bloody waters of the Chaydash run down its features, making it almost feel alive. As you study its features, you are unsettled to realize that its gaze is piercing into you, examining your thoughts. Your mind drifts to your experiences in Seregost's prison and your successful escape. Suddenly, your mind is grasped by the spirit, and a stream of images comes to you, hazy and dream-like.
You see a man and woman, walking together through beautiful fields, hand in hand. They are clearly very much in love, but you notice the woman does not seem entirely normal. Her features are ever so slightly monstrous. Regardless, the man is enraptured by her. Emotions come to you that are not your own. Love and happiness, but in the background a deep and growing sorrow.

The spirit sees that you finally understand and shows you another image, this time different, clearer. This must be somewhere nearby, not a memory. You see another statue, a twin of this one, standing in the Chaydash. The red waters pass through an iron gate and stone walls behind it. It must be behind Seregost itself, further upstream. You can feel a forlorn attachment to this statue, as if the spirit yearns to be closer to it. The man's face appears in your mind for just a moment, and the spirit shows you an almost tangible connexion through the waters. You get the sense that you could pull on this connexion to travel to the other Watching-stone. The image fades away and you can feel the spirit trying to form a word in your mouth.
You allow the word to form: 'Bargain?'

Talk to Taerthon in Celondim

'${PLAYER}, have you heard the good tidings? The time has come at last to sail to Mithlond and to blessed Valinor!
'We have waited only one month, but each day has seemed a year since we arrived in Celondim. The burdens of this realm shall soon be behind us, but I am curious if the sons of Elrond found what they sought in the ruins of Edhelion. I have heard many tales of the sorrowful history of that place, and how it came to ruin by the hand of a disreputable dwarf named Skorgrím Dourhand, but it has laid empty for many long years now. I wonder if anything remains to be found there....
'I have never walked upon the shores of the blessed realm, but I have heard many tales of Valinor. Your forebears who once dwelt there, did they not? Did you as well?'
Taerthon pauses a moment and studies your face.
'You look restless, my friend. What troubles you on such a joyous day?'

You arrived in Celondim with the sons of Elrond one month ago, and the time soon approaches to sail to Mithlond. However, Elrond's decision to offer you a choice of whether to leave Middle-earth or remain to aid its peoples has weighed heavily on you during your travels. The Elf, Taerthon, has also come to sail to the West and you have spent much time together in preparation for your journey since Elladan and Elrohir departed for Edhelion.
The time has at last come to journey to the West, and Taerthon awaits you at the docks of Celondim.
Prologue: A Sea Unsettled

You arrived in Celondim with the sons of Elrond one month ago, and the time soon approaches to sail to Mithlond. However, Elrond's decision to offer you a choice of whether to leave Middle-earth or remain to aid its peoples has weighed heavily on you during your travels.
Reflect on the paths of your friends and kin (${CURRENT}/${MAX})

'Ah, so you return. Where has your reflection led you, ${PLAYER}?'
You tell Taerthon that you desire to remain in Middle-earth.
'It is not the choice I make, but I understand it, friend. You have made it your purpose to confront the forces of evil wherever they take hold, and though it does not seem so here in Celondim, it is true that great evils are again at work in this realm.
'You see, while you were reflecting, Elladan and Elrohir arrived in Celondim and asked to speak with you at once. I told them I would deliver their request when you returned, and they now wait for you near the stable-master.
'My path leads to the Uttermost West, but it seems yours now leads elsewhere. May the Valar guide you, and may you one day come to find peace in Valinor!'

You reflect upon the path of Gil-galad, the High King of the Elves, and the bravery he possessed as he fought and fell to purge the evils of Morgoth and Sauron from the world. You consider the loss of the Elf, Thelaron, and the pain of losing a companion during the War as Gil-galad did. You consider the loss of your King, and you understand what his sacrifice meant for the peoples of Middle-earth.

You reflect upon the path of Glorfindel, who has remained in Middle-earth to stand against the evils of the Enemy and the most vile of his servants. You think upon Glorfindel's deeds in the Elder Days of the world, and how his resolve has never faltered, even when confronted with death.
You reflect upon the decisions of Círdan the Shipwright, who remained in Middle-earth that others of his kin might depart for the blessed realm of Valinor.

You reflect upon the decisions of your dearest friend, Harthalín, who has chosen to remain in Middle-earth and free it of evils before the time comes to bequeath it to Men. You consider her duty to the people of this realm, and that she hoped that you might remain to aid her in the battles against the evils of the world.

You reflect on the decisions of Elrond Halfelven, once the herald of Gil-galad, whose time in this realm draws near to its ending. You consider Elrond's words, for he said that you might depart for the Uttermost West if you truly wished it and that the burdens of this realm no longer fall to you. You consider that he kept you in Imladris that the choice might one day be yours, rather than sending you to revive in the Uttermost West.
Your reflection on the path of Gil-galad fills you with determination!
Your reflection on the path of Glorfindel fills you with hope!
Your reflection on the path of Círdan fills you with grace!
Your reflection on the path of Harthalín fills you with courage!
Your reflection on the path of Elrond fills you with wisdom!

Elladan and Elrohir can be found to the west of the docks by the stable-master of Celondim.
Taerthon is sorrowful, but understands your choice to remain in Middle-earth. He has also mentioned that Elladan and Elrohir have suddenly arrived in Celondim and wish to speak with you. You should find them by the stable-master of Celondim.
Talk to Elladan in Celondim
Find Elladan and Elrohir by the stable-master of Celondim
Talk to Taerthon in Celondim

'What troubles you, ${PLAYER}?'
You tell Taerthon that your thoughts are drawn to your friends and kin and to the choice that was given to you to remain in Middle-earth if you so wished it.
'Why would you wish to remain here? As you must know well, the lands of Valinor heal all ills and replenish our spirits. The concerns of this realm are ours no longer!'
Taerthon senses that his words have not convinced you.
'I see. Perhaps you should reflect upon the paths of your friends and kin to guide you?'

'${PLAYER}, I am glad you have not yet departed! I feared we would be too late....'
Elladan and Elrohir's faces betray grave concerns.
'There are grim forces at work in the Ered Luin, my friend. The terrible Gaunt-lord, Ivar, has bound vile spirits to the corpse of the Dwarf-lord, Skorgrím, and now the Dourhands think him their leader reborn! Our foes escaped, and now the Enemy has beguiled the Dourhands into his service!'
Elrohir gives Elladan a knowing look.
'Indeed, the truth must be told, brother. When Father spoke of the shadow in the East, he spoke of Sauron. The Dark Lord has returned once again, ${PLAYER}, and he has sent his servants across the many lands of this realm in search of the Ring that was lost. If Sauron recovers the Ring, no host shall remain to stand against him and all will be lost.
'The time shall soon come when the peoples of this realm are called to war, and I beg that you remain to guide them and make safe the lands of Middle-earth. It is a great demand to make of one as storied as you and at so final an hour, but I would not ask it if the need were not dire. It shall soon be a realm of Men, and it must survive for them to inherit it! I beg you -- will you remain?'
You tell Elladan and Elrohir that you have chosen to remain in the realm of Middle-earth.
'To have you among the forces that stand against Sauron brings me new hope for the days that lie ahead. You should aid the folk in Celondim and the lands beyond to hone your skills for the battles that surely await us. When the time comes, we shall call on you to join us!'
Prologue: Reflections of the Past

Completed: Abyss of Mordath (Tier 1)

'It seems our paths once again converge, ${PLAYER}!
'We battled through the ruins of Barad-dûr, and hitherto, we have silently pursued the Order of the Eye into these depths. Both Megoril and I have known \qbelievers\q of their kind before...for they first rose after Sauron's defeat upon the slopes of Orodruin. Fate proved their beliefs to be true, and now they will never be turned from the hope that Sauron shall once again return.
'However, their presence here appeared both unannounced and unwanted, and we believe it might be turned to our advantage. They have passed through the Black Pits, crossed the Abyss itself, and battled deep into the foundations of Barad-dûr all while chanting their hatred of an accursed foe - one they call: Greytooth. I know not what dispute they have with this Greytooth, but from their wild shouts and chants, I fear it concerns the Rings of Power. Even with their power fading, the Rings remain a symbol of status and strength to those that dwell in these lands.
'Do what you must to combat the Order and keep the forces of this Greytooth from the Rings, and we shall search for any sign of Thelaron. If he yet lives, he must be hidden in the depths of the Mordath.
'We cannot face so many foes alone, but we have found secret ways through these depths. If you find your way into the deeper chambers of the Mordath, we can help you return to them swiftly.
'Let us hope we both find what we seek in this Abyss, friend.'

They have been known to dent all but the finest of dwarf weapons. We needed some means of replacing our warriors' gear, as efficiently as possible, and I came up with just such a way!

If you collect weapons and shields dropped by the Orcs, they can be melted down and used by our smiths. I sent Vágrek to Udûn, and he will wait there with his cart. 'Ah, you have a package for me from Vétha? What has my wife sent me this time?'
Góthur carefully unfolds the leather satchel and removes a smooth, round ball. With an exclamation of delight, he brandishes it in your direction.
'This is a loaf of cram, ${PLAYER}, as the Men of Dale are wont to make, but they did not bake this one. No, my wife Vétha has sought to learn their recipe and has made some improvements to it. This one is tougher and hardier than others of its type... much like my Vétha, as she would be the first to tell you!
'Thank you, my friend! I would offer you a bite, but surely you need to be off on your own adventures; I do not wish to keep you from them for as long as consuming a serving of this cram would take!'

'You defeated some of the foes throughout Dor Amarth? I suppose that is enough, and now you can deliver the package from his wife to Góthur. He should be near a lake of fire south-west of the ruins of Barad-dûr, in Dor Amarth.'

'Ah, you have a package for me from Vétha? What has my wife sent me this time?'
Góthur carefully unfolds the leather satchel and removes a parchment covered in tiny, angular letters. He studies it for a moment and then sighs.
'Gossip from home, ${PLAYER}. There is a lot of talk of our neighbours, rumours of the king, assorted petty grievances and hurts, and the family's minor triumphs and accomplishments. I do not think I will read it all right now, and it would be of no interest to you, but it does achieve two useful things. First, it helps Vétha pass the time while I am away, for it takes her a long time to write all this out. Second, it helps me pass the time when boredom threatens, even here in Mordor. And so such gossip helps to pass twice as much time!
'I have had a lot of time to think up this justification, my friend, for while I enjoy news from home, there's always just so very much of it. It is rather exhausting. At any rate, I thank you for bringing it to me! Perhaps I will see you again.'

'Ah, you have a package for me from Vétha? What has my wife sent me this time?'
Góthur carefully unfolds the leather satchel and removes a parchment with a brief message written in a messy hand.
'It is a message from my son, Gárni! He misses me, and has written to wish me well as I adventure in... well, he has not mastered his runes as of yet, but I believe this word is intended to represent Gorgoroth. See how he began writing it, but did not know when to stop? Ah, he is clever, more clever than me by far!
'He has asked what he always asks: he wants to know about the monsters I have encountered in this land. He is still too young to hear about them in all their beastly glory, but one day I will return and have many fine stories to tell. Vétha may not like it, but I know that it will whet Gárni's appetite for adventure! Who knows? One day he too may journey in this land, and he too may have a son who desires to hear tales of it! Wouldn't that be something?'

'Ah, you have a package for me from Vétha? What has my wife sent me this time?'
Góthur carefully unfolds the leather satchel and removes a parchment covered with precise, angular runes. He is about to show it to you, but suddenly he flushes and keeps it to himself.
'My temperature rises. It must be the lake of fire! Yes, that must be it. This message from my wife is not intended for anyone's eyes but my own, ${PLAYER}! I thank you for the delivery, and I thank you doubly-so for not reading it!'

'Ah, you have a package for me from Vétha? What has my wife sent me this time?'
Góthur carefully unfolds the leather satchel and removes a small, but very shiny, stone, and a piece of parchment.
'This is a small nugget of gold. Ah! My son Gárni has been learning the basics of mining, and this is one of the early results! The ore does not appear far from the vein, does it not? My son will be a fine prospector indeed if he is already so adept at such a young age!
'Nay, he will be even better than I, for I did not have much of a taste for mining. Is that not why I chose the adventuring life? Still, I am so proud of him for surpassing me in this, and already! Thank you for bringing me this, ${PLAYER}!'

'Ah, you have a package for me from Vétha? What has my wife sent me this time?'
Góthur carefully unfolds the leather satchel and removes a parchment with a charcoal drawing on it. He studies it for a moment and then smiles.
'A drawing of the Lonely Mountain! My son Gárni has become quite the artist, has he not? Look at this fine representation of the Mountain, ${PLAYER}! My son is quite an artist!'
Góthur tilts his head to the side and studies the drawing more carefully.
'Oh, wait a moment. I see now that my wife has written her name in the corner. Vétha drew this picture for me. Well, it is quite good, is it not? She is as fine an artist as her beard is long, ${PLAYER}! Thank you for bringing this to me, and I look forward to what you might bring next time!'

'You delivered the package to Góthur? I hope that is enough for Vétha, but I am not foolish enough to believe she will not have another one to send him in a few days!
'Perhaps you will come back in a day or two and deliver that one as well? And the one after that? By Durin's Beard! When will Góthur return home and put an end to all this package delivering? Not soon enough, that much is clear, ${PLAYER}!'

'One of our scouts, Góthur, adventures in Dor Amarth and has faced many dangers there already. His wife Vétha has prepared a package for him, and insists that someone deliver it to him. It seems to me that every week she has a new package to send him, but I do not want to tell her this cannot be done, ${PLAYER}. Will you bring this week's package to Góthur? Before you deliver it, perhaps you can defeat foes in Dor Amarth? That way there will be some justification for making the journey!

'Thank you for returning the shield; I will ensure it is brought to the man to whom it belongs. It is a wonder to me that the Thandrim can still strike at their enemies, even now, a thousand years after their deaths.
'We are their instrument in this: not of vengeance, but of justice. And of course you will be rewarded for the work. Come back tomorrow and there will be more work, and more reward!'

'A shield was given to me, a shield that was once cloven in two but has now been repaired with leather straps. I believe you know the man who lent it to me, for he has repaired a number of them and bears one himself.
'It is a shield of the Thandrim, who once held the fortress of Durthand and were slain by the forces of Mordor. This man does not want the Orcs and other evil creatures who now inhabit it to forget the steadfast Thandrim, and he wishes for brave warriors to bear this shield to the keep once known as the Black Shield. He asks that you hang the shield upon a wall, and then defeat a number of foes within the fortress.
'Once you have done this, retrieve the shield from the wall where you left it, and return it to me. This man will be glad to have the shield returned, but more than that: he will be glad to know that the memory of the Thandrim lives on, and can still strike out at their hated foes.'

'Forgive me, ${PLAYER}, I am out of breath. I have been running, and I need a moment to catch my wind. You want my report? Here it is.
'Something terrible crept up on me while I was leaning against one of the dead trees that inhabit this awful place. It put such fear into me that I was compelled to run until my breath gave out and I could run no further. Even now I can see the spectre of the hideous sight that surprised me so.
'What was it, you ask? It was spiders, ${PLAYER}, a whole pile of the things. Can I leave Lhingris yet?'

'You want to hear my report?
'I got caught in a web! I did not think I would ever get free! I can still feel its clutching tendrils... it was terrible! I thought the spiders of Lhingris were bad, and now I think they are worse! When you return to Gondor, tell them that I have done everything I can hope to do here, and it is time for me to come back. Will you do that? This web-business would be the last straw for me, if every spider I've seen hadn't already been!'

'I will give you my report, but only if you tell the people back home that it is time for me to leave Lhingris. I am ready to return to Gondor!
'Here is my report: there are spiders here. Spiders! More spiders than you've ever seen! Now go tell Tancram it is time for me to come back to the city!'

'You are here for my report? Well, here it is.
'I finally saw something other than spiders! It was a dwarf, and he seemed to enjoy being around the terrible things! His name was Atli. Perhaps he can scout for Gondor, and I can return home? Just make the suggestion, ${PLAYER}, that's all I ask. How long must I remain in this land of crawling spiders?'

'You have returned, and I trust that you have Fairdal's report?'
You relay the message given to you by Fairdal in great detail, leaving nothing out. When you are finished, Tancram nods.
'Spiders, eh? That sounds about right. Well, we will give him a few more days of scouting before we call him back to Gondor, just to be sure that we know what is going on in Lhingris. Come back tomorrow for more work, ${PLAYER}!'

'Defeat enemies in Lhingris, and after you have done that, find Fairdal north of the cross-roads east of Cirith Ungol, in Rath Cail. Make sure he still lives. Then hear his report and bring it back to me, and we can decide what should next be done.'

'You want to hear my report? I'll tell you what it is!
'Spiders. There are spiders here! What am I supposed to say?
'When you return to Gondor, can you ask if I can return from Lhingris? I think I have seen everything I need to see!'

'You want my report?
'There weren't very many spiders! I could hardly believe it! It seemed as if my luck had finally changed, and the winds of light and hope had swept into Lhingris!
'But then I turned around, and there were dozens and dozens of spiders, after all. When you return to Gondor, can you ask if I can leave Lhingris yet?'

'You defeated many foes in Lhingris? Now find Fairdal north of the cross-roads east of Cirith Ungol, in Rath Cail. Make sure he still lives. Then hear his report and bring it back to me, and we can decide what should next be done.'

'You are here for my report? Today it is brief, for my excursion was short-lived.
'I explored part of the way into Nargroth, the great fortress delved into the depths of the caverns to the north. It is a place of horror, full of Ghâsh-hai and spirits of flame. I mapped a portion of the fortress, but had to turn back before it was complete.
'I hope to return in the days ahead and find more success.'

'You have come for my report? It is good you arrived when you did, for I am lately returned from my last excursion.
'I climbed the slope of Orodruin, and crept as high as I could given the great devastation of the southern face. If you dare to go that way, you will find the footing treacherous and the climb quite dangerous. It was a worthwhile endeavour, however, for from that height I was able to observe the movements of many enemies.'
Candithil relays the information to you. You commit it to memory and thank him for the report.

'You are here for my report? Very well, but I warn you it may not be of much help, for I am still considering the significance of the behaviour I observed.
'There is a town to the north-west of here, rent by a great river of flame that snakes from the summit of Orodruin. The inhabitants of that town war upon each other, north and south, finding no common cause with the other. It is a curiosity to me, but I hope this infighting may be turned to our advantage. It bears further study, but as of now I am unsure how best to capitalize upon this turmoil.'

'You are here for my report? Very well, but know that it looks to the future and not the past, and will be of limited use for those wishing to adventure in Talath Úrui.
'The gate to the south-east is held against us, for the moment, but I have been trying to form a plan to seize control from our enemies. If we could but gain access to the gate of Ennyn Ûr, we might pass through into the lands of Nurn. What awaits us there? I will continue my excursions in Talath Úrui, but my eyes ever turn to the gate, and wonder what lies beyond that sealed fastness. Curiosity was always a weakness of mine, ${PLAYER}. I believe that is one of the qualities for which I was chosen to walk in Gorgoroth, but I do not know for certain.
'Return with my report, and I hope one day you come back to me with a command from the Lord or Lady to pass beyond Ennyn Ûr!'

'Thank you for the report, ${PLAYER}. Candithil continues to provide useful information concerning the situation in Talath Úrui. I hope he does not push his good fortune too far, but for now his adventures are of use to the Court of Lothlórien, and his daring is a credit to his people.
'Come back to me tomorrow and I will have further responsibilities for you.'

'I ask that you defeat any of the hostile creatures that inhabit Talath Úrui. After doing so, if you find yourself near the cross-roads south-east of Orodruin, return to me with Candithil's report and be rewarded for your efforts.'

'You have come for my report? There is little to say of this land I have not already reported. Let this then be my account.
'I miss the sun, ${PLAYER}, and the cool breezes of Lothlórien. I miss the greenery of my home: the plants, and the trees, and the flowers. This is a harsh and unforgiving land, blanketed by fire and smoke and the smell of sulfur. My mouth tastes of ashes. The weather is unchanging, or if it be changeable the difference is from disagreeable to distasteful; a small one only, and of little account to my eyes.
'Return with my report. It should not be surprising, but perhaps my next will be of more use.'

'You are here for my report? I give it to you gladly.
'From a small rise not far from here, I beheld a small group of Orcs bound for the prison-fortress of Naerband. Nurnhoth slaves were chained together in the centre of the marching lines. I could not leave them to their cruel fate; I nocked an arrow almost before I knew what I was doing, and let it fly only slightly after my mind caught up to my heart.
'I left the captors where they fell, and sent the Nurnhoth along with friends of mine, to freedom. May they find happiness where at last they settle. That is my report.'
'If you find yourself near the cross-roads south-east of Orodruin, return to me with Candithil's report and be rewarded for your efforts.'
Defeated hostile foes in Talath Úrui (${NUMBER}/${TOTAL})

'Lord Celeborn dispatched scouts to many of the regions of Gorgoroth, and they journeyed to each side of Orodruin. We have received many of their reports in the last few days, but Candithil journeys in Talath Úrui, and his reports are sometimes delayed.
'I ask that you defeat any of the hostile creatures that inhabit Talath Úrui. After doing so, if you find yourself near the cross-roads south-east of Orodruin, return to me with Candithil's report and be rewarded for your efforts.'

'The corruption in Agarnaith has had a withering effect upon the beasts that roam that foul swamp-land; they should be given an end, for that would be a mercy. As for the Orcs and Uruks that lurk, it is not mercy I would wish for them, but an ending that will safe-guard the unfortunate wanderers that must walk in that land. See to both of these aims, and return to me for my thanks and a small reward.'

'Hello there, ${PLAYER}. I have been collecting requests in order to determine how best we can help our friends and neighbours, but today the request is from one Aster Hayward. Yes, this request is my own!
'You see, a number of former prisoners have been freed from the yoke of slavery in Gorgoroth, and now they seek to make homes for themselves in Gondor. Many of these freed slaves are Nurnhoth, the people of Nurn, to the south. I have not studied their family trees as sufficiently as I would like, for while I am a student of lineage and ancestry, my specialty is in that of the larger hobbit families of the Shire. Still, I understand that the Nurnhoth are of Easterling descent, and have Easterling customs and habits.
'This is a long way of saying that many of the freed Nurnhoth have different tastes than the rest of us, and while they have freedom they still lack some of the things that would make them most comfortable. I speak of food, ${PLAYER}! I have conversed with some of them, and have learned that they would enjoy a few traditional meals: Khingal, Lavang, and Pishi Badam, which they have described to me but I have never sampled. We do not have the ingredients for these meals, but we might take them from some of the Easterlings in Gorgoroth who are hostile to us. Deprive the Easterlings at Rhûd Vorn, on the eastern side of the vale of Udûn, of their food jars, and I may be able to cook up some of these meals for the freed Nurnhoth. I want them to feel welcome, ${PLAYER}, and this may help them feel more at home!'

'I believe this is it, ${PLAYER}. Are you prepared to face the horrors within?'

'Here we are again, ${PLAYER}. I had hoped we wouldn't need to return to Seregost, at least not so soon! Alas, we must steel our hearts and put on our bravest faces. All the Free Peoples are counting on us now.'

'The day is won! You should be proud, ${PLAYER}. We would never have been successful without you.
'The defeat of Dulgabêth and the departure of Lhaereth will mean another shakeup in the power structure of Mordor. This can only be good news for the Free Peoples!
'I am certain this is not the last we have seen of Lhaereth the Stained. Her threat made that abundantly clear. We should celebrate while we can, but keep a wary eye out for her in our future travels in Mordor.'
Word has reached you that Faeron of the Grey Company has a plan for penetrating the defences of Seregost, and has asked for you by name. You should return to Agarnaith and see how you can help.

'Ah, ${PLAYER}! Per usual, your timing is uncanny. The threat of Lhaereth's plague still exists, and the time to act is now. I hear you have discovered another way into Seregost. Is this true?'
You explain that the Watching Stones in Seregost consider Lhaereth an enemy as well, and have allowed you safe passage to and from Seregost.
'Watching Stones? Can we really trust such fell beings? We must take the risk.
'Here is my plan. I have gathered some soldiers, and more will be coming. They will move into Kala-gijak and create a bulwark there. My hope is that this will trigger an attack from the majority of the forces left in Seregost, and distract Lhaereth from our true intentions.
'That is where we come in. We cannot risk a full invasion, even if that were possible, because of the plague. Only the three of us are inoculated against it, and even then, I am unsure if we will survive direct exposure to it in a concentrated form.
'We have no choice. The threat to our homelands is too great. We will form a small strike team and enter this den of evil ourselves. Gather some companions, be sure they are inoculated themselves, and meet us in Seregost. We will find a way to Lhaereth's throne room, and do what we can to end this threat.
'And no, I will not allow Viznak to come this time. He is but a child, after all.'

'I am very excited about this autumnal mystery, ${PLAYER}! I have read many scary stories, and they always delight my imagination, but I have never been involved in one myself! Tell me once again what the ghostly fellow had to say?'
You recount the words of the spectral vision.
'Hmm. There can be no reparations for the hurt that has been done. In one year, all will fear the parting of the wood! None will escape the curse of the eerie acres! Despair and repair to your holes, for none but one will laugh when all is done! Do I have that right?
'I have to admit I do not know what any of this means, ${PLAYER}, but it sounds to me like we have a year to figure it out! I will do some thinking. It sounds to me as if next year's Harvest Festival might be something, though! I can't wait... but I guess I must!'

'My cousin Prisca has brought her children to visit, and we are all going to enjoy the sights and sounds of the Harvest Festival together. You simply must join us! I will not take \qno\q for an answer, and you know how stubborn Boffins can be when we set our minds to it. Legendarily so!
'You can find my various cousins enjoying the games around the Party Tree. I would appreciate it if you help them make the most of their time here, and later in the evening we will all meet on the Greenfields to tell spooky stories. I can't wait!'

'You saw what? You... you... you should go see what it wants!'
'Perhaps you should... tell cousin Bingo... what you saw. I don't think I need to hear about it. I don't believe in... in that sort of rubbish! No indeed!'
'Hullo there, ${PLAYER}! You found him!'

'Bingo has come here, and he apologized for the trick, and all is well now and we don't need to discuss that thing I told you, ${PLAYER}, all right? Good.'
You give Dinodas his pack. After a moment's thought, you tell him that you saw something unusual nearby.
'Oh? What... what was it? Actually... perhaps you should... tell cousin Bingo. I don't think I need to hear about it. I don't believe in... in that sort of rubbish! No indeed!'

'I apologized to Dinodas for our scary trick, but I think it did him some good. Now, what has whirled you up into such confusion?'
You quietly tell Bingo about the spectral vision you saw in the wood, and he looks at you skeptically.
'Is this a joke, or a trick of your own? You really saw this thing?'

'I was on my way back to the Greenfields when you caught up to me. I turned around because I heard something scary and dropped my pack, and ran back this way. Do you think you can retrace my steps to the north-west and find my pack? I don't think I have the courage to go back and look for it!'
Unnatural blue fires blaze in the darkened wood

'Now you know my secret shame, and I trust you will keep it to yourself! It all began some time ago, when I offered to walk Celandine Brandybuck back to her home after a dinner party my mother hosted. Celandine was very happy to have the company, but as we began the walk I saw that the hour was much later than I had thought! The night was dark and the shadows were deep, and my blood ran cold at every creepy sound! I knew if I did not do something, Celandine would know me for a coward. Cry disaster! In order to mask my fear, I adopted a brazen attitude and mocked every fear I felt. It was all an act, an act at which I have become all too practiced!'
Dinodas frowns.
'Still, Bingo is my cousin, and that was a mean trick for any family member to perform, at any remove and no matter the distance! Speaking of distance, I was on my way back to the Greenfields when you caught up to me. I turned around because I heard something scary and dropped my pack, and ran back this way. Do you think you can retrace my steps to the north-west and find my pack? I don't think I have the courage to go back and look for it!'

'Yes, I gave Bingo and Esmeralda permission to carry out their joke on Dinodas. He will not be happy when they tell him it was a trick, but everyone had a good laugh about it, and he will too. Eventually.'

'Many, many years ago, long before our family trees had so much as sprouted, there was a small village on the banks of the Brandywine, not far from where Stock is located today. One of the prominent figures in this village was a fellow named Gerd Goodcliff; he had the respect of his neighbours and was consulted about many of the matters that faced the town. It was widely-held that when the time came for the Mayor to step down, Gerd would easily be chosen to take his place.
'One day, Gerd was walking among the reeds at the river's edge when he heard a small voice among the rushes. \qHow curious!\q he thought to himself, and he squatted down in the mud to find the owner of the voice. Finding nothing, he prepared to stand once again, but before he could a large black cat padded out of the reeds. \qWell, hello there,\q he greeted the cat, and turned to go.
'\qHello yourself,\q it said to him.
'Gerd was most surprised, for this was the first time a cat had ever spoken to him. Once he recovered himself, he found that the cat was not simply talkative, but quite friendly as well. It introduced itself as Green-eyes, and said that it came from a far-away land in search of a home. Gerd was happy to offer Green-eyes such a place at his own humble burrow, and Green-eyes contributed in his own way: keeping mice and other undesirables away from Gerd's pantry.
'In time, Green-eyes proved capable at finding much more than mice. He would stalk throughout the village, creeping into half-open windows and pushing open unlatched doors. He learned many interesting rumours and overheard much gossip about the hobbits of the town, and he recounted each salacious morsel to Gerd with delight.
'Gerd began to look upon his neighbours with distaste and distrust, and he found he could no longer stand to engage in conversation with them. He became cold and distant, and other hobbits avoided him when they saw him on the road, crossing to the other side rather than speak with him. When they returned to their homes, Green-eyes would follow behind and listen while they called Gerd off-putting, odd, and unfriendly. The cat recounted these stories to Gerd with regret, but his tail twitched back and forth happily.
'\qI don't need these liars as friends anyway,\q Gerd told him one day. \qI have you, Green-eyes, and you're the only friend this hobbit needs.\q Green-eyes nodded, his tail twitching.
'Not long afterward, a day came when Gerd could not find Green-eyes anywhere. Despairing, and certain that one of his neighbours had done some harm to his friend, he ran screaming out into the centre of town. Folk watched his raving progress through the village, and their whispers were no longer hushed or hidden. Madly, Gerd ran down to the banks of the river, and there at last he found his friend.
'Green-eyes stood among the reeds, and with his two front paws he pushed a small boat out into the river. He clambered onto it, and turned back to face Gerd as it floated out on the current.
'\qWhy, Green-eyes? Why must you leave?\q Gerd called out to him. Green-eyes did not respond, but only watched him silently until the current bore him away and out of sight.
'No one knows what happened to Gerd Goodcliff after that, but he never came back to town, and he never became Mayor. But there are some who say that if the moon is high in the sky, like it is tonight, you might catch a glimpse of Green-eyes on his boat, floating away down the river, his tail twitching, twitching, twitching.'

'You all know I love napping, and it has been the subject of some teasing throughout the years. But I tell you this! Mother told us this story when we were very young, and if some of you forgot it, well, I never did! Once you have heard it again, you will be jealous of my afternoon naps and my early bedtimes, I don't doubt it!
'Many years ago, a hobbit named Hamson Broadbeam lived in the town of Overhill. He was a woodworker of much renown, and folk came from all throughout the Shire to buy his crafted goods. You can still find oaken chests bearing his mark in hobbit-holes throughout all the four Farthings, though Hamson himself is only remembered in this tale.
'He was a victim of his own success. There were so many orders from so many customers that he had to stay awake late into the evening to finish each crafted good, stumbling into bed as the first beams of light began to shine through the trees onto Overhill. His work began to suffer, and he feared that his reputation would be tarnished unless something changed, and quickly.
'One day, Hamson was drowsily walking through the Bindbole Wood to an area where he was accustomed to felling trees for his workbench. As he approached the location, he felt the hair on his toes stand up; something was watching him from the tree-canopy.
'\qHullo? Is anyone there?\q he called.
'\qI live here,\q a thin, reedy voice replied. Hamson squinted up at the branches, but he could not see the speaker.
'\qI don't see you,\q Hamson said. \qAm I asleep? I must have fallen asleep somewhere on the trail, and now I am dreaming. I hope no animals find my body while I sleep!\q
'\qYou seem pretty awake to me,\q the mysterious voice answered. \qAt least, you're not asleep, but perhaps you should be. Your limbs hang loosely, your eyelids droop, and I see exhaustion in every part of you.\q
'Hamson was impressed that this strange new acquaintance could read the situation so clearly, and he described the many demands on his time that prevented him from sleeping. \qIf only I didn't need to sleep,\q he exclaimed, \qI need worry about nothing!\q
'At first, the voice from the tree-canopy did not respond. Then, a small twig with red berries fell from aloft, landing in the dirt by Hamson's feet. \qWhat's this?\q he asked.
'\qI do not need to sleep,\q the voice responded. \qEat those berries and you will not need to sleep either.\q Normally, Hamson would not have trusted such a gift from a stranger, particularly from one so strange as this, but he so desperately wanted the berries to do as the voice promised that he did not give it a second thought. He ate them greedily, but felt no different. He asked how long it would take for him to notice their effect, but the voice did not respond. Angrily, Hamson went home. He didn't even care to collect the wood that had brought him into the forest in the first place, so disappointed and out-of-sorts was he.
'That night, Hamson fashioned a set of chairs requested by a wealthy patron, and the work was delicate enough that he found himself quite engaged and still awake by dawn. In fact, his drowsiness had departed, and he worked all the rest of the day and into the following evening. \qCan it be?\q he asked his empty burrow. \qDid those berries take away my need of sleep?\q It seemed to be so, and Hamson had never been so happy.
'The following weeks were a delight for the woodworker, and he finished every order set before him. When there were no more orders to fill, he read his small collection of books, and he felt he had become a much smarter and more cultured gentlehobbit. When there were no more books to read, he took long walks through the Shire at night, and marveled at the night-time beauty of the countryside. When that finally lost its lustre, he returned to his home and lay awake in his bed. He had exhausted everything he wanted to do, and now he was bored. All he wanted to do was to close his eyes and sleep, but try as he might he would never sleep again. As bad as he had felt before, now he felt worse. Every day felt like an eternity, and every night felt like two.
'Hamson walked every inch of the Bindbole Wood, calling for the mysterious voice to return and give him different berries, but as far as I know he never found it. He might be walking there still, just over there, seeking an end to his endless wakefulness.'

'When we came here to see cousin Bingo and celebrate the Harvest Festival with him, we crossed the Brandywine Bridge and took the road by Stock. Do you all remember looking across the water and seeing the farms of Budgeford? My story took place at one of those farms, and the events told therein happened not so long ago. I know these events are true, though they sound unbelievable. The story was told to me by someone who would know the truth of the matter.
'The farm stood right on the river's edge, and belonged to a hobbit named Everard. He was a Bolger, as are many of the folk of Budgeford, but whereas most of the Bolgers are fine farmers, Everard struggled daily to maintain his crop. Either it was taken by blight, or savaged by crows, or munched by rabbits, and on many occasions he had to depend upon the charity of his neighbours for his family to survive.
'Everard blamed his scarecrow most of all. No matter how hard he tried, he could not fashion a suitably frightening scarecrow; every day, the birds came to feast on his crops, undeterred. He was at his wit's end on a Tuesday, and even as he glowered at his failing scarecrow, a raven flew down from the sky and lighted upon it.
'\qOh, I'll teach you what you deserve!\q Everard growled as he swung his trowel at the bird. The raven flew just out of reach, and then landed once again upon the scarecrow's straw hat.
'\qYou seem upset, friend,\q the raven said. This set Everard back a bit, for while he had heard stories of speaking birds he had never encountered one himself. \qUpset?\q he managed. \qOf course! You birds won't leave my crops alone, you vile things!\q
'\qIt does seem like you deserve better,\q the raven responded. \qIf you like, I can speak to my people and see if perhaps we could come to an arrangement. I'd be willing to do this for you if you let me sample some of these grains.\q Everard thought it over and could see few drawbacks to the raven's proposal. After all, one bird's appetite would be less than a whole flock, and by giving up some of the crop he might secure safety for the rest. \qI agree,\q he told the bird, and watched as it devoured some of the crop and flew away.
'The next day saw little improvement, and birds continued to harry his crops. He was certain he would not see the raven again, but to his surprise the bird appeared and spoke. \qThey said they want to help you out, but they just can't resist the taste of the crops you're growing here. They said what you need is a better scarecrow. That would make it much more difficult for them to fly near.\q
'\qI have tried to make this one scarier,\q Everard told him, \qbut it's just no good.\q
'\qLet's see what we can do,\q the raven replied.
'The Wednesday sun crossed the sky, and as dusk approached, Everard's wife sent their daughter Holly to bring Everard in for supper. As Holly approached the field, she marveled at how life-like appeared the second scarecrow her father had made. He must have spent all day fashioning it; it looked just like a hobbit. As she watched, a raven hopping among the grains squawked and flew away.'

'Odo Grubb was the finest fisherman the Shire had ever seen, and none who cast their lines today can hope to rival his skill. Nor should they, if you believe the tale I am about to tell. I believe it, for it is surely true.
'Odo's name was known far and wide throughout the Shire in his day, and it seemed he could find fish in any body of water; not just fish, but fish of a size you would hardly have expected! Where most hobbits would pull minnows of middling sizes from their hooks, Odo could cast into the river and take from it fish of incredible beauty, their rainbow scales glittering, creatures of a size that no hobbit had ever drawn before.
'So skilled was he that he dared clamber into a boat of his own making and fish far from the banks, which was very unusual for hobbits of his day, and indeed remains so! Yet it also proved unwise, for there came a day when a great behemoth of a fish seized his line and pulled his boat rapidly along with the current. Most hobbits would have dropped their rod and rowed to safety, but Odo had a reputation to uphold; he braced himself against the sides and held onto the rod for dear life.
'\qI will make you mine!\q he proclaimed to the great fish as it pulled him along. \qI will be the victor in this contest, or my name is not Odo Grubb, Master Fisherman!\q
'The battle lasted for days, and the mighty fish pulled Odo's boat far from the Shire and into lands unknown to all hobbits. At last, consumed by hunger and weariness, Odo released his hold on the fishing rod and it flew out of the boat and into the water. \qI give up,\q he said to no one as his boat slowed from its rapid pursuit. He picked up the oars and prepared to begin the long journey homeward.
'Then something bumped into the underside of his boat and the oars broke from their locks and fell into the water; but his rapid journey southward continued. \qWhat is happening?\q he cried aloud, and peered over the side into the water below. The great fish had not left him, but remained, pushing the boat on its southward course. \qWhere are you taking me?\q Odo demanded, but the fish did not respond.
'This continued for many days, until Odo was faint with hunger. He collapsed in the base of his boat, and once again wondered when the great fish would let him go. \qDid you bring me here just to let me die?\q he cried aloud, too weak to even shake his fist at the cruel skies. Then he heard a splash, and another: small fish were leaping from the water and landing in the boat. \qWhat... what luck!\q he gasped, and grabbed them with both hands. He ate them raw, which he would have found distasteful back home, but on this terrible day he was glad for the unexpected gift.
'His vigour renewed, Odo was now strong enough to keep watch from the front of his boat, and that is how he saw the Great Sea approaching, and the river's end. The boat slowed, and the great fish halted its pushing. It lifted its great head from the water, and Odo saw that the creature was not alone: there were fish of every imaginable size and shape surrounding his boat. \qWhat do you want?\q he asked.
'As Odo surveyed the vast variety of the diverse species that surrounded him, he found that he recognized every type of fish. At one point or another in his esteemed career, he had caught at least one of each of these types, and in some cases many. \qYou hold me responsible?\q he whispered. \qYou came for me. You came for me... for revenge?\q
'The fish stared at him with bulbous eyes, their gills working silently just beneath the surface of the water.
'\qBut... but you fed me. Why keep me alive?\q
'There was no response from the silent assembled, but suddenly they moved as one. Hundreds of fish pressed against the sides and bottom of Odo's boat, and the silvery, rainbow multitude forced the boat from the fresh-water of the river into the salt of the Great Sea, dying as they went.
'And so Odo Grubb paid the price for his success. Give a thought to him on this night, floating on the Great Sea far away, never to return.'

'My story is a cautionary tale, but I urge you not to discount it for it is also true, very true. The events of this story took place not so very long ago, shortly after the new homesteads were made available in the Shire.
'A very old and by most accounts rather unpleasant hobbit, the widow Spinner, was enamoured of one of the homes on Myrtle Court, and she greatly desired to purchase it. She was not the only interested buyer, of course, but she had the most money to spend and she was able to outbid her chief rival, a young hobbit named Bob Newbuck. She purchased the most desirable home on Myrtle Court, and she lived there for several months, much to Bob's consternation.
'Well, Bob wasn't one to give up, even when losing a contest, and he made it a point to pass by Myrtle Court as often as possible, scowling in the direction of the widow Spinner's home at every opportunity. One night as he passed by the lane, he heard a strange voice calling in the darkness. He looked more closely and saw the widow Spinner standing in the yard beside her burrow, wearing a long nightshirt and a sleeping cap.
'\qCrazy old bat!\q Bob thought to himself as he continued down the lane to his own, comparably disappointing and cramped burrow.
'Thinking back on that curious sight some time later, Bob decided that he might have been the last person to see the widow Spinner before she disappeared. Indeed, no one else could tell the Shirriffs what had happened to her or where she had gone. Bob was as helpful as he could be, and he told them what little he knew, but it was not long before the widow Spinner was declared dead and 6 Myrtle Court was once again available to purchase.
'Bob wasted no time and purchased the house, and it was everything he hoped it would be. He decorated it to his liking and lived there happily for several months. He was lying in bed one night sometime after midnight when he heard a voice. \qHelp me,\q it called from somewhere outside Bob's cozy bedroom.
'\qWhat is that?\q Bob wondered to himself, and pulled the covers up to his chin. \qHelp me,\q the voice called again. Bob squeezed his eyes shut, but then decided that the morning was too far off and there would be no escaping the plaintive voice. He followed its call out of his bedroom, down the hall, and finally outside.
'The air was cold and the night was dark, but he was able to hear the voice clearly enough to follow it to the side yard, where the well was dug. Sure enough, the voice echoed up from the dark hole in the ground. \qHelp me,\q it asked again. Bob leaned over the hole and scowled. \qSpinner, if that's you down there,\q he began, but he wasn't able to finish the thought before something slammed into his back and he slipped on the wet grass. Bob tumbled down the well, and everything went dark.
'When he awoke, he was lying half in and half out of the water, deep inside the well. A crevice in the wall opened into a chamber dug out of the dirt, and he was wedged painfully in that crack. He felt woozy, and it was hard to make his eyes focus. Gradually they did, and he saw the widow Spinner sitting on the floor, leaning against the wall of the dirt chamber, a teapot and several plates arranged around her.
'\qHelp me,\q the voice said once again, and Bob realized that it came not from the widow Spinner, but from somewhere much closer, right by his ear. \qHelp me set out the tea,\q it continued. \qShe will be so happy to have someone over for tea.\q Something pulled at his arm roughly and Bob disappeared into the dirt chamber. He was never seen again.
'I heard that 6 Myrtle Court is available for purchase again... if you don't mind tea at midnight.'

'I overheard this story when I was very little, and it made quite an impression! I vowed never to let fear be the master of me, and so far it hasn't, and won't! Some hobbits could still learn that lesson, I'd say!
'Long ago, a wealthy hobbit named Longo Proudfoot lived alone in a fancy manor in Michel Delving. He enjoyed expensive things and employed many servants, and it was a poorly-kept secret that he did not treat them well. He enjoyed the food they prepared for him, but he was consumed with distrust, and he feared they would sneak into the pantry and steal the ingredients within for their own families.
'So it was that Longo had strong locks and heavy bars installed on his pantry, and carried the only keys. When it was time for his servants to prepare his dinners, he would march them to the door, carefully unlock everything, and stand by watching while they removed what they needed. He carefully marked the quantities of each foodstuff, and if it seemed more was being withdrawn than was necessary, he had strong words at the ready.
'This continued for some time, but still Longo was certain that his servants were stealing his food. I cannot say for sure, but it seems to me that the extreme measures he used to prevent it must have enflamed the servants' desire to perpetrate some thievery, but that might just be my perspective as a rebellious hobbit!
'At any rate, there came a day when Longo's suspicions were at their greatest level and he called all of his servants into the sitting room. \qI no longer have need of your services!\q he proclaimed, and dismissed them all. \qGo steal from someone else's larder!\q he cried as they streamed from the manor.
'That night, as Longo lay in his bed, he found that his suspicions had not been eased by dismissing all of his servants. On the contrary, now he worried they would not be bound by loyalty and might break into the manor to gain access to his pantry. Where were his keys? Ah, here they are. Still, they might have already performed the deed, and replaced the keys when they were done!
'Longo hurried to the pantry and found the many locks as he had left them earlier in the day. He unlocked every one and threw open the door, revealing shelf upon shelf of useful ingredients and foodstuffs. As he went inside for a closer look, he brushed the door by mistake and it swung shut behind him. If he had not been so focused on counting the bags of flour and inventorying the pickling jars, he might have heard the heavy bar fall into place outside the door, but he did not.
'No one knows how long it took before anyone noticed they had not seen Longo Proudfoot set foot from his manor for some time, for he had told his servants not to return and he had no friends or family to check on him. He might have lasted for quite some time in that well-stocked pantry, but in the end, after all, does it really matter if it was days or if it was months?
'But hobbits in the Shire have reported feelings of discomfort in their own pantries late at night, as if they were being watched from behind the shelves, and some folk have claimed to see eyes peering out at them from between the bags and boxes, eyes full of jealousy and distrust.'

'What fun! What do you think, ${PLAYER}? It seems to me that Esmeralda should try acting at the Frostbluff Theatre... that was a convincing performance!
'I'd say we certainly gave Dino a taste of the season, wouldn't you?
'Oh, it's all in good fun. He'll be fine. He just needed a good scare. We wouldn't have carried out this trick if Prisca hadn't given her permission, and she thought it might do him some good, just as we did. It's the season for scares, after all!'

'The story I am about to tell is older than each of the others we have heard tonight, for it dates from the earliest days of the Shire and is recorded in very few places. I found it in a book that ${PLAYER} retrieved from the library of Great Smials, but it seems to me there were few copies of that book ever made. Once I tell you this story, it will live on, and you should all remember it.
'Even in the earliest days of the Shire, festivals were already important to our distant ancestors. Were there Boffins, even then? I'd like to think so, although I have not seen a family tree that extends back that far. Certainly some branches of our family trees bear similar names to those earliest inhabitants of the Shire, and I have seen accounts of Esmeraldas, Marigolds, Griffos, and Foscos. But I am getting distracted!
'A young girl by the name of Menegilda desired to win a dancing competition, but her chief rival, one Peony, excelled at the art and bested her at every opportunity. Menegilda was obsessed with winning the great prize, and she became convinced that Peony owed her success to the violet shoes she always wore. Menegilda hatched a plan to steal the shoes.
'She surprised Peony on the banks of the Brandywine and demanded she hand over the shoes. Peony refused and said there was a spell on the shoes; they would work only at her command, and they would do Menegilda no good at all. Menegilda was not dissuaded. In fact, the revelation that the shoes were enchanted filled her with happiness. At last, an explanation for her continued failure to beat Peony at dancing!
'Peony removed the shoes and threw them at her rival. \qFine!\q she cried, \qHave them! I will tell my father what you've done, and you won't be allowed to dance at all!\q This was a mistake, but Peony did not understand the rage that seethed within Menegilda's heart. Menegilda charged at her with arms raised, and she pushed Peony into the river. She never surfaced.
'Menegilda put on her stolen shoes and returned to town. There were whispers, but no one had seen her encounter with Peony, and it was believed that Peony may have run away, seeking her fortune beyond the borders of the Shire. Menegilda did not care; her every thought was bent on winning the next dance contest.
'A few weeks later, Menegilda wore her new shoes and danced on the stage before all the assembled hobbits. Everyone cheered and applauded, for they had never seen such dancing before, not even when Peony had participated. Menegilda was the clear winner.
'And yet, something was wrong. Someone tried to present Menegilda with the winning ribbon, but she merely continued to dance. Everyone applauded again, but she showed no signs of stopping. \qI think that's enough, dear!\q someone called, but now there were tears streaming from Menegilda's face and the assemblage came to understand that she wanted to stop, but could not.
'Folk rushed the stage and sought to remove the violet shoes, but they wouldn't come off. Menegilda's feet flew left and right, here and there, but even when she fell into a stupor the dance continued. At last it stopped, but Menegilda's dancing days were done. The shoes were packed into a box and it was sealed away, hidden in a dusty corner of a forgotten burrow. Hobbits spoke for a time of Menegilda and the cursed shoes, but eventually the story passed into legend, and folk doubted if it had ever really happened, even as they feared to speak of it.'
