'Maybe I am too hasty to dismiss that offer. After all, there is something to serving the people of Gondor and not the corrupt leaders who reach into our pockets for coin or extract their price in blood.
'Is it then, that I fear my strength would be wasted not on hoisting sails but on spreading pitch to patch the leaks?
'Would we, perhaps, learn better the skills of swordsman, so that we are not skewered on the blade of some Corsair? Or, would we be a sacrifice in early battle so our captain could gain advantage and keep our coin?
'I think, I fear that I would be under the heel of a terrible captain who wants only glory and naught the thing they try to sell in that post.
'Listen to me ramble. I am sorry, friend. I fear I am in a grim state this night. Let us lighten the mood. A toast to kinship, and to friends who travel the road that rises to meet us on our journey.'

The sound of plunderers echoed in the tavern. The flagons were not meant for us, after all.
'We best be prepared to draw weapons, friend. They are from Umbar and the very Corsairs that threaten Gondor.'

'For the people of Gondor, yes. I see the merit in that, but our stewards are degenerate and never leave the safety of Minas Tirith. When was it they last set foot outside the white city?'
He scoffs and looks toward the bar.
'The innkeep must have known of our arrival. Come, my friend, let us toast to our lives... as they are and ever shall be.'

'You fight well. You should consider joining my crew. You just saw firsthand the menace that Umbar presents.
'Come down to the harbour on the morrow and speak with me.'
'I did not expect any of this tonight, my friend. Perhaps, come the morning I may visit this ship and speak with this captain. I have never been so exhilarated.'

Gondor expects...
and Gondor must not, and will not, be disappointed.

'Another night of libations to clear the dirt from our throats. This life, my friend, is lacking. How I yearn for something beyond the dust of the road, or the fires of a smith shop.
'Where is adventure and wonder?'
He pauses, looking sullen.
'Youth is wasted on wonder, when in our most fruitful years we are tied to the land, then to a partner, and then to children. What nonsense. That life is not for me. I want more.
'I want wonder! I want every day to forgo the rote mechanics of life and be new and inspiring. I want to never know what lay on the other side of the horizon.
'Alas, I am but me. You are but you. And we, together, are merely labourers with only a few coppers between us to seek our wonder at the bottom of a mug.
'Come, let us enjoy the night before I grow too grim.'
Mission: A Life at Sea
I made my way toward the bar, not noticing yet that the inn was bereft of clients, something that should have alerted me to the curious nature of the night. Along the way, a posting caught my eye....
The poster was meant to entice the reader to the sea, to service, on some it had that effect. On others...
We made our way to the bar and took up the flagons....
I raised my flagon and awaited the same of my friend. Our toast, however, was only the beginning of a harrowing event....
For in the back of the inn, Corsairs had set to plunder. Killing the innkeep after he dared ask them for payment for the drinks we now consumed....
There were no more words between us. The Corsairs drew blades and we fought. It were not luck that brought us through....
Was it in the commotion that the captain appeared? It was unclear. I only know that after the fight was done, there they were....
The Captain's words lingered with me as I rejoined my friend.

The woman in hand-me-down armour and threadbare boots almost felt bad for the flock of Corsairs laid out on the ground.
Almost.
Her travelling companion, a woman in a grey cloak, got up from the rock she was sitting on and came to stand next to her.
'What was their first mistake?' she asked.
Threadbare Boots pondered the question. \qThey underestimated us!\q she declared. \qThey saw two travellers and thought six people would be enough to best us.\q She smiled triumphantly.
'Close, but not quite correct. They did underestimate our strength, yes, but they made a bigger mistake first.' She gave Threadbare Boots a few moments to consider, but the silence stretched a little too long.
'Look at us,' Grey Cloak said. 'Do we look like we are worth robbing? I wear a dull cloak and your armour is scuffed and dented. We travel with light packs that could not hold more than two days' worth of supplies. What could we possibly have that is worth risking a confrontation? It would have been better to save their strength for a better target like a merchant with a cart full of goods.'
'But a merchant would employ an escort,\q Threadbare Boots retorted.
'And? A beast is only as hale as the prey it devours. A hard fight is worth the risk if the spoils are commensurate. If you are to make it as one of us, you would do well to remember that.'
The Corsairs of Tathrendalf

Rhúdon stands beside a toppled cart and iron ore lies strewn about the ground.
'And now he's sent someone to check on me? Master Boradan is going to have my head for this! Would you help me deliver this ore to Master Boradan? I was also supposed to help clean up the loose ore strewn about the village from when the Orcs took Tingobel, but now it seems I'll have no time for that.

'It is done, then? Very good.

A Dangerous Dare

'Ah, you're back!
'Thendor and Glamion returned not long after you left, and Randis just ran back into Lancrath. She had quite the grin on her face. I trust they weren't too much trouble for you?'
You tell Berthalend that the Ruthless Dead appeared at the Stone of Erech.
'I see. I hoped they would not, but I feared as much. We still tell tales of the Shadow-men because there is truth to them, but too often the children think they are just that—stories! I am just grateful that you were there to protect her, ${PLAYER}. Now that she is safe, I hope Randis will take this lesson to heart.
'The other children look up to her, after all!'

'I was going to go with Randis, but then Thendor got scared, so I didn't want to leave him alone!'
Glamion appears visibly nervous.
'Randis said she wasn't going to come back until she touched the Stone, but it's been a long time....'
You tell Glamion to take Thendor back to Lancrath, and that you'll find Randis.
'If you say so!'

'W-who are you? Why is it so cold?'
You tell Randis you've come to bring her home to Lancrath.
'But I was so close! I... only stopped because I heard those voices. Do you hear them, too?
'I can't go yet, I've got to....'
'Don't worry, I've learned my lesson. Next time I'll bring a sword!'

'Hail, friend.
'I don't believe we spoke the last time you were in the Vale, but I remember your face. I am Berthalend, a simple craftsman of Gondor. And you are?'
You introduce yourself and inform Berthalend that you are one of King Elessar's emissaries.
'Ah, I did not realize you worked in service of the King! Might I ask a small favour of you? You see, some of the children in Lancrath have taken to daring each other to do this and that, and it is usually harmless fun. However, I overheard one of the older girls, Randis, talking about the Stone of Erech. You have been to the Vale before, ${PLAYER}, so surely you know what lurks on the Hill of Erech. Such a dare could lead them into grave danger!
'Randis set off with two young boys named Thendor and Glamion. Would you go find them? Tell them to come home before it is too late!'
Randis stands before the Stone of Erech, clearly uneasy

Deliver word of King Elessar's gratitude to the people of Alagrant

The Vale Left Behind

'At last you return, ${PLAYER}.
'What had the folk of Alagrant, Tingobel, Sardol, and Lancrath to say of King Elessar's gratitude? I hope they were a more welcoming sort than you encountered here in Morlad!'
You tell Malthellam that the inhabitants of the Blackroot Vale were largely accepting of King Elessar's gratitude, but that the people of Lancrath, in particular, have taken issue with the choices of King Elessar.
'I see. I commend you for taking on such a task, my friend. It is a difficult thing to stand before people and speak on behalf of another, knowing that words alone will not satisfy them. Always there are questions you cannot answer, fears you wish you could comfort, and promises that you cannot make—knowing you may not fulfil them. As Steward of the Vale, I am no stranger to being put in such a position, but for one to speak with the voice of the King carries even greater expectations. I do not envy you!
'It shall be some time before Lord Duinhir is able to return to his duties, ${PLAYER}. In the meantime, I shall try my best to serve in his stead.'

'Hail! What business do you have in Tingobel? Has the Lord sent you to check on our progress?'
You inform Drabnir that you have come on behalf of King Elessar to deliver a message to the people of Tingobel. Drabnir summons the other inhabitants of Tingobel over to you and gestures for you to speak. You offer your sincere gratitude to the people of Tingobel, and they appear somewhat heartened by your words. You make certain to mention that the hardships that Tingobel, in particular, endured during the War of the Ring have not been forgotten to Gondor and that King Elessar mourns those who were slain by the Orcs of the White Mountains. After you finish speaking, the crowd murmurs in assent and disperses.
'I know, for my part, that many here will appreciate the King's words. You see, I lived in Tingobel before the War, and it was a great pain upon my heart to learn what became of it while I served with Lord Duinhir in the defence of Minas Tirith. I know firsthand what battles we fought and what sacrifices we made during the War, and I know well the role that King Elessar played in securing this newfound peace for Gondor. I was there, ${PLAYER}, but many of these folk were not. It is important that they know that Gondor remembers them and that the King works in their best interests.
'I thank you for your visit on the King's behalf, ${PLAYER}. There is much work to be done still in Tingobel, but we shall see it to its end!'

'Oh, hello! I haven't seen you in quite some time, ${PLAYER}. I'll have to tell Sarnir that you're back! What brings you to Sardol?'
You inform Mellien that you have come on behalf of King Elessar to deliver a message to the people of Sardol. Mellien gathers the other inhabitants of Sardol, introduces you as an emissary of the King, and gestures for you to speak. You offer your sincere gratitude to the people of Sardol, and they appear to be heartened by your words. You apologize on behalf of King Elessar for the severe edicts during the War, including the brief suspension of their hunts by order of Malthellam, and for the failure to make safe the road through Tarlang's Crown. At the mention of Tarlang's Crown, a few hushed voices whisper to each other in the crowd. As you finish your remarks, the inhabitants of Sardol offer you their thanks.
'I had no idea you'd become an emissary of King Elessar, my friend. What an honour! It is good to know that the King has not forgotten us, and that he was thoughtful enough to send someone who was a great help to us during the War. Like many others in the Vale, we lost some of our young men in the War, for they were among Lord Duinhir's company when he marched to Minas Tirith. Your words have soothed some of our hurts, but only time can heal what remains. But I would not lay such things at your feet or at those of the King—it is the enemies of Gondor who slew our bowmen, and the King has made certain that many of them have been repaid.
'I must warn you, though. There are still some unsavoury folk lurking along the road through Tarlang's Crown, but it is not like it was... not like when that so-called Heir of Castamir, Azruthor, first set his encampment upon it. It is good to see you again, ${PLAYER}, and you are always welcome among us.'

'Ah, ${PLAYER}. What an unexpected return! What business brings you to Lancrath?'
You inform Osbenn that you have come on behalf of King Elessar to deliver a message to the people of Lancrath. Osbenn calls for the other inhabitants of Lancrath and they gather about you as you begin to speak. You offer your sincere gratitude to the people of Lancrath, and while some appear to be heartened by your words, a few others seem dismissive of your presence in the Blackroot Vale. You apologize on behalf of King Elessar for the hardships that Lancrath endured during the War, including accepting the refugees of Tingobel after it was sacked by the Orcs of the White Mountains. At the mention of Tingobel, a few in the crowd grumble in protest. After you finish your remarks, the crowd disperses.
'I am afraid gratitude alone is little comfort to those who have lost their sons in the War. Not to mention, you have forgotten another matter entirely—that of the Sleepless Dead. When the King summoned them, they followed him past Lancrath. Do you have any idea how scared our children were? How heavy that dread laid upon the hearts of our elders? No? Short of banishing the last of the Dead, there is little else that troubles us here now that the War is ended. If that authority is King Elessar's alone, then I ask why he has not used it for the good of his people! Forgiveness or no, what further use could those Dead Men have to Gondor? They endanger us by their very presence, so I must believe that King Elessar deems our lives a worthy cost.'
Osbenn pauses.
'Forgive me, ${PLAYER}. I apologize for my harsh manner, but you must understand that not all is well simply because Gondor has won the War. As always, you are welcome in Lancrath, but King Elessar has much still to prove to us!'

Alagrant can be found to the south of Morlad, Tingobel can be found to the east of Morlad, Sardol can be found far to the south-west of Morlad near Tarlang's Crown, and Lancrath can be found far to the south-east of Morlad near Tarlang's Neck, in the Blackroot Vale.
Malthellam has asked you to deliver word of King Elessar's gratitude to the people of the Blackroot Vale. You should travel to the hamlets of Alagrant, Tingobel, Sardol, and Lancrath.

Talk to Malthellam in Morlad

'Much has changed since last you visited the Vale, my friend. The War exacted a heavy toll upon us, and many of our bowmen did not return from their journey to Minas Tirith.
'Morlad has borne the greatest loss in the Vale, with many of its sons being slain in the War, and in especial, the Lord's sons: Duilin and Derufin. They were beloved among the people of Morlad, and it is a great sorrow that neither of them will be heir to the Lordship of the Vale. Between the news that King Elessar would not come to the Vale and of the baseless rumours that Lord Duinhir slew an emissary of the Haradrim in Minas Tirith, the people of Morlad believe that the Blackroot Vale has come to be known as a place of disrepute—a place of low-born criminals not worthy of the King's attention. Such a thing cannot be true, of course!
'After all, King Elessar was swift to pardon the Lord when the true culprit was identified, but alas, voices carried through Minas Tirith and out into Gondor. That is another matter, though.
'If you have come on behalf of King Elessar, then let us continue your work. It is true that you are an emissary of King Elessar, but more importantly, you are held in high regard among many people in the Vale. Your presence could do much to ease their misgivings in the aftermath of the War, ${PLAYER}.
'I would ask that you travel to the hamlets of Alagrant, Sardol, and Lancrath to deliver word of King Elessar's gratitude to their people. Oh, and Tingobel. It has been rebuilt since last you were in the Vale, and its people would be pleased to see you again.
'May you find good fortune in this errand, ${PLAYER}. Let us hope that peace is closer than it seems!'

'Welcome back to Alagrant, ${PLAYER}. To what do I owe this visit?'
You inform Calennen that you have come on behalf of King Elessar to deliver a message to the people of Alagrant. Calennen calls over the other inhabitants of Alagrant and steps back to allow you to speak. You offer your sincere gratitude to the people of Alagrant, and a few among them appear heartened by your words while others appear entirely uninterested. You apologize on behalf of King Elessar for the severe edicts during the War, including the brief suspension of their hunts by order of Malthellam, and a few people in the crowd grumble in affirmation. As your speech concludes, the remaining crowd disperses.
'I appreciate your words, my friend, and I think many in the Vale would find them a comfort. However, whether the King visits us or not is not of terrible concern to many of us here in Alagrant. Although we are all thankful that that terrible War is ended, it is no secret that we were sheltered from the worst of its horrors. We are simple hunters, after all. If King Elessar wishes to offer his gratitude to us, though, I would not refuse it. Perhaps he can visit Alagrant himself when next he wishes to see the Blackroot Vale!'
After learning that King Elessar will not visit the Blackroot Vale, many of its people believe they have been cast aside and forgotten, left only to mourn those they lost in the War of the Ring.

'It has been some time, ${PLAYER}! I mean no insult, but I did not expect you to return to the Vale.
'What business brings you to Alagrant?'
You ask Sarnir if he spoke to a man named Egnir and if he knows where Egnir meant to go after leaving Alagrant. You inform him that Egnir is remiss in his duties and must return to Morlad.
'Ah, yes, Egnir was here for a brief time. He told me he had a matter to attend to in the woods just outside Alagrant, but he would not say more of it. I must confess, my curiosity got the better of me, so I followed him at a great distance. I spied him carving something into one of the trees just to the west of Alagrant, but I dared not interrupt him and I made my way back to Alagrant before his work was finished.
'I did speak to Egnir when he returned, and he said that he was going to meet someone, but I cannot remember the name of the man he mentioned. It started with an 'L', but... what was it?
'I haven't been back to see his handiwork in the woods, so why don't you find out what he was carving? In the meantime, I'll try to remember that man's name.'

'Well, were you able to find it?'
You tell Sarnir that you found a carving on a nearby tree, but its appearance has been marred by several, deep slashes hewn into the tree's bark. However, despite being defaced by Egnir, you tell Sarnir that it still clearly read: 'E+D'.
'Defaced? Perhaps I was mistaken. Maybe it was carved some time ago then, by another's hand or even Egnir's own. As you describe it, it seems to me a sort of lovers' mark, but I say some sorrow must lay heavy upon Egnir's heart. For what other reason would he travel so far from Morlad to try to rid himself of it?
'I suppose the 'E' is meant to refer to Egnir, but 'D' could refer to countless people in the Vale. One thing is for certain, and that is that it does not refer to Dírion over there—I don't believe he and Egnir have ever exchanged a single word!'

'What can I help you with, ${PLAYER}?'
You ask Calennen if a man named Egnir came to Alagrant.
'Egnir, you say? Yes, a man by that name did pass through the other day, but he left not long after he arrived. I must admit, I didn't take the time to speak with him. He had a grim look about him, and it seemed to me that he would not welcome a conversation.
'Even so, Sarnir tried to talk with him. It seemed a bit one-sided, but I did hear Egnir answer him on a few occasions. Why don't you ask Sarnir if he knows where Egnir has gone?'

'Might I trouble you with a more private matter, ${PLAYER}?
'One of my bowmen, Egnir, has taken an unexpected leave of his duties here in Morlad. It is not like him, at least not as he was before he set off for the War with Lord Duinhir, but now... and it pains me to say it: I can scarcely recognize him. Before he left, few could contest that he was one of Lord Duinhir's most skilled bowmen—only equaled by the Lord himself and his two sons, Duilin and Derufin. When Egnir returned, I saw in his eyes a sorrow not unlike that of Lord Duinhir and Lady Rosfin, but I do not know why it has taken hold of him. I have asked him, but he will not answer... and now he has gone so far as to leave Morlad.
'Do not misunderstand, my friend. I would not see him punished, but I worry for him... and I worry that he may not return to us at all.
'From what I've heard, Egnir was last seen travelling southward toward Alagrant. Will you seek him out and ask him to come home to Morlad?'

The Dead and the Living
Egnir appears lost in thought.

'Hail! Take care, traveller, for the road ahead is treacherous. Turn back or...
'Oh, wait a moment, I remember you. You were the one who came through the Paths of the Dead! ${PLAYER}, was it? What can I do for you?'
You ask Ludhír if he has seen a man named Egnir. Ludhír's face sinks and he sighs.
'Yes, I have seen Egnir, but... he is unwell. He's gone up the road toward Fennas Dûr, and he's been loosing arrows at the Ruthless Dead for hours. I do not know what has gotten into him, but he must carry some terrible burden on his heart. I have heard him call out to them, taunt them, scream at them until his voice was hoarse, and still he continued... as if he laboured in service of some unknowable quest.
'The Dead will tire of him sooner or later, and I would not see him throw away his life now after he survived the War. He would not listen to me when I told him he ought to return to Morlad, but perhaps he'll listen to you. If nothing else, at least convince him to leave this place!'

'What do you want?'
Egnir does not turn to face you, and his gaze remains fixed on the Ruthless Dead along the road ahead. You tell Egnir that you were sent by Uidor to ask him to return to Morlad, and you mention that Uidor seemed worried about him.
'Uidor is a wise man, but grief does not make a good bedfellow of wisdom. That is the very reason why I left. When my grief turned to anger, I found my own hand destroying something dear to me... something irreplaceable. I stopped myself before it was too late, but even so, I could not shake the anger in my heart. In my journey back from the War, I learned that not all of the Dead heeded the summons of King Elessar and that those wretched spirits still haunted the Vale. And so, I turned my anger upon them, hoping beyond hope that I would find some reprieve from my grief.
'Alas, I have not. I have vanquished dozens of these Ruthless Dead, but always they return and I feel no better for it. And now my anger has all but burned out....
'It is curious, though. Each time I 'slay' one of them, they leave behind a pile of glimmering dust. Is it their essence? It always seems to fade away to naught after a time, and then, there they are again—reborn into restless death.
'Have you ever seen such a thing? If you would gather some of it, I can show you.'

'Do you see?'
Egnir takes the dust from you and casts it into the wind. It appears to vanish before it ever touches the ground.
'It seems that no matter how much of this dust I collect, they still remain. How can you take so much of someone and expect anything to be left? How queer to think that I might envy such a fate!'
Egnir chuckles weakly.
'I try and I try to make sense of this world, but how can I do that? Look at these turncoats and murderers! They persist evermore, flitting through the world of the Living, and we are made to think they suffer some terrible curse. But when good men—a good man—perishes, no matter how valiant his deeds or how pure his love, he is simply dead and there is nothing that can be done for it. O, if only Derufin had broken an oath!'
You notice Egnir has begun to weep, and his once-stern countenance has broken. You comfort him as best you can. He begins to sob, and after a time, he steadies himself and turns to face you.
'I... mourn the life I had wished to live, my friend. Derufin had not even told Lord Duinhir of us before—before the War took him. And so, who now am I to the Lord? One of half a thousand bowmen, but perhaps the only one who truly knows his loss. And maybe that is enough.
'You need not ask again, ${PLAYER}. I'll return to Morlad.'

Egnir appears lost in thought.
Perhaps it is best if you finish collecting the glimmering dust he mentioned.

'Ah, ${PLAYER}, I finally recalled the name of that man Egnir meant to meet: Ludhír.
'I believe he's one of the Lord's archers, but I couldn't say where to find him. Who sent you here again? Uidor, was it? You ought to ask him, then. I know him to be one of the Lord's finest captains in Morlad, so he would surely know better than I!
'I do hope you can find Egnir, my friend. It seems his sorrows have taken hold of him, and I know all too well how difficult that embrace can be to break.'

'${PLAYER}! Have you found Egnir?'
You inform Uidor that Egnir passed through Alagrant to deface an old carving on one of its tree, but then left to meet with a man named Ludhír.
'Ludhír? What business could Egnir have with him? Ludhír patrols the northern road that leads to Fennas Dûr—to the Paths of the Dead. After the King pardoned the better-hearted of their kind, we thought the Dead would not trouble us any longer. How wrong we were! Ludhír's even had to shorten his patrols of late, since the Ruthless Dead now dare to drift further from the darkness of the Haunted Mountain. Why would Egnir want to go there? I have not known him and Ludhír to be particularly close, friendly as they are to each other.
'I do not like this at all, my friend. Seek out Ludhír, and see if Egnir is still with him!'

'When those soldiers of Gondor passed over the great bridge, heading east, they did not come down here to the water's edge. I am not surprised: their eyes are ever on the horizon, dreaming about the great things they plan to accomplish for the lord that gave them their orders. It falls to common folk like me and my fellows to take care of everything else.
'In this case, that means the Orcs that hid down here when the army passed by. We are going to take care of these stragglers. Come! I will tell you about that rigging-hook while we work, and you can tell me how you came by it.'

'It is now your turn, stranger. How did you come to find Dírharn's rigging hook?'
You tell Nathlad that it was found within a stronghold in Mordor, and you hoped to cleanse it of the corruption that ensnared it.
'In the depths of Mordor, you say? There is a story here, to be certain, for I watched him cast that rigging-hook into the Anduin not far from this very spot. Did an Orc or some other fell creature fish it from the river and bring it on dark paths into the Black Land? That is a better answer than the one I suspected, the one for which I led you down here.
'I thought to test your loyalties, and if you proved a friend to the Orcs I would have buried my sword in your back for the murder of my friend. But I think now you are what you claim to be.'

'I have also given up the free-booter's life, if you must know. Shortly after my captain left, I changed the name of the ship to Valatëa, and we are now mostly honest men. Mostly.
'Thank you for hearing me out, stranger. I think it did me some good to remember my former captain, and to speak of his choice. You are welcome to keep that rigging-hook, if you would desire it. It was named Anchor of the Past by my friend Dírharn, but it need not be such a weight for you. May it be a help to you in the journeys that lie ahead.'
'Goodbye, stranger. I will count you from this day forward a friend of mine, and of Dírharn.'
Nathlad has brought you down to the bridges that now cross the Anduin, above which stands the city of Osgiliath.
Nathlad has ended his patrol and now stands before you, deep in thought.
Nathlad has ended his patrol and now stands before you, deep in thought.
Nathlad has come to a conclusion.
Nathlad has agreed to tell you what he knows about the rigging-hook you recovered from Mordor, but he wants you to help him with his work along the river.
Talk to Nathlad in Osgiliath and learn what he knows of the corrupted rigging-hook

'I know why you have come, ${PLAYER}. If you are to journey beneath the shroud that covers Gorgoroth, you will need the aid of a light that can pierce the darkness. Now that this rigging-hook has been cleansed of the corruption that settled upon it, perhaps it can serve that purpose for you.'
Elrond takes the Anchor of the Past from you and dips it into the font beside him. When the artifact emerges from the glowing circle, light drips soundlessly from it and pools like water in the basin. Elrond smiles at the sight, and his voice contains both determination and joy when he speaks again.
'With the Light of Eärendil, you will be able to walk where the shadows lie, and overcome them.'

'What's that? You think I might know something about a rigging-hook? Most captains and every mate need one, which you'd know if you were truly a Mariner. I cannot give you mine, if you've broken yours. I still make my living on the river, or would do if there weren't Orcs still hiding in the city and along the river-banks.'
Nathlad turns the rigging-hook over in his hands, and a dark cloud passes across his features.
'Wait... I do know this particular hook. How did you come by it, and why does it fill me with such a feeling of dread?'
You stare Nathlad in the eye and say that you can tell him some of the story, but you want to know what he knows about it first. He sighs.
'Well, I am not going to tell you here. There's work that needs doing. I'll tell you what you want to know, but you are going to need to help me first. Otherwise we will go around in circles, and no one will learn anything. Do we have an agreement?'

'You are the Mariner here, my friend, and if you say this artifact is a rigging-hook of the sort used by sailors I will not say otherwise! But this symbol here tells me where you should begin your investigation, for these markings seem to indicate a number of buildings built upon a bridge over a rapidly-flowing river. Whoever once owned this rigging-hook may have operated out of Osgiliath. Now that the Host of the West has passed through the city, it should be safe to ask sailors in that city if they know about this artifact.'
'I will meet you at the Haven of Orladion, ${PLAYER}.'

'Very well, are you ready to help me with my work? I will tell you what I know, and you will tell me what you know, and we must each be satisfied.'
<rgb=#FF0000>This is a Solo quest and cannot be completed with a Fellowship.</rgb>

Mithrandir believes you should ask sailors in Osgiliath if they know the story of the rigging-hook you found in Mordor.
Now that soldiers of the Host of the West have passed through Osgiliath, the city should be reasonably safe for you to search for such a sailor.

'I have studied the artifact that Ayorzén stole from the vault of Durthang. It bears a powerful corruption, but it was not made in the land of Mordor. It came from elsewhere, and the corruption that envelops it stems from its stay in the Black Land. If this evil could be cleansed, I believe that Elrond could imbue it with a powerful and vital force for Good.
'Before that can happen, however, we must do something about the corruption that Mordor has worked upon it. There are different methods to accomplish this, though the Wise disagree upon the effectiveness of each. My preferred means for such a cure is to bring the corrupted item to the place where it was made, or to places of some significance upon its path, and to thereby diffuse the foul touch of Mordor that has, in the interim, claimed it. We must learn the story of this heirloom before it came to Mordor.'
The Wizard turns the artifact over in his hands, studying it for some clue to its origin.
'The metal with which it is made is bronze, and fashioned into a hook of some kind. I cannot identify the purpose of this artifact. Perhaps there is none, and it was merely a decorative element of a larger piece?'
You cannot help but smile, for while the Wizard may not have seen this type of artifact before, to your eye it is most familiar. You tell Gandalf that the artifact is a rigging-hook, used by Mariners to rapidly descend along the ropes of their vessels without burning the palms of their hands, made of bronze so it will not rust in the damp.
'You are the Mariner here, my friend, and only a fool would not defer to your wisdom on such matters! But this symbol here tells me where you should begin your investigation, for these markings seem to indicate a number of buildings built upon a bridge over a rapidly-flowing river. Whoever once owned this rigging-hook may have operated out of Osgiliath. Now that the Host of the West has passed through the city, it should be safe to ask sailors in that city if they know about this artifact.'

'Oh, hullo. Did mother send you? Thanks for clearing a path through those awful turtles. When mother said they were bigger, I never thought… well, I can get home on my own now, but please – I lost my sword! It was a gift from Cangwen, and she always says a knight doesn't leave their sword on the ground, but when the turtles showed up I stabbed at one of them and it got stuck in the shell, and and and…'
She sniffles and wipes at her eyes.
'Please find Thumb-cleaver! I think I ran here from over that way.'
She waves an arm towards the north and swallows.

'Words alone cannot express my thanks to you, traveller. I hope she's learned her lesson. I might not be able to keep her from following in Cangwen's footsteps, nor would I want to, but hopefully she'll be more careful going forward.
'There's bravery and then there's… well, this was a learning experience, I suppose. Oh my poor girl, I am so glad she's home safe.'

'I wanted to name my sword something fierce, like Foe-cleaver or Goblin-head-lopper, or something. But, the first time I drew it I cut my thumb right badly on its edge and my sister named it Thumb-cleaver on me and even laughed when she bound me up! I miss her. And I miss my sword. I hope you find it soon!'
'You found it! You found Thumb-cleaver! Oh thank you, thank you! I... think I'm going to train a bit closer to home from now on, until I'm at least taller than those turtles.'

'Help! Oh, have you seen my baby? My little girl, Dorach, is missing! That fool of a child is always wandering off pretending to be a knight like her older sister. I only looked away from her for a moment and she was gone!
'Her sword is missing too, and I fear she's gone on to challenge the turtles on Loeg Thangalf. I tried to explain to her that they are enormous, fierce creatures, and not at all the small turtles she's seen in the river nearby, but I fear that made her all the more determined. Oh please find my girl!'

'I should've known Anoch would tell someone eventually. The truth is, I... I wanted to avenge Father. Those Corsairs took him away and I couldn't even do anything about it. 'And I want to. I want to run in screaming and tear them apart. I'm so angry. But I'm also so scared. I've never hurt anyone. I don't want to hurt anyone. But they hurt Father. He must be dead by now.

'Hedra told me she was going west, where there's a lot of Corsairs. The Corsairs already took Father... I don't want them to take her too!

'What I need from you is strength! I need your strength of spirit and arm. You alone understand the terror wrought upon the first Nenglor... what we lost.
'I will not be pitied. I will have my vengeance for those who were wronged. I will pursue this quarry like the dog he is until the very end of the world if I must.

'There is only one payment that will sate me, and it is blood!'

'I know my mind. I do....'
The captain calmed down.
'This map, containing only four points - four spokes - is but thin parchment and yet, mightier than the halyard that hoists our sails to drive us to our quarry.
'Out there, beyond the depths that swallowed my brethren whole and drove them down into the deep, there is an enemy in need of reckoning and by the stars above, I will set right the course of history.
'Should we be complacent, instead? Should we not revisit upon this enemy the same sentence they passed on Men and Women earning their wage?'
He shakes his head violently.

The captain sighs deeply.
'It is not madness that consumes me, it is grief. It is humiliation. Twice this scoundrel evades my capture. And the last...'
He cuts himself short and offers a sob.

At last, Yarikh came into view. Two of his lieutenants flanked him near a serviceable launch they were trying to get into the sea. We wasted no time to engage.
Yarikh's boat slipped out of sight as my blade wet itself on Akhât's corpse. Behind me, I heard a gasp and sputter for air... my friend.
Corsairs defeated (${NUMBER}/16)
With a new ship, the vengeful captain set out in search of Yarikh....
Speak with the captain

'All noble pursuits, young one. And in time, you shall see them come to pass.
'For now, my friend, we should both be content in the knowledge that we are friends. We have fought and bled together. We have saved people in Gondor and beyond and we safe-guard their future by our very actions.
'Ours is a noble pursuit. We should never think otherwise.
'On the morrow we sail again into the Bay of Belfalas. Let us hope that our quarry, this Yarikh makes his presence known that we might finally end his reign of terror on the good people of our land.'
'The night grows old, my friend. Let us rest while we can, we launch at dawn's first light. Let us see, together, what that new day holds for us.'
We sat in a simple study, each enjoying a smoke and spoke at length about our goals....
Often he would be like this, jovial and open, a warm companion. I listened quietly and drew on my pipe....
When it was my turn to speak he listened intently and responded....
Speak with the captain
Smoke with the captain

'When I was a boy, I was a ruffian. I fit in nowhere, much like you have confided of your early days.
'Ah, but when I found the sea. There, on the waves, was freedom. There, beneath the endless blanket of the sky was life. There was no substitute for what it offered, no greater joy.
'Dawn wakes over the horizon, drawing all from their slumber. The rocking of the waves give way to the bustle and commotion of boots on the deck, the promise of a new day, new adventure, new wealth and new shores... something new at every turn. There is no course that is set but the one you make.
'That is the life I covet and seek.'
Mission: My Bosom Friend

Mayor Will Whitfoot can be found outside the Town Hole in Michel Delving, in the Shire.
Despite your protests to the contrary, Fridolin Took believes you to be a long-lost and unusually tall cousin of the Tooks and thinks you ought to visit the lands of the Shire. You should talk to the Mayor of the Shire, Will Whitfoot.
Talk to Mayor Will Whitfoot outside the Town Hole, in Michel Delving

'Well, well! That is more than enough excitement for today, I think! I don't recall seeing you around Mossward, traveller. Although, I imagine it would've been hard for me to see anything at all while I was hiding in one of these fine folks' cabinets during that raid! I hear you helped to put an end to those oversized goblins, though, and I must thank you for that. What is your name?'
You introduce yourself, and Fridolin Took introduces himself in turn.
'${PLAYER}... a curious name for a most curious hobbit. Why, you bear a striking resemblance to old Bandobras Took—the Bullroarer, as we Tooks call him—yes, very alike indeed, at least where your height is concerned! Might you be one of my long-lost cousins? No? Perhaps you're of the North-tooks, then?'
You tell Fridolin that you are not one of the Tooks, a North-took, a Bullroarer—whatever that is—or anything of the sort. You say that you hail from a place beyond the Misty Mountains, and that you have travelled to Mossward as but one of many destinations on the long journey from your home-land.
'Yes, yes, that is all well and good, but you might still be a Took of some sort. Hah! I jest, of course. Even if you are not a Took, I say you are a cousin of mine, and it would be terribly rude of me not to invite you to visit us in the Shire. You'll need to follow the road up to Bree-town, and then you'll want to head west. Once you cross the Brandywine River, you're in the Shire! Ah, but first, you'll want to stop into Michel Delving to talk to the Mayor, old Will Whitfoot. He'll want to give you a proper Shire welcome!
'Oh, and if any of the Bounders give you trouble, just tell them Fridolin's invited you for tea!'

'Hullo, hullo! Are you a visitor come to the Shire?
'It is my duty and pleasure to welcome you to our great country, then! I am Will Whitfoot, Mayor of Michel Delving, and of all the Shire. Who are you and from where to do you hail?'
You introduce yourself to Mayor Whitfoot, and he bows in turn. You tell him of your home, saying only that it lies beyond the Misty Mountains, and of your long journey through countless lands that led you to the village of Mossward in Swanfleet. It was there you met Fridolin Took, you say, and Mayor Whitfoot chortles to himself.
'It would be Fridolin, wouldn't it? Tsk. It is always a Took! Well, I, for one, am glad you have come to visit us. If you and your kin are indeed distant cousins of ours, then I say you are kin of mine! You are welcome to remain in the Shire for as long as you wish, ${PLAYER}. There are many fine towns and villages in the Shire, so I would suggest that you visit them all. After all, I have heard more than enough complaints about my purported favouritism!
'Nevertheless, I am certain the good folk of the Shire would welcome the help of a ${CLASS} of your... stature!'
A Hobbit's Home From Home

After a long journey from the lands of Misthallow led you to the border village of Mossward in Swanfleet, you have encountered a most curious hobbit! Not a fellow River Hobbit of Lyndelby, nor one of the Stoors of Swanfleet, nor still their elusive cousins rumoured to dwell in Enedwaith: he is a hobbit of a land called the Shire.

'Before you leave, we would love if you could join us for dinner. Surely even you must need a rest after such hard labour?'

'I cannot believe you have truly decided to leave us, ${PLAYER}! I know we have spoken about this possibility for many years, but... well, I must admit I always thought I would be the first of the Holbytlan in living memory to leave this hidden vale, and the first to return!'
You tell Valaric that he is welcome to accompany you, and to his credit and his surprise he almost considers it. Then he shakes his head.
'Oh, no,' he stammers at last. 'It is a big world out there, they say, and I do not think I am quite ready to see it. But you are the tallest of us, and grew for the longest. If any of us have the courage to leave Misthallow, I believe you are the one!'

'So what has gotten my Heldric all in a bother, ${PLAYER}? And I have not seen Valaric this excited since... well, since Gísla accidentally doubled the recipe for her famous pie-fillings, but to speak honestly that was quite a day for all of us.'
You tell Grandmother Maddy that the time has finally arrived for you to leave Lyndelby, see the wider world, and have an adventure. She nods silently, and taps you on the nose.
'It was bound to happen sooner or later, dear ${PLAYER}. You have always been different, in your own way: more outgoing than the rest of us, and more curious about what lies beyond the mist-shrouded dells. And taller, too! The blood of the ancient Holbytlan is very strong in you, I have always said it! Haven't I, Heldric? Oh, he has stopped listening to me. That old goat!'

'You are up early today, ${PLAYER}. Are you planning to...'
Ogiva's cheerful words trail away into nothing, and her amiable expression is replaced with one of shock.
'This is the day! I knew it! I told Vilihad you were finally going to go and set out on your wanderings, and sure enough I was right! I did not know it would be this morning, perhaps, not exactly, but I have known for awhile that you were planning for just such a journey. That is terribly exciting, ${PLAYER}. You'll go and make us proud, see if you don't!'

'Today is the big day, then? Ogiva has been telling me you are soon to set out on some adventure or another, but I figured it wasn't really our business. I can't imagine leaving Lyndelby, but I suppose every one of us is different, after all.
'You be careful out there beyond Misthallow, ${PLAYER}. Who knows what dangers you might run into? The shrews are always getting into my crops and spoiling my lettuce, and I expect there are larger and more dangerous creatures out in the wide world. GIANT shrews, I wouldn't doubt it!'

'I just cannot believe you are leaving us, ${PLAYER}!'
Erma wipes away a tear and makes you promise that you will return after you have had your fill of adventure. You tell her you are certain to return to Lyndelby when you can, after you have seen what lies beyond the distant ridges on the horizon.
'The mountains are awfully tall to be climbed by one of the Holbytlan,' she says. 'I know Valaric says our people went that way, once, but he says a lot of things. Maybe you'll be the first of us to see what lies on the other side of them? If that's true, you be sure to come back and tell us all about it!'

'You are leaving Lyndelby in search of adventure? Good-bye then, ${PLAYER}. I will see you when you return, and...
'Oh! You should say good-bye to Croaker, too! He is simply the best frog-friend anyone's ever had, you know he is! You definitely need to say good-bye to Croaker, too. It will be some time before you come back, after all.'

'I saw the goblins from high above, ${PLAYER}, but I saw something else as well: I saw you bidding farewell to your folk, and I knew your mind. I have known what you intended for several weeks now, and have kept watch upon your steps. I hope you do not mind.
'I will continue to safe-guard your folk, as I have for all the years I have known you. But you will need to be properly-equipped if you are to survive the adventures that await you! You do not have the mighty talons of my kind, after all, though you are unusually tall and strong... for one of your folk. You are still very small when compared to the Great Eagles, and to the other peoples you will encounter beyond the ridges that surround your village.
'These goblins were thieves, and their leader possessed a bag of weapons. Perhaps you should avail yourself of this equipment; the goblin has no claim upon it, and its former owner cannot make use of it any longer, but in your hands it may yet do some good.'

'Do not forget to equip your new weapon, ${PLAYER}. I will not be able to protect you when you leave Misthallow, and you will need to rely upon your skills and the equipment you are able to find if you are to survive the challenges ahead of you.
'It is a dangerous world out there. Are you certain this is the life you have chosen? Most of your kind do not leave their homes, choosing to remain near the land of their birth.'

'I will not ask for you to stay, ${PLAYER}. I see that your mind is made.'
Grandmother Maddy smiles at you, and fondly tugs upon your ear.
'Now listen to me, dear one, because this is important and I will not repeat myself. You are to keep your eyes on the road ahead of you, and you will not worry about us; we have Fanglind and the other Eagles to keep watch over us, and Lyndelby will be fine while you are gone. But remember this: we are only letting you go so you can bring help to the folk you find out in that wide and dangerous world. You are to make yourself useful, ${PLAYER}! There are people out there who will need your help, and you should help them. I think that is the calling that draws you away from us, and it is only so you can answer it that I will permit you to go.
'Are we agreed? Then <rgb=#00FF00>wave</rgb> to us all and be off on your grand adventure, ${PLAYER}! And remember what I said!'

'Hello and welcome to Bergraw! We produce Pinnath Gelin's prized Calengaran. Bottles were sent up to the table of the king and his lady themselves for the wedding! Have you tried it?
'Yes, we pride ourselves on our wine, however this season's batches are in serious peril. So much has been going strangely lately on our Green Hills. Talk of goblins and Southrons. Something happened to Cornworth Farm and I haven't been able to get yeast from them for months! I've had to make due with yeast made from our very own grapes. It'll change the flavour, but will still be Bergraw worthy, of course. Only problem is, I can't get near the barrel the yeast is growing in to collect it! One bee sting could mean my death – my own gran had her throat close up because of it, many years back. We've all been careful since.
'Maybe you can help. I have some honey to distract the bees with, but you'll have to be quick! Take up that honey there, bring it a distance away from the barrel of grape yeast, and then make a run for it! You should be able to gather yeast in time, before they get back. I'm… nearly sure of it!'

'Are you all right, ${PLAYER}?'

I figured if it was above the water, it would have been picked clean ages ago. I left that detail out, of course, but now that we know where it is, I'm sure my crew can find a way down to it. 'I think it is time we sailed back to Mekhem-bizru, ${PLAYER}.'

'Ah, the Saervig is a fine ship, my friend. And look, Durin himself greets us!'
Byrski takes a moment to look around on the decks of the Saervig.
'Very good! Let us begin our search for Durin's Crown, ${PLAYER}. And remember, you're looking for seven stars in the shape of a crown. I'll start over here, so why don't you have a look from larboard?'

'${PLAYER}! Are you all right?
'You were looking into the Mirrormere and then it seemed to me that you became lost in some deep reverie. Is this a common occurrence, my friend? I do not mean to alarm you, but it has been nearly ten minutes! What happened? Did you see Durin's Crown?'
You tell Byrski that you were engulfed in a brilliant light, and that its warmth lifted your spirits and granted you a renewed sense of purpose as a Mariner. You suggest that it could have been the fabled Star of Eärendil, but you remain uncertain.
'The Star of Eärendil?! I thought that was just an old Mariner's tale—a guiding star to find shelter upon the Sea. And besides, I didn't see any light! I may be one eye short, but I would think I'd have noticed something like that! Perhaps your adventures have been too taxing of late, my friend.
'Ah, but I am... fairly certain that I spotted Durin's Crown! It had the proper number of stars, and it did appear to be in the shape of a crown, so I think our expedition was a success!'

'Nothing? No luck at all?'
Byrski sighs.
'I had hoped it would be easier than this, my friend. I'll take one last look, and then we can sail back to Mekhem-bizru. I just don't want to let the Iron Garrison down!'

Listen to the concerns of your crew
'I am not much of a teacher, but I hope to be a help to you. What do you want to know?'
'The sails have been taken down, but we are not yet safe! There is a presence in the wind, and it seeks to batter our ship beneath the waves!'

'I have never been to Umbar, ${PLAYER}, and neither has my brother... unless he has somehow managed to escape my notice and had some adventure about which he has told me nothing! But I find that unlikely.
'I wonder if Elves live among the sea-folk that call Umbar their home? I will have to put this question to the Corsair Daxamat sometime in the next few days. It could be he has seen Elves in the city or along the cape during his time there, before the Kindred came to power.'
Gwallang the Limlinn hops excitedly up and down, occasionally cracking the shell of a snail he has caught on the railing of the Wave-hunter. He seems very happy to be sailing with Sirgon again.

'This blade has to earn its name, ${PLAYER}. I cannot give it a name that might prove to be the wrong one! Weapons are like children, or so I have heard it said.
'The Elves of Lórien called my brother Corudan \qthe River-walker,\q for he was often away from home, exploring the lands up and down the Anduin. Will this adventure now make him \qthe Sea-strider,\q or \qthe Bay-rider?\q
'I will have to tell him this when we rescue him. He will laugh to hear it, once he is safe.'

'I have not yet needed the seasickness remedy you and Legolas procured for me, ${PLAYER}, but all the same I believe I will stay below decks for now. Do you think I should share it with Caebar? I will have it ready if he asks me for it, but I do not want to give it all away, just in case.
'We are not yet out in the Bay, after all. Legolas says he expects the rocking of the ship to become more pronounced when we leave the river behind us.'

'I have given some thought to our voyage, ${PLAYER}. I believe the City of the Corsairs must remain a bustling port-city, despite the defeat of Balakhôr the Scourge and the Heirs of Castamir during the War of the Ring. Do you think the arrival of the Wave-hunter can go unnoticed when we draw near the port?
'I cannot decide if it is more or less suspicious of us to arrive by night. Perhaps some of Golasgil's sailors will give me their opinions.'

'How fares my husband Rossaran? No doubt he gawks at the scenery through which the ship passes?
'Oh, he is a dear man. Two things he loves besides me, ${PLAYER}: faithfully serving his King, and marvelling at the great feats performed by the prospectors and stonemasons of Gondor. Sometimes I wonder if he should have been born a dwarf!
'But I have been checking our store of food and water, and it seems that we should have enough for the voyage to Umbar and back. The Wave-hunter is well-prepared for the journey; I confess to you that it is our arrival at the City of the Corsairs that now most concerns me!'

'This ship is unlike those of my people, ${PLAYER}. No, I do not intend that to be an insult! Even a ship made of rough-hewn timber is still to be prized if it stays afloat and keeps you from a watery grave! I think it is simply the way of the Men of Gondor to value the use of a thing higher than the beauty of its form.'

'What's that? Oh, nothing. I am just thinking.
'What goods do you think the people of Umbar might value? If I were to establish a market along the docks of the city, what things would fetch the highest price? Will items from Gondor be considered valuable or worthless, ${PLAYER}? I cannot decide! At least I will have a few days to think it over.'
'Thank you for keeping me company, ${PLAYER}, but I will not ask you to remain below decks for the whole voyage! Feel free to go above and take in the fresh air.'

'I have not felt this youthful in years! Our course leads down the Lagorduin to the Bay of Belfalas, and then we will truly be on our way.
'Like young Caebar, not all of the Wave-hunter's crew have before been at sea. I suggest that you speak with the folk you recruited and learn how the river-passage treats them. The waters in the Bay will be more unruly than this, and if the rocking in Lagorduin disturbs them it may be helpful to know, and guard against further upset! I understand the dwarf Gimli has in his possession a remedy for seasickness? He may need to share it, with Caebar at least, and perhaps with others!'

'I am all right now, ${PLAYER}. It was simply the sight of Daxamat clambering out over the railing of the ship that made me feel queasy. I think I will remain below decks for the rest of the voyage, unless you need me above. I cannot imagine you will. The sailors of Anfalas seem very capable.'

'The one who abducted my son Thorongil, this Nakási Wave-reaper... you said you know who she is?'
You tell Nauriel of the cellar encounter between Nakási and the Heirs of Castamir that resulted in the death of her husband Tumúldo. Nauriel stares at you with narrowed eyes.
'She will have no sympathy from me. Bad things happen. If she does not return my son to me, unharmed, I will send her to see her husband at once. I may do this anyway. Let her and her masters beware: a Knight of the Green Hills does not grant mercy without good reason... and the mother of an endangered child never does.'

'I have been thinking about something, my friend. So much good stone is covered by rivers and by lakes... and by the Sea as well, I imagine! What precious gemstones lie hidden down there, out of our reach? Is that the secret of the Temámir? Do the arid lands of their birth yield such valuables to them more easily than ours? And yet they still need water to drink....
'I look forward to learning how it is done when we arrive in Umbar. The gemstone worn by Khôltekh the Cunning is an intriguing mystery, but it is one I intend to solve!'

'Oh, excuse me, ${PLAYER}, I did not mean to be rude. I was contemplating the bridge over the Lagorduin: such an impressive feat of stonework!
'The City of the Corsairs has been many things over the years, but for some of that time it was a sea-haven of Númenor. There must be architectural wonders there too, and I am eager to see them. My wife Bruidis cares less for such things. Where is she now? She has gone below decks, intending to assess our stock of supplies. I told her the voyage itself should not take more than a few days, but still she wanted to ensure we have food and water enough.
'I told you before, did I not? I am a swan-knight, and my martial skill is well-developed; but my wife Bruidis is the strategist of the family. If there is thinking to be done, she is the one to do it!'

'Thanks for checking in on me, ${PLAYER}. You say the Corsair Daxamat spoke about what we can expect when we reach Umbar? I should have liked to hear that... assuming it was good news!'
You tell Caebar what you learned, and he nods.
'A little good and a little bad, then? It sounds to me as if we have our work cut out for us when we arrive. At least the sailing has been easy. I expected worse!'

'The storm rages and the seas are wild! We have to take down the sails, or the wind will tear our masts to splinters! The sailors and the Elves have gone above, but I cannot tell if they are still alive!'

'The voyage is well underway, and now our thoughts turn to our arrival at the City of the Corsairs. What will we do if the Kindred of the Coins greets us at the dock, ${PLAYER}? I said we would once again become the Hidden Guard, but there is very little that will be hidden about our mission if our foes see us arrive from atop the walls or from the watch-towers of Umbar.'

'I am not much of a teacher. My brother Jajax is the talker in the family.
'But I hope to be a help to you. What do you want to know?'

'The storm chewed up your ship and spat you out, stranger... but it must not have liked the taste of you. Most of the ships devoured by Shedax Khîn arrive upon the Shield Isles in more pieces than this, and with fewer survivors.
'Shedax Khîn? That is the Umbari word for the rocks that surround the island of Bakhjâd. It means \qthe Grinding Jaws,\q and theirs is the smile that welcomes strangers to these isles. But someone else must smile upon you and upon your crew, for while your ship will not sail again, you have your life, and that is more than some retain when they come here.'

'Mattân and I listened to the driving rain of the storm last night and it told the two of us a new wreck would decorate the islands this morn. We arose early, before any others, and came here in haste... but we were rewarded with disappointment. The isles have their new decoration, aye. But the Grinding Jaws did not finish their meal, and too many survivors guard the wreck.
'There will be little for us to salvage today. But I tell you this: life in the Shield Isles is hard, and not all who arrive here as you have can endure it. You survived the storm, but will you survive the week? Will you survive the day?
'Oh, it is no threat, stranger. I am simply making conversation.'
'These isles are not deserted, ${PLAYER}, and the men who live here may seek to do us harm.'

'I knew I did not like sailing, ${PLAYER}! How can it be that Sirgon missed it? A sailing-ship is a hateful thing, as unpleasant a creation as I have ever known!'
You remind Caebar that were it not for the strong hull of the Wave-hunter and its brave crew, he would not have survived the storm. Caebar shakes his head.
'Yes, yes,' he mumbles. 'I suppose it could always be worse. But I am done with ships! You mark my words, ${PLAYER}! From this day forward I will take the land-road, no matter how out of the way it may run!'
'You are more fortunate than most who come here, stranger.'
'An unguarded wreck is free to all who dare search it. Perhaps Mattân and I will come back tomorrow.'

We have our lives, after all, and the successful conclusion of your mission still lies ahead! This is not an ending, but a beginning! I have lost friends to the rocks that guard the Shield Isles, it is true... but today the strong hull of the Wave-hunter and the resilience of his crew has delivered us here safely. Rejoice for that, and celebrate the good fortune and the blessing of the Powers that aided in its accomplishment!

'Aye, it is coming back to me now. Let us see what I can remember.
'This island chain is a rocky archipelago composed of numerous isles running from north-west to south-east, but three of these are larger than the others. The southernmost island is the largest, Zamarzîr, and it lies in view of the cape upon which Umbar stands. It is a place of jungle and mountain, and when I served the Steward of Gondor in years past it was the haunt of pirates and freebooters. We left it alone as much as we could, for it was a dangerous place.
'The middle island is nearest to us, and it is Bakhjâd. The jagged rocks that surround Bakhjâd are responsible for the reputation of this place as the bane of sailors, for the dangerous currents surrounding the Shield Isles sweep strong ships and braver men to their dooms. I have lost good friends to those rocks, which the men of Umbar call Shedax Khîn. I understand that there may be a settlement somewhere in the centre of Bakhjâd, but I have not seen it.
'The northern island is uninhabited. I believe it is called Jeb Khâtel, but the steep cliffs surrounding it make it inaccessible from the coast.
'This is a place of adventure, ${PLAYER}! If we meet the challenge it sets before us, we are certain to survive and see the successful completion of our mission!'

Yahîm lowers his voice, and looks to either side before continuing in a hushed tone.
'The life of a Corsair is not what it once was, I confess it. I blame the Heirs of Castamir for that, but when I do so I make sure not to do so loudly, or when not in the company of those I know well. I make an exception for you and for your Elf companions, for if you cannot trust those who save your life, who can you trust?
'I promised you knowledge. Here it is: after the death of Balakhôr the Scourge in Gondor, his widow Saklaphêl thought to claim the rule of Umbar, acting as regent through their young son Balakhâd, but the rioting in the streets and the rise of the Kindred of the Coins caused her to abandon both that plan and the city; she fled to the Shield Isles, and now lives in exile here in Mâr Naphra. None see her. She issues orders to her servants through Galadaith, her spokesman. Supporters of the Heirs of Castamir believe she will organize the remaining Corsairs and attack the city and the Kindred who control it.
'But I have heard there is a reason she cannot. Some say Balakhâd died during the fighting when the city fell, but others say that the Kindred hold him hostage, and Saklaphêl dares not attack the city for fear he will be slain.
'Once again I thank you and those Elves for the rescue, and for the return of my sword. I hope my information is of help to you.'

'Yahîm said you should bring his sword to him at his home by the water on the eastern side of Mâr Naphra. It may be he will know something useful about the Heirs of Castamir or the Kindred of the Coins. Once you have spoken with him, we will meet you back at the Wave-hunter.'

'This is a very strange adventure, ${PLAYER}, where we must save our foes and rely upon what they can tell us to free our friends. My head spins, but I think Elrohir and I did the right thing. We could not leave Yahîm to be devoured by the kergrim, whether his allegiance is to the Heirs of Castamir or not. Corsair or no, he is still a Man, and he needed help.
'My brother feels the same, I am certain of it.'

'What did Yahîm have to say about the Heirs of Castamir and the Kindred of the Coins? Elladan and I would have rescued him no matter what information he had to share... but if his information is useful then so much the better.'
You tell Elrohir what the Corsair had to say, and he mulls it over for a moment.
'He does not know if the son of Balakhôr and Saklaphêl is alive and held by the Kindred of the Coins, but I think we have seen enough to know that they are the type to take prisoners. It could be Thorongil and Corudan and Balakhâd are all being held in the same dungeon, the easier to keep an eye upon them. The Kindred can then use each of them as leverage upon their respective families and friends.
'It is interesting, too, that Saklaphêl fled to Mâr Naphra. At least we will know from where the Heirs of Castamir might be organized, should they once again become a threat. It is worth keeping an eye upon, anyway. As if there was not enough to do already!
'Thank you for helping us with Yahîm, ${PLAYER}. Elladan and I will see what else we can help with around here.'
'Once again I thank you and those Elves for the rescue, and for the return of my sword. I hope my information is of help to you.'

'My brother and I thought to scout Bakhjâd and avoid the attention of the Corsair settlement we discovered in the island's interior, but it was not long before we heard the sound of someone calling for help from within the ruin atop this hill. We could not remain idle, ${PLAYER}, you understand. We went to investigate and only then discovered that he was clearly a Corsair; by most accounting he is a foe of our mission, but we could not leave him to be devoured by the kergrim that threatened him.
'We saved him and brought him back here. Have we done wrong?'

'You are a friend of these Elves? I am not accustomed to speaking with such as they, but I cannot deny that if they had not come along I would now be dead.
'My name is Yahîm, and I am not one to refuse aid when it is offered! It is true: I am a Corsair, and Mâr Naphra is my home, but I confess I am currently without a ship. If you hold a grudge against my kind, I understand it, but we are not currently at sea. On land can we not remain friendly?
'I appreciate the timely intervention of these Elves, and I do not mean to be ungrateful... but when I followed them to safety I left my sword behind. If you will return to the kergrim-infested ruin atop this island and retrieve my sword for me, I will see that you are rewarded. The Elves seemed more interested in what I might know than what valuables I might give to them, if you take my meaning. I will tell you what I know about the Heirs of Castamir and the Kindred of the Coins... if you bring my sword to me at my home by the water on the eastern side of Mâr Naphra. Unless I have misjudged your intent, that is what you want to know, is it not?
'If you will do this, can I ask for one more favour? Slay some more of the kergrim for me, will you? They are disgusting creatures, spreading filth and disease, and they should not remain among the old ruins. It is not right.'
'We saved him from the kergrim and brought him down here, though he is a Corsair and a foe of our mission. Have we done wrong?'
'Watch yourself among the wrecks, ${PLAYER}. The kergrim are dangerous.'

Gangur turns the corroded rock samples you retrieved over and over in his hands, but his scowl deepens the longer he looks at them.
'These rocks are like the others. The only difference is they are melted by the corrosive breath of the drakes. I admit it is not what I was hoping to see. I thought Khôltekh the Cunning might have gotten the shiny material that was embedded in his medallion from these islands, but if so its location remains a secret.'
He sighs heavily and then looks at you with a more open expression than you are accustomed to seeing on his face. He seems almost haunted.
'When I fell in the water I swallowed too much sea-water, and I felt the life leaving me. I cannot tell you now if my eyes were open or shut, but I believed them to be open, and before the blackness took me... I saw it.'
Gangur pauses, as if gathering the strength to go on. You let him wait until he is ready to continue.
'It was a great shelled beast, all tentacles and siphons, and its spiral shell was encrusted with the shining jewel of my dreams, glimmering like an opal but with every facet a riot of colour. Huge the creature was, but it paid me no mind even as it filled the great expanse of my vision. And then it was gone.
'Was this the dream of a dying dwarf, ${PLAYER}? Maybe it was. But I cannot forget the sight of it. That vision will haunt me to my last day... I know it.
'Thank you for listening to my story, but please do not tell anyone else of it. I will try to put it from my mind and help with the mission... as much as I can.'

While you look for those, could you also retrieve some rock samples for me from the islands hereabout? I am curious about something. I will be... well, I will be right here. 'The Steward Denethor came to believe that Belondor cared more for the people of Umbar than he did for his native Gondor, and he distrusted the man he had named Warden of the Firth. He believed Belondor had fallen under the sway of the Church of the All Seeing, a religion that had at the time a small, though growing, presence in the city of Umbar. This was impossible to believe, and even today I do not believe it, but the Steward had other reasons to distrust Belondor.
'My old friend had fallen in love with an Umbari noblewoman named Mêshka. I do not know how the Steward came to learn of this, but the rumours eventually came even to the White City. There must have been spies aboard one or more of Belondor's ships, or lurking in the court of Mêshka's home... but I cannot say for certain. When paired with Belondor's recent missives, which counseled mercy and fairness for the Umbari people, these whispers painted a clear picture of betrayal that the Steward of Gondor could not disbelieve.
'He commanded the master of his navy to pursue the traitor Belondor, relieve him of his duties, and bring him back to Gondor. I could not refuse the command, ${PLAYER}.'

'I am not a man for whom deceit comes easily, ${PLAYER}, but I could not think my old friend a traitor without good cause. On any other day, a call to dinner at my manor-house would have been the signal for a time of merriment and joyful reunion, but on this day it was a lure. Belondor answered the summons, for he had no reason to suspect the orders given to me by the Steward Denethor. Over dinner I asked him where lay his loyalties... and his answer did not dispel my worries.
'\qThey lie with Umbar Baharbêl, the City of Sails, my old friend,\q he said to me. \qThey lie with my Mêshka, to whom I am betrothed. And only then do they lie with Gondor. Can a man not serve three loves equally in his heart, if he is wise and fair?\q
'\qThe Steward Denethor does not think so,\q I told him, and our raised voices would have proven to me that our friendship was at an end, even if the drawn swords had not followed. Each of us sustained injuries in that duel, and Belondor fled through the shadowed streets of Pelargir to where his ship lay moored. For three days I pursued him in my own vessel across the tumultuous Bay, when at last he dared draw too near the Grinding Jaws; among the rocks of Shedax Khîn his ship perished. Some of his crew we rescued, but of Belondor there was no sign, and I believed him drowned, lost at sea. The Steward Denethor praised me for the pursuit, but I mourned lost Belondor, and cursed the duty that made me drive my friend to his death. But I cursed it silently, for still I served the Steward.'

'Thank you for indulging me in this, ${PLAYER}. I owe you so much for allowing me to join the crew of the Wave-hunter and come with you on this voyage. I would follow you to the very ends of the earth, know that I would, and never complain or say to you a cross word. I have always done my duty as I saw it, first for the Steward of Gondor and then for the King Elessar, and now for you, as the leader of this mission. So I will not still my tongue now, and I will tell you the source of my fear. May it prove without base!
'The name spoken by the young scribe: Belondor. I knew a Belondor when I was a young man. He was born in Anfalas and grew up along the Langstrand, and we both served at the command of the Steward Denethor. Belondor and I were well-nigh inseparable, and together sailed this very Bay of Belfalas and up the coast of Gondor to more distant shores. He was at my wedding, by the Valar, and gave the toast before all the gathered company! Celebros had me keep the stuffed birds he gave us for a wedding-gift in my hall of keepsakes, even when later events made their reminder a painful one.
'We rose in the estimation of the Steward. Even as I was made master of the fleets of Gondor, Belondor was named Warden of the Firth, and worked faithfully to keep the city of Umbar under guard, its pirates quelled and under control. He was an empathic guardian of the city, fair and just to the Umbari people, and they loved him. But this love proved to have a cost.'

You tell Horn what you know about Corudan's captivity by the Kindred of the Coins and your mission to Umbar. When you have finished, he rubs his eyes.
'After the Battle of Pelennor Fields, I wandered without purpose. I came to this land because I did not want to get involved, but even that proved a lie. I called myself Bymerë at first, and told myself Horn was dead. But as I lived here, drowning my old sorrows with ale and trying to forget what I had done and what I had been, I saw crimes I could not forgive; as I opposed them I took on a new name: Driftwood. I believed the Heirs of Castamir might again threaten Gondor... and if they had victory there, would not Rohan be next? So I made things difficult for them, as I could. I thought I might gain an audience with Balakhôr's widow if I claimed to have slain one of her enemies, and so end the threat of the Heirs of Castamir.
'Most of my plans ended in the bottom of a mug of ale, ${PLAYER}. When I was Horn, and fought alongside friends, it was different. Driftwood is alone, and accomplishes nothing. It is useless.'
You tell Horn that it could be different, and he shakes his head.
'This is my place now. I spend my days fighting Corsairs and my nights here, drowning in my cups. I suggest you defeat the Corsairs of the Shield Isles, for the sake of our past friendship, and then return to your ship. Horn is dead; only Driftwood remains, and he cannot help you.'
'Would Corudan come to your aid, if your positions were reversed?'

'This is my place now. I spend my days fighting Corsairs and my nights here, drowning in my cups. I suggest you defeat the Corsairs of the Shield Isles, for the sake of our past friendship, and then return to your ship. Horn is dead; only Driftwood remains, and he cannot help you.'

There can be no mistake. This is Horn of Rohan, though months of hard living on the road and in the wild have weathered his clothes. His face is still familiar, but the war and its worries have left their marks upon it, and he seems more aged than you remember.

'I do not wish for you to leave anything behind, my friend.'

'It is unfortunate to hear of Hithgol's continued ills, but I hold hope he shall soon recover as you have, ${PLAYER}. You see, when the battle came at last to Barad-dûr, Sauron himself felled Hithgol with a deadly blow, and it seemed only by the grace of the Valar that he was not at once ended. Even still, the steel of the Dark Lord's weapons was tainted in much the same way as the blade that pierced you, and he has suffered its effects as you did for many long years. Now then... we have spoken enough of the past, let us turn our minds to the days ahead!
'Much has changed since we last travelled together from Imladris, my friend. It seems now an age of Men, and I sense the time of the Elves in Middle-earth draws near to its end.
'Indeed, many have departed this realm for the Uttermost West by the ships of Círdan, our friend of old. He is now called the Shipwright by those who know his works, and he dwells in Mithlond with the few that still remain in his service as skilled crafters. Much of the wood used by Círdan is ferried to Mithlond by way of the port of Celondim along the Ered Luin, and it is there you must journey to reach the Havens.
'${PLAYER}, I have gathered your belongings and a few supplies for your journey. I have set your ring in its case upon the table across the room, and your armour rests in a chest at your bedside. It is still marked from battle, but time has not worn it elsewise. Indeed, the passing of an age has dimmed only our light... and given rise to the shadow in the East. Concerning such matters, I have also prepared for you a tome of writings on the history of the Third Age thus far. You are free to claim them ere you depart.
'Once you are prepared, we shall speak more of your journey to Celondim.'

'Very good, ${PLAYER}.
'In time your strength will return, my friend, and the power of your ring shall rise with it. I hope my writings prove to be of use to you as well. I recount much of the time that passed while your wound healed, but even I cannot be aware of all that has transpired since the end of the Second Age.
'As for your journey, my sons shall see you to Celondim in the course of their own travels. Elladan and Elrohir are to follow an expedition to the ruins of Edhelion led by the Elf Dorollas on my behalf. Speak not of this to any outside their company, but I had a strange premonition... and in it, amidst a field of blurred visions, a voice rose saying:
\qBlood-red footsteps Upon snow-coloured black, Where the Dour King walks to take back his throne and finish what was begun.\q
'It is a troubling riddle, my friend, and one that I do not think soon solved. Have you any thoughts on its meaning?'
You hear a muffled creak as the doors to Tham Send open.
'Ah! It is just as well; such troubles are best left to Dorollas and his expedition. My sons await you by the door to the central courtyard, and when you are ready to depart, they shall guide you to Celondim along the Ered Luin.
'May your journey be swift and free of hardship, my friend. Namárië.'

'These are the rock-scrapers I requested, and I thank you for them. Now tell me: did Yared cooperate? Did he know where these could be found, and was able to retrieve them quickly and easily?

'But do not tell Yared what I have said to you! Let him and the others think they are getting away with something.
