'Well met, ${PLAYER}! Your arrival at Jiret-menêsh is grist for the mill, as they say! You are quite the lively topic of conversation. I have not spoken to a visitor in one hundred years!'
The jovial dwarf chuckles and bows to you.
'But how rude of me, I should introduce myself! I am Gôbezhir Firmhand, master smith of Jiret-menêsh. I have heard you are well-travelled! I envy the sights you have likely seen, though I am no warrior and am happy to live a quiet life.
'I wonder, though, if you would be willing to keep an eye out for something for me. Since returning to the surface, I have had unusual dreams. I dream of a starlit night with falling stars trailing fire, streaking across the sky. They look so close, you could almost touch them. It is not unheard of for such things to be seen from the Height of the Sky, but I cannot help but feel like these dreams bear a message.
'When these stars land, they leave iron ore unlike any from a mine. It is stronger, resistant to rust, and must be worked at a higher temperature. We call it birêt-kibur, 'the noble iron'. I believe in my heart that I am to use birêt-kibur to craft an axe. Not just any axe, but my life's masterwork. I must do this thing, but I am only suited for the forge, not for adventures in the wilds.
'If you happen to come across birêt-kibur during your travels in An Shêru, would you collect it and bring it to me?'
Iron from the Sky

'The Ordâkhai mine is an open pit to this day? Zigêt! I hope that one day we are able to oust those worthless wretches. Or better yet, someone else does it for us! This Arch of Adazâr is intriguing. From your description, it sounds like it is the work of Shagâni Men, before the coming of Ordâkh.

You have visited the locations of other mines in An Shêru and assessed their condition. You should return to Kufâro in Jiret-menêsh.

'Well met, traveller. I have a question, and I was wondering if you could help me find the answer. Historically, we have had many problems with Men coming to An Shêru to pillage its once rich resources. The result is the landscape you see around you today.
'In an earlier age, we went to war with Men who wanted the greatest treasure of all, Jiret-menêsh. This war ended with an agreement that Men were allowed to mine in other parts of An Shêru, but there were provisions that they cause no harm to the land and do not mar its beauty. Their king swore an Oath to this, and for many generations of Men, the Oath was kept.
'When these Ordâkhai arrived from the south, they did not know of this oath, though it was made on behalf of all Men. But I do not think they would have cared, even if they had known about it. They cut down and hauled off all of the trees to fuel their war machine. They dug pit-mines... horrible things, those.
'Their final blow was the Din of Stone, causing massive unnatural earthquakes that surely collapsed many mines and stopped the flow of the Usâl River. It was then that Châmelek Gêta had had enough of Men and sealed the doors of Jiret-menêsh shut to the outside world.
'I cannot help but wonder, though, did all of the other mines collapse? Could any of them be reopened? In what state will we find the pit-mines? Since you are unafraid to traverse this land, would you be willing to visit these locations and tell me how they fare? I am most curious about Erakúndo, Gebarakór, Adazâr, and Lâkindar.'
Mine Inspections
Men have mined in An Shêru for hundreds of years, but the Din of Stone was powerful and likely collapsed the mines not of dwarf-design.

In fact, there was a grove of those sarláshi trees that the Elves tended.
'I do not doubt that the Elves are gone, but perhaps something remains of the trees? I apologize that it is far to the east, but would you mind going to where this grove once was, Zakhûr, to see if any wood remains? It is a hearty wood, and if any fallen branches remain, they may yet be usable.'

'${PLAYER}, what brings you to me?'
You ask Halshûm if he has any interest in a trade agreement with a Temámir jeweller from Jiret-menêsh.
'Interesting... I myself am not, but I know many people and may still be able to help you. I would need you to do something for me first, of course.
'I sell supplies to the Ordâkhai at Kôth Rau. It is why they allow us to keep Khanâg Gur in business. Among those supplies are foodstuffs that resist spoilage - very useful for an army. I happen to find myself with more of these rations than the Ordâkhai wanted to buy, and I need to sell them. There is gold invested in them, and I need it back.
'Should you find yourself in Kôth Rau, and the rations they bought from me happened to go missing, they would need to replace their lost supplies. Do you follow me? If this thing happens, I will see to it that this jeweller of yours has a buyer.'

'${PLAYER}, you were gone so long, I thought you had forgotten me, but you went all the way to Zajâna on my behalf? I do not know that I am worthy of such effort, but thank you! I have many rings and pendants ready to trade, but I look forward to talking to this Zarzûmir about what is best for selling, and make more of that!
'This brings me so much joy, ${PLAYER}! I cannot wait to get back to my workbench!'

Upon seeing you return with the crates, Halshûm laughs.
'You did it! If you want to become a Khanda-khêl, let me know. I think you would fit in well.
'I do not want those rations, though. My men have finer tastes than Ordâkhai soldiers do, and I do not expect the dullards to buy them for a third time.'
He chuckles before waving his hand in the air dismissively.
'Do with them what you will. Just get them out of here.'
'Now, on with our business. In Zajâna there is a man named Zarzûmir. You will find him lingering in one of the marketplaces. He would give your jeweller a fair price, and he has caravans that pass through An Shêru, so he could pick up the goods.
'I do business with him myself. He pays me to ensure his caravans make it through An Shêru without being attacked by bandits. Which is very easy to do. I just order them to leave him alone.'
Halshûm laughs again at his own cleverness.
'Anyway, tell Zarzûmir Khanda-mashár sent you, and he will not refuse your offer.'

'${PLAYER}, you return! But why?'
You present the Ordâkhai rations to the leader of the Jatsakóri and ask Nabatínu if he wants them.
'By the stars, yes! You know we would not turn away any unspoiled food. Thank you for remembering us. You are a treasure.'

'Saráz záro-dan, what can Zarzûmir do for you?'
You tell the man that you were sent by Khanda-mashár and that there is a Temámir jeweller in Jiret-menêsh who is looking for a partner to whom she can sell her creations.
'Jewellery? Made by a dwarf in the legendary Jiret-menêsh? Yes, I think I could sell those kinds of goods, no problem, and make a tidy sum at the same time.
'Not that it seems I have a choice, but you do not need to tell me twice to do something that brings in coin. I will assume Khanda-mashár will want a cut, but I will work that out with him. He will also tell me where to find Jiret-menêsh. There are few things he doesn't know. Thank you for bringing me this.'

Mêshaget laughs at your skepticism.
'Truly, if she did not like you, she would have said very little and would have told you to finish your business here and be on your way.'

'My grandson speaks very highly of you. I wonder if you are truly worthy of his praise.'
You bow and hand her the box of treasure. She opens it and briefly appraises the gold and gems within.
'You have done well. I am told this was taken from the Ordâkhai of Shêru. A difficult deed as well as a noble gesture, though I am sure you received counselling from one who knows me well.'
She hands the box off to her steward as Mêshaget's cheeks grow flush with embarrassment.
'It is of no matter. Thank you for the fine gift. For the sake of all, I hope you did not lead our enemy to our front door. I know not if you are aware of the danger Mêshaget has put himself and some of our kin in. My grandson fought hard to have the doors of Jiret-menêsh reopened. It is an understandable desire for those of less than one-hundred years, but it is foolhardy nonetheless.
'Though Barkhûsh is no more, evil has not died with him. Evil lives ever on in the hearts of Men, and has broken the land beyond repair. Even the Avabár-kinta have not the power to heal this land. But still, the mountain provides all that we need. We do not need to involve ourselves with anything outside of our Halls, and to do so is to invite disaster.
'Mêshaget is naive and does not know what the real world is like. He and others of his generation have been sheltered their whole lives. I understand the yearning for more, but the world that they yearn for does not exist. I must allow them to make their own mistakes, and only hope that the lesson does not cost them their lives.
'After much debate, I relented and allowed those who wished to surface to do so, with some terms. My first priority is to protect these halls and the dwarves within. Therefore, should we be subject to attack, the doors will close immediately. We will not hold them open for anyone, including my grandson. We will send no help, and they will be left to whatever fate befalls them.
'Honestly, I regret my decision to allow this. I see no good that can come of it. But a promise from a Gêta will not be broken.'
She leans back in her throne.
'You may come and go as you will, ${PLAYER}, but know this: should you lead the Ordâkhai to Jiret-menêsh, you would be responsible for the deaths of many innocent dwarves.'
Time to go!

You spot a chest loaded with treasure
To make her more amenable to your presence, he suggests you bring her a gift, a treasure stolen from the Ordâkhai at Onabóha, their camp to the south of Jiret-menêsh. You should travel to Onabóha.

'I would like to introduce you to Châmelek Gêta. She can be a stubborn old mule, though. I can say this only because she is my grandmother!'
He gives you a hearty laugh from his belly, and you get the sense that, despite his words, he loves the \qstubborn old mule.\q
'She is not fond of us being on the surface at all, so I expect her to be disagreeable about having visitors. I suggest that by bringing her a gift worthy of a Gêta, she would look upon you with a more open mind.
'The Ordâkhai outpost of Onabóha is comically close to Jiret-menêsh, considering the men there have yet to notice us! It would be more humorous if they didn't pose a deadly threat to us. Should Kôth Rau send them troops to support an attack on us, we would stand very little chance of survival.
'Regardless, if you went to Onabóha and stole a treasure from the Ordâkhai, it would be doubly impressive! Not only would you give her a treasure, but one from her feared enemy! Not being able to pay their soldiers would also make things difficult for them. It would also show the Gêta that they are not as invulnerable as she seems to believe.'

'${PLAYER}, there you are! I wanted to thank you for all you have done. Getting me here safely was no small thing, and rescuing Tâklu was an extraordinary act. I dare say I have never met another like you, so willing to help others. I will make sure Doorward Azagâya knows of your heroism.'
Khagâmi gives you a respectful bow.

'Who is this, then, a friend of Mêshaget? A ${RACE} offering help, no less! Interesting indeed!
'I am Mísikir and see after the safety of all at Jiret-menêsh. I assume you are quite trustworthy, else Mêshaget would not have sent you to me. Aye, there is one simple task for which I could use someone's help. I apologize that it is not very exciting, but still, it must be done!
'An Shêru is as dry as Châmelek Gêta's sense of humour, and standing guard is thirsty work. Please, take this water-skin to Cherêka, who is keeping watch over the road that all must take to approach the mountain. She will be somewhere nearby, looking down upon the road.'

'By my mother's beard! You have good timing, my friend. My own water-skin is empty, and I was just thinking of my thirst.
'I must tell you that I have never spoken to a ${RACE} before. You are taller than I expected! Only recently has the Gêta allowed us to come to the surface, and I am a mere forty-seven years of age, so I have only recently seen the open sky for the first time. Its vastness is intimidating, and I have no love for the wind!
'This is a good experience, though. One must be comfortable with being uncomfortable if they wish to travel, or so I am told, and I would like to see the Shoreward Stone one day!
'My thanks for the water, friend, and send the captain my thanks as well.'
'I thank you for your help! A woman came by earlier, asking after your whereabouts. She said she wanted to talk to you, but I am unsure where she went.'
'Khagâmi's words speak true, my friend. Your willingness to help people tells much about your noble nature. You are exceptional, indeed!'

'His name is Sâdikiz, and he is a Temámir who was banished from Jiret-menêsh many years ago. He also pushed for opening the doors and was so wilful that he angered Châmelek Gêta. She dubbed him \qthe Sky-hungry\q and cast him out from the city, telling him that if he craved the sky so much, he could go die under it.
'I expect she thought he did just that, but the world is not as perilous as she believes. He has had many adventures and has returned to An Shêru. He can often be found in Khanâg Gur.
'You should meet him! I admire him in many ways. He may yet prove to be a valuable ally to you, as he has been for me. Look for his boar. If you see it, he cannot be far.'

If you were able to collect eight of these glands, I could sell them to the right buyer for enough to cover my debt. Would you aid an old, battered dwarf?

Talk to Mêshaget
Talk to Châmelek Gêta

'Châmelek Gêta, you are wise, and only want what is best for all of us. That, I understand and respect. I was not unaware of what lurks within the Quelling-house, and I chose to enter this forbidden place, risking my own life, for the chance to bring safety to our people without sacrificing their freedom.
'I do not believe that things must be only one way or the other. We can have both security and freedom if we fight for it! Barkhûsh and his priests are gone. Ordâkh has no Hûl... or perhaps too many Hûls, I am not sure. By all accounts, they should be weakened! We can surely defend ourselves against them, and can do so with allies, if only we allowed ourselves to make some.
'If Zajâna were to find value in trading with us, they would likely be willing to help defend us, should it become necessary. Evil does not lurk in the hearts of all Men. It was Men who killed the Hûl in Gondor, and it is said that the same Men helped bring Barkhûsh to his knees. And what of the Shoreward Stone? As Temámir, we are not friendless or alone.
'I only ask that you examine the works of Semayâti the Unyielding, and allow for further discussion.'
Mêshaget bows to the Gêta respectfully as he ends his argument.

After a moment of silence, Châmelek Gêta responds.
'It will be as you say. I will look upon what is in this book, and we will discuss your proposal. You have not won, Shakâr-inik, I only agree to a discussion!'
She leans forward conspiratorially.
'Speak to me, ${PLAYER}, do you have children? Grandchildren? If not, avoid it at all costs! I fear that as Mêshaget comes into his own, he is becoming more stubborn than I am! One day, he will be Gêta and may do as he wills. Why he is impatient and chooses to spend all of his time fighting with me, I will never know.
'There is a part of me that wishes to punish you for allowing him to endanger himself on such an unwise adventure, but I do not think you would have been able to talk him out of it if you had tried. Instead, I suspect that you are the only reason the fool is still alive. Am I correct?
'Thank you for returning my rough gem to me. I am glad he has you for a friend.'

'I am relieved you came! This place has a foul air. It strikes fear in my heart and makes my hair stand on end! I do not think I could enter were I alone.'
Mêshaget is sweating, visibly afraid of this place and is fighting to gather his courage.
'It is said that inside Lâkindar lies the tomb of a legend, Semayâti the Unyielding. At the time of Lâkindar's height, she was a celebrated Temámir crafter, inventor, and engineer. It is said that there was nothing she could not do well!
'It is believed that upon her passing, she was entombed with her journal, which was filled with many inventions and designs that were never made into reality. According to the history I have read, one of these designs was a plan to fortify Jiret-menêsh against attackers.
'We have been relying on secrecy and ignorance to protect ourselves for one hundred years, ${PLAYER}. It is only a matter of time before those who envy our great wealth decide to take it for themselves, and our lives with it. We will find the tomb of Semayâti the Unyielding and recover her journal. I will convince Châmelek Gêta to make these designs a reality so that we may live as part of the world, and yet also live without fear.
'Please go in ahead of me. I should remain behind for a few minutes to ensure neither of us has been followed, and then I will catch up to you inside.'

'That went better than I expected, ${PLAYER}! Châmelek Gêta may be stone-headed, but she is not blind to reason when it is in front of her. Jiret-menêsh has a bright future ahead, and she will soon see that.
'Thank you for all the help you have given me. You are a steadfast friend, and you came at the right time for when I truly needed one. Sâdikiz crafted his own fate, which I know in my mind, but my heart hurts for what I have done, regardless.
'Should I have shown him mercy? I do not think he would have shown me any, but does that make my wrath warranted? Was a death blow truly necessary? It will be some time before I can sleep easily at night, I think.
'I wish you the best on your travels, ${PLAYER}. May we meet again in more prosperous times.'

'Explain yourselves! Why is my grandson injured, and why is he in my hall instead of my hale-house?'
Châmelek Gêta appears to be furious. Mêshaget hobbles forward and kneels before her, holding out the journal of Semayâti the Unyielding. She snatches it out of his hands and looks it over, flipping through the pages before she pauses, and her look of anger is replaced with one of wonder.
'What is this?'
Humble, and without looking up, Mêshaget says, 'The designs of Semayâti the Unyielding, that we may use to build defences to protect Jiret-menêsh and its people.'
She sets the book aside as Mêshaget returns to his feet.
'You fools went into the Quelling-house!? Did I not tell you that this place is forbidden? Tell me why you disobey me, Mêshaget!'

It pains me to question the motivations of one I have long considered a mentor and friend, but since we have succeeded in opening the gates, he has started asking many questions he should not. He seems to have no ill will for the hall of his fathers, but I cannot help but wonder now if it was all a lie. A false face to earn my trust and then use me to the ruin of our people.'
The young dwarf looks thoughtful for a moment.
'There is something I must do, and I wonder if you would help me. To the south lies the ruin of Lâkindar. Many refer to it now as The Quelling-house. Lâkindar was once a wealthy mine of the Temámir, but many years ago, the priests of Barkhûsh turned it into a slaughter-house and sacrificed many innocent people there, Man and dwarf alike, to their wicked deity. As you may imagine, Châmelek Gêta has forbidden us from going there. The place is surely cursed.
'But go there I must. Would you accompany me? I will tell you more of our purpose once we arrive. Meet me at the top of the great stair. You will know it when you see it.'

'${PLAYER}, I should tell you of my task and destination. I am on a quest to find an ancient dwarf city called Jiret-menêsh. Tales claim that it has been in An Shêru longer than the sun has been in the sky. It is well documented in the libraries of Zajâna that the Temámir were avid trading partners with Zajâna and others for centuries.
'When Urash-zâl, the Din of Stone, shook the ground and dried the Usâl, the people of Zajâna had their own difficulties. It went unnoticed for some time that all contact with Jiret-menêsh had been lost. Most believe that the Temámir were either all killed or they abandoned this forsaken land, which is quite plausible.
'However, there have recently been whispers that the hearty Dwarves of Jiret-menêsh have emerged from the ground, where they have been hiding in isolation for one hundred years. Doorward Azagâya sent me to investigate the rumours and see if this is true. Should it be so, I am to establish friendly relations with them, and if possible, negotiate terms of establishing trade between our cities.

Without the rivers to sweep them through, they festered, creating bogs where previously the land had been green and rich with forests.

'These oranges are perfect. I would have taken five, but seven is even better.
'Here is the book you requested. Give Khâbakh my regards.'

'Saráz záro-dan, friend. Yes, I have that book. I don't want coin for it, however. I have a powerful desire for oranges. They grow freely on the hillsides outside Zajâna, beyond the Khab Kitâx, this time of year. Yes, I believe I will accept oranges in exchange for the tome.
'How many oranges are you willing to get for me?'

'Three? You don't seem very skilled in negotiation friend. You are supposed to get closer to the number I suggest, not farther away.
'I suppose I could accept a paltry ten oranges in exchange for the book.'

'All right, all right. You'd see me driven from hearth and home, and leave me destitute with no oranges, but I will accept your terms. Seven oranges in exchange for the book.
'Now go, bring me the oranges before I change my mind.'

'Ah yes. This is the book I needed. Let me see, yes, this is the relevant passage for you.
'You were asking about the Pale Blight, yes? Here it is. Travelling scholars mention a legend among the Kintai that may be relevant. They speak of Sívigush the Earth Terror, a great beast of unimaginable size and ferocity. These accounts say that Sívigush carried within it a great plague, that corrupted all it touched, turning the forests pale and dead wherever it strode.
'These accounts attribute this Pale Blight to Sívigush, and claim it emanated from a place in Adagím once said to be Sívigush's abode. This site was later settled by a group of Men who excavated the area. It is known amongst the Elves as Nagakhêdi's Folly. Apparently the Men who were excavating the site were building a grand abode for their king, Nagakhêdi. Reports disagree here on the details, but each claim that the workers perished to a man within the cursed tunnels.
'This is all rumour and happenstance. But if you are indeed searching for the source of this Pale Blight, you might explore Nagakhêdi's Folly in Adagim. Then tell me what you find. I would love to publish something new about Adagím - as long as I don't have to go there myself. Dreadful place.'

'I don't believe the Kalmakhíla has a copy. You should head to the Court of Larinâsta here in Zajâna. There is a book-seller I know there, Merbâna. Here is some coin. I believe she has a copy of the book. Bring it here and I will find the relevant passage for you.'

'It is not Men alone that threaten Kighân. The spiders to the east snatch and claw at passersby, harassing the many caravans set along the Great Road. They and their dread brood-mother - the one we call Jûkhtar the Ravenous. The spiders have set up their vile lair in Jâr Obadal, in the dusty caves east of Zajâna.
'Please, go there and set fire to their network of webs, and cull their number - so that travellers can again feel safe both on the road to Zajâna and throughout Kighân.'
'You are a miracle worker! I can scarcely believe that you defeated Jûkhtar and ended the threat of her brood. We shall make a ballad of your deeds this night!'
'Your mission is clear, ${PLAYER}. Defeat the spiders and set their burrows ablaze.'

'This is alarming, not least because Charganpâta is quite hostile to all but the zizani. Could you investigate these claims, and if they are true, try to speak sense into this man?'

'A hoardsman? I can scarcely believe it. Still, we will make sure all these possessions return to the people he stole from. I hesitate to call these valuables - but they will be returned.

'We have a problem, outsider. The Pohâni, our learned class of scholars and sages, have just informed me that one of our oldest and most important texts, \qThe Farings of Kábuzar,\q has been stolen.
'The Jewelled Council raided the Kalmakhíla last night, and stole many books. They have burned them in the past, seeing these stored learnings as sacrilegious and profane. We cannot allow this text to be burned.
'Will you go to the Halls of Lajór and retrieve this book before the Jewelled Council has a chance to figure out what they have in their possession and destroy it?'
'You have it? Praise be. The Pohâni were beside themselves this morning when they thought it lost forever. You have my gratitude - and theirs - for returning this, my friend.'
'This book is truly irreplaceable. Do whatever you must to ensure the Jewelled Council does not destroy it.'

'Sen Chatâk sent an urgent request for aid this morning. It seems their village is beset by raiding goblins. They have been killing locals and setting fire to their houses. This is something the Doorwards take most seriously.
'Luckily we believe they have sown the seeds of their own destruction. Our scouts report that they have explosive weapons, barrels of black powder they are preparing and gathering for some foul purpose. But we can use that against them.
'Break into their camp, and use the black powder to destroy their structures and war machines. This should cause them grievous harm, and might even hasten their retreat fully from Kighân. Will you help us?'
'You bring me bright tidings on a dark day. I wish I was there to see the battle itself. That fire sounds glorious. We are once more in your debt.'
'These goblins have reigned down destruction on the innocents of Kighân for too long. It is time for them to taste the sting of fire and iron.'

Complete Mission: Chopping the Woods

'Although our troubles are many, those who find their way from Adagím have it worse. There is a sickness there, one that threatens to take hold here in Kighân.
'We cannot allow that. Already it has found a toe-hold in northern Kighân, a place locals call the Moulder-grove. There as in Adagím the trees are restless and violent, and the plants twisted and strange. We cannot save Adagím - but we can contain its evil.
'Please, seek out the strange and twisted plants in the Moulder-grove, and set torch to their progeny. It is the only way we can be sure this affliction does not spread and take over Kighân as well.'
'You set fire to them? It heartens me to hear it. We shall be rid of this blight yet, if not by salves or miracles then by flame. Thank you, friend.'
'Sometimes the only proper answer to a problem is a good flame. May fortune guide you, and bring you swiftly back to Zajâna.'

Complete Mission: The Sweetest Reward

'The farmers of Sormedan recently came to us with an urgent matter. They can no longer harvest honey from the caves of Medân Makhai. Many here in Zajâna depend on them for the harvest. The farmers tell a strange tale.
'They say that recently a new dark queen installed herself, defeating and exiling the former queen. The farmers found the queen, injured and broken, not far from the caves, and were able to nurse her back to good health. However, they are not warriors - they cannot contend with this new queen or her warrior acolytes.
'Please, help them. They are not warrior folk like yourself. Defeat this new queen and harvest the stockpiled honey, so that the farmers may work with the bees as partners once more.'

'It warms my heart to hear it! The farmers will be happy to be able to return to Medân Makhai, and all of Zajâna will be heartened that the supply of honey is once more flowing, a delicious amber river.'
'We are relying on you. Defeat this new dark queen, that our relationship with the bees may be healed and returned to the fruitful partnership that it once was.'

'If you should find the unsullied seeds of Nisigím, gather them with care. In them lies the memory of what once was and the hope, faint though it be, of what might yet return.
'We offer you tools to claim and harvest, or the means to make them. Choose as you will, and know this: even before your hand turns to aid us, we are already in your debt.'

'Welcome, ${PLAYER}. Your honoured name reached us from our groves to the North. Your coming renews our hope that virtue yet walks among us.
'Our stores are thin, as in the North, and what we can grant in exchange for aid is little beside its worth. Yet we will deal in good faith.
'As the blight spreads, still there remain unspoiled roots and seeds in Adagím. We ask this: gather what is pure. Take the seedlings untouched by corruption; bring us the seeds that hold the memory of the Emerald Wood.
'Here, beneath the boughs of Sul Madásh, hope clings still. With your help, the forest may yet be reborn.'

'Well met, ${PLAYER}. Word of your valour in the North has reached us, and you are welcome as a friend of the Kintai.
'In the West, the once-hallowed forest Nisigím lies stricken. Now it is named Adagím, for it is shadowed by blight, and foulness spreads where once light dwelt. Trees and beasts alike wither, and though some persist, most fall silent as the Mother Trees perish. Only Sul Madásh endures, untouched.
'Seek Quartermaster Aralath. They will tell you what aid we can spare—and what we ask in turn.'

'As our fortunes rise, so too shall your reward. The stores shall swell, and with them, the treasures set aside in your name. We shall see this venture through to its end—and you shall not be forgotten in its telling.'

'We have witnessed your strength—in arm, in spirit. You have stood beside us through triumph and grief. We have spilled blood, not as strangers, but as comrades. And now, we draw near to the ending. Hamât shall rise again, renewed by Mizâdi's hand.
'There is no other she would call to my side in this hour, ${PLAYER}. The campaign must find its end—and before that hour comes, she shall call upon you again, if you will attend her.
'Captains and lieutenants clamour for aid as there is much to do and prepare; all that you do in her name shall bring you honour, and raise your standing among her host. Lumgâna will keep your share of the spoils safe, and grant you access to our deeper stores.
'Stay steady, ${PLAYER}. The road narrows, and the end draws near. We will need your strength before the last banner is raised.'

'From many corners of the land, your name is spoken—not loudly, but with growing admiration. You have walked the narrow path, and not turned aside. For this, we offer not only reward, but also our trust.
'Zajâna is a city of memory. The Doorwards seek to restore what time and tyranny have buried. Whether through relic, script, or shard, we gather the truth of who we were.
'Among the ruins of our foes or carried by their hands, caches remain -- sealed by the craft of the Ordâkhai. These keys will pass their locks. Take them, or if your hands are skilled in metal, learn the means to forge your own.'

'We are settled now. You know us, and we know you. Aid us as we return to the old ways upon the surface, and together we shall see prosperity grow, stone by stone.'

'Ho there, traveller. Our return to the surface is met with both marvel and mourning. When last we looked upon these lands, they were green with life and bright with running water. Now dry beds, and pools turned foul.
'Yet the shadow recedes, and so we step forward to trade, to speak, to mend what was broken. Aid us, ${RACE}, and in return, you shall see a share of our wealth and craft.'
You have spoken to Quartermaster Semanísi

'A rare day indeed—and welcome. Few have come, and fewer still returned. Long have we laboured in the deep, far from sun and sky. Now, by craft and council, the gates are unbarred.
'The elder and the cautious remain in the halls of stone. Those who yearned for light and the green earth have returned, and we behold the scars left upon the Mûr.
'Through dark years and bitter days, we held fast in Jiret-menêsh, our beloved hall. We kept it whole, though the world above faltered and threatened to shake her apart. When the time came to look beyond the doors, many refused. We, who rose, heard whispers that the long shadow was lifting, and that light once more touched the land.
'Thus came we forward, to trade anew, and to see if the old pacts may be struck again. To see if Elves and even Men would share their wealth. Now we seek the trader, the wanderer, and the warrior alike; and by your bearing, you may be all three.
'Seek the quartermaster. We have wrought much in the silent years. If you would aid our return to the world above, there is work to be done and reward for those who earn it.'

'Another face unknown to me. There are many such now. Not long past, those like you would go west to the cells of Emax Dûl. Civility returns and Zajâna stirs, and the Doorwards seek again the name it bore of old: a city of esteem, and cross-roads of the wise. The City of Keys.
'If you would earn regard of our folk, your deeds shall be weighed, and your worth measured. Speak with the Quartermaster—they will show what task may earn you standing.'

'To make a name here, you must act in service to Kighân and more, to Zajâna. Our land, like our people, stands at a turning. We seek again the freedom we once knew, and still desire.
'Aid us truly, and your name shall be writ among those of good repute. Cross us, and it shall be stricken, and you marked foe. The choice lies with you.
'Prove your worth, and we shall speak of trade and reward. For now, begone; I have much to address.'

'Take no offence at our reserve. Zajâna has suffered long, and we have learned to be wary of open hands. Too often have gifts masked chains. We will watch. We will judge. Let your actions speak until your voice has earned its weight.'

Otibúk's condition is much the same. His whole body glistens with sweat, fighting both his wounds and an ever-returning fever. He occasionally thrashes in the bed, softly moaning. Is he having nightmares of the battle? I could not know, and was being consumed by my helplessness. How can a mother watch her son suffer so?

My daughters should be in bed at this hour, but I noticed that my youngest, Khêjiba, was missing. I asked my eldest, Lokóya, if she knew where she was.
'She said she was bored and went to explore. I tried to stop her, but she ran off before I could block the door. I think she went to the garden. Sorry, mother. Please don't be too angry with her.'

I asked Khêjiba who she was speaking to, growing increasingly concerned.
'I don't really know. We call her the Pale Lady. She talks to me sometimes.'
I was alarmed, and asked if my other daughters knew about her.
'Yes. She talks to all three of us. I've seen her staring at Otibúk before, too. Do you think she can help him?'

I asked Lokóya if she knew about the Pale Lady. She turned white as a sheet at the mention of the name.
'I... Yes. I don't know what she is or what she wants. She has appeared to all of us. Aunt Barkhuráni warned us not to mention her to anyone, so I haven't....'
She starts to cry.
'Mother, I'm afraid to leave our bedroom! Can we please go back to Ordâkh?'

'I assume you overheard some of that. Mizâdi's rebels approach from the East while the upstart servants of Aradûn approach from the West. Our enemies are nearly at our doorstep. We must strike before they form an alliance and encircle Emax Dûl.
'But do not worry, I will oversee our forces and ensure we are victorious. We cannot abandon Emax Dûl. We cannot fail the Hûl. We cannot abandon Emax Dûl. We cannot fail the Hûl...'
Góramul seems momentarily entranced. He snaps back to normal when he hears someone else enter the room.

I inquired as to just who this dark ally is, and why I was not made aware of an important guest in the palace before this.
'My apologies, sister! I would have thought your husband would have informed you. If he has not explained, he must not want to trouble you with it, and I would not want to displease the Sai.
'All you need to know is we have a powerful ally on our side, who will ensure a prosperous future for us and the empire.'
She flashes an innocent smile, but does not elaborate any further.

I demanded answers. Yes, my husband is the crown prince, but something was deeply wrong, and I would not allow it to threaten my children.
'You forget yourself, Kotráka. I have everything under control.'

Góramulâ's eyes welled with tears. Somewhere inside, he knew he was losing the fight, both for Mûr Ghala and for his own mind.
'Kotráka... I am sorry.'

'I had hoped you would find me. There are many here in your debt. Were it not for your action, our lives would be at an end. There is no recompense we can provide, as destitution is the plight of our moment, but we would invite you to entreat with us, those you saved, for a modest gift of story-telling.
'Across this bridge to the north you will find Dabâr. Beyond him, beneath the canopy and near the sheep pen, Vilgêra, and beneath the canopy nearest the stable-master you will find Malgâras. Each has a story to share.
'Will you meet with them, and then return to me?'

'The King and the Pale Blight? A tale passed down through countless generations. Yet the memory of Men is fleeting and few recall with true clarity.
'Like others, I weave the tale with embellishments to soothe eager ears. But mark this, friend; no maps speak of the Citadel of the King of Folly. No written lore survives to hint at its bearing. So great was the horror the king wrought, his reign was erased from history, passed only in oral tradition, as a warning.
'Yet… among the Temámir dwarves, there may be maps of those peaks they dared not scale. Dwarves, unlike Men, can recall the ancient history of stone; they will know of the place they would not delve.'
A Celebration of Life

The dwarf's eyes meet yours with a rare intensity, and his tone grows firmer.
'It is a treasure that would make me the envy of many, and you will have done me a service beyond measure. I will honour my part of the bargain, as I always do.'

Bêtam explained that he will provide you a map for the price of collecting a prized smith's hammer from the resting place of Kojomedên in the Quelling-house. He warned that others fear to enter to the place due to horrors wrought there.
Speak with Bêtam the Couth at Jiret-menêsh

'Whispers among the prisoners you freed spoke of the Temámir opening their doors once again. If such words are true, then perhaps you may seek out Bêtam the Couthful. Should he, or any of his kin, yet walk this earth, they will know the lands where even they dare not tread. But be warned, for I have heard it said that dealing with the Temámir always comes at a price.'

As you explain your quest, the dwarf exhales deeply, his voice thick with both weariness and resolve.
'There is a region of mountains in these lands where none of my kind will venture. I can provide you with a map, should you wish it, but it shall require time and a service in return. Grant me these, and I shall keep my word.'
He pauses, his gaze growing distant as if recalling some dark memory.
'The service I ask is this: you must find the resting place of Kojomedên, within the Quelling-house, and bring me his hammer. It is a prize long coveted by my kin, though, I confess, it is one we have feared to recover, given the dark fate that befell those who sought it before.
'The time collecting the hammer will grant me the time I need to craft your map, should you return to me.'
The Penchant of Dwarves

You claimed the hammer from the despoiled corpse of a once great dwarf artisan. Return Kojomedên's hammer to Bêtam the Couth at Jiret-menêsh. If he is an honourable dwarf, he will provide you with the information you seek.

Though a teller of tales and a historian, Phardâli does not know where the Fool King's citadel may be. He suggested visiting Bêtam the Couthful of Jiret-menêsh for more details.
Bêtam provided you a map and directed you to compare it to the maps in the library of Zajâna. He warned that where the edges do not match, there shall you find the Fool King's citadel.

'I am as true to my word as you are to yours. Here is your map. If what the tale-weaver told you is true. You should take it to the libraries of Zajâna and compare it to the maps of Men. Where the edges do not meet, there shall you find the fool's citadel. Seek out Valukhâri, she oversees the keeping of tithes at Zajâna. She will know more.
'Go now, I have something to forge.'
'Maps? We have many. Is there a specific map you wish to view?'

As you compare the maps, you see a distinct difference in the south-eastern corner of Adagím's border. 'Strange indeed. Our maps are renowned for precision and care. It may be that the cartographer who crafted yours has, perhaps, erred in their reckoning.'

Make your way to Viznak in Adagím.

Make your way to Viznak in Adagím.
You embark on a journey back to Viznak and learn that travel through Mûr Ghala grows more harrowing by the moment.
Viznak directs you to return to Rhadrog and Faeron in Zajâna, convinced that the Blight Lady they pursue has arrived here in Adagím.
After speaking with Rhadrog, he is resolved to seeking out Lhaereth and asks that you inform Faeron at the fountain in Zajâna.
Speak with Rhadrog at Zajâna
Speak with Faeron near the fountain in Zajâna

'You must hurry to my bodyguards. They will want to know. They may want to help. Be quick, I will wait here and study more.
'They are still in Zajâna.'

'That wretched imp yet finds new ways to confound my expectations. If indeed there is truth in the rumour that Lhaereth has come, seeking to reap some vile gain from the pestilence that defiles this land, then we must learn her whereabouts with all speed. Go now—tell Faeron what has passed. I shall make ready to depart.'
'Our road southward has not been in vain. If the tidings prove true, then the one we have long hunted may at last be near. Let us turn our path east and press on into the very heart of the blight.'
Seek the Citadel
Viznak is concerned that the Blight Lady has come to these lands. He directs you to return to Rhadrog and Faeron at Zajâna.
Present your story to Ildimár at Sul Madásh
Hear Dáthlil's response to your story
Return to Irsinith at the Mother Tree and see what she learned

Ildimár and Dáthlil listen to the retelling of the King's Folly, and all you have learned since. They share a glance, and Ildimár speaks.
'Men tell this story in a manner different from what we recall. Ages have passed, the king's bones have long been dust, but a persistent memory endures.
'Bitter woe came to Nisigím, and many reaches of the great wood went unwatched after. Our people fought not only the cruelty of Men, but also the endless creep of Sívigush, the blight that rises now to consume all. In truth, we have always striven against Sívigush. It is as old as the stars.'

'When the blight returned, it was as in the old tale of the forgotten king: a thin, devouring veil that left naught but ruin behind.
'If the tale holds true, the place of its binding was sealed. But Ordâkh came with sorcery, broke the land's back, and the blight was loosed again.
'If dark things now stir in the North, seeking its source, they must be stayed 'ere all falls. Go to our daughter, Irsinith, upon the Hill of the Mother, and hear what Amûma has revealed to her.'
'Amûma remains silent; her pain is too great. We should heed my parents' words. Viznak's insight may prove invaluable.'
Dáthlil responds and bids you return to Irsinith
You shared your story with Ildimár
Viznak wants you to bring the tale and news of the king's story to Irsinith, the Warden of the Mother Tree in Adagím.
Irsinith, inspired by your story, will commune with the Mother Tree. While she does, she asks that you visit her father and mother at Sul Madásh.
Irsinith, inspired by your story, will commune with the Mother Tree. You have spoken with Irsinith's father. He asked that you speak with her mother before returning to Irsinith at the Mother Tree.
Speak with Irsinith at the Mother Tree

After your explanation and description of the enemies setting upon you on the return to him, Viznak looks off into the distance before speaking.
'Morvul, troll, Orcs, all pawns for Blight Lady. Not spiders, though. Not that I ever see. My bodyguards are smart to send you. We should tell the sad Elf-lady about Blight Lady. Her name is Irsinith. She is a very sad Elf-lady. This news will not cheer her up, but maybe give her a new purpose. You go and talk to her and see if she can teach you more.'

Irsinith listens to the tale of the King's Folly with great interest. As you explain the variance in maps from the Temámír and Men, she nods in assent. When you finish, she pauses and looks to the Mother Tree.
'The Temámír map speaks true. In elder days, we held pacts with the dwarves; the defence of Nisigím was a charge borne by all. There were peaks even they dared not climb.
'The Kinta stood firm in that age, though it lies beyond my remembering. My father and mother may recall what I cannot.
'Take your tale to them at Sul Madásh. I shall seek Amûma's counsel—if her grief permits, she may yet speak.'
Enlightenment of the Suspicious Mind
You learned some more about the blight from Ildimár and Dáthlil, return to Irsinith at the Mother Tree in Adagím and see what she learned from her communion with the ancient tree.
Irsinith bids you seek counsel from her parents in Sul Madásh
Viznak is curious and precocious, a frightening combination. He directs you to seek Irsinith's counsel at the Mother Tree.
Deliver the peculiar mushroom to Viznak at Sul Madásh
'This is not good. Look at the gills. They are very different. None of the fungus here is like this. The ground here is too moist. This fungus is from the north.'
Irsinith enlists you to gain Viznak's aid in learning more about the missing section of the map. Return to him at Sul Madásh.

Viznak directs you to scour the area in the south-east section of Adagím in search for something out of the ordinary. He believes that you will find a fungal growth very different from the others near the location not on the maps.

You discovered a mushroom at the foot of the mountains in south-eastern Adagím. The mushroom was certainly different and out of place from the rest. Return the mushroom to Viznak at the Mother's Hill.
Speak with Viznak at the Sul Madásh in Adagím
Collect a peculiar-looking mushroom from south-east Adagím

'Viznak's counsel shall be of great value.
'Seek him out, and ask by what signs we might discern whether the 'Blight Lady' has come to this place, drawn to a hidden wellspring of the Earth-terror.'
'We must hurry. Go to the place on the dwarf map. Look for Uruks, look for trolls, and look for morvul! If you see blighted fungi different from others, collect one for me.'
Insight into Action
Collected a peculiar-looking mushroom
The Kintai of Sul Madásh welcome the assistance of you and the others against their ancient enemy, Sívigush. Irsinith directs you to enlist Viznak's further assistance.
Ask Rhadrog how to proceed at the south-west gate in Zajâna

'Viznak's insight—or his paranoia—may yet serve us. At the very least, you can tell him the tale of the King's Folly and see if he can establish the connexion between the blight we face and that which claimed a generation.'
Faeron agrees and suggests you ask Rhadrog what next to do

Valukhâri is dismissive that the tale is nothing more than a child's fable spun for a new crowd and age. Something does not sit right with you. Take the map to your allies Rhadrog and Faeron, recently arrived here in Zajâna and gather their opinions.
Rhadrog believes the tale may have merit and wants you to share the story and map with Faeron at the fountain square in Zajâna.
Speak with Rhadrog near the south-west gate in Zajâna
Share the story with Faeron at the fountain square Zajâna

'I fear I have nothing more to offer. The map you hold is likely flawed. The tale of the Fool King's Folly is little more than a children's fable, meant to frighten them from the night or keep folk from venturing into Adagím. It has served its purpose. No expedition has ever sought the fabled citadel's location.'

You show the map to Rhadrog and recount the tale of the Fool King.
'You were wise to bring this here, ${PLAYER}. The dwarves are long-lived and masters of stone, unless, of course, they are driven by greed and seek to hoard a treasure. Ask Faeron what his counsel may be.'

'Had the Temámir not believed in what their map suggests, they would have long ago established an outpost. But they are wary. Men, however, are prideful and secretive, prone to hiding uncomfortable truths. I side with Rhadrog—tell him I believe we must inform Viznak and compel him to learn more.'
Failure Erased?
Faeron and Rhadrog agree there is a reason to investigate further. Faeron suggested you ask Rhadrog how to proceed.
Rhadrog asks you to speak with Faeron

The difference in the maps provided by the scholars of Zajâna and the Temámir are pronounced. The Doorward leader believes that the map provided by Bêtam may be a fraud, or errant. You should consult with your allies from the north, Rhadrog and Faeron.
'Make haste to Viznak. Be warned, the pathways through Adagím grow darker and more dangerous.'

Rhadrog and Faeron ask that you gain Viznak's insight and input on the story of the King's Folly and the map you discovered. Perhaps the goblin can tell you how the story may coincide with the blight he studies in Adagím.

You made a harrowing journey through the wilds of Mûr Ghala, beset by spiders, Orcs, trolls, and a morvul. At the journey's end a friendly face appeared, the goblin Viznak. He wishes to speak to you in Sul Madásh in Adagím.
Complete the Instance: The Road to Adagím
Deliver Bêtam's map to Viznak at Sul Madásh

You share the tale of the Fool King and the map of Mûr Ghala with Viznak. After a moment of quiet contemplation the goblin speaks.
'My bodyguards did right by sending you to me. I think the story is real. The blight is real. Look around you.
'We should look to the south-east. If dwarves do not go there. It is because of nasty Orcs, or worse. We should find out, maybe it is where the blight is born.'

'Make haste, ${PLAYER}. Return to Viznak and seek his counsel on the tale of the King's Folly. His perspective may yet reveal something we have missed. With his insight, perhaps we can offer the Kintai aid in what yet unknown to us.'
Viznak's Insight

Rhadrog and Faeron believe there is a reason to investigate the fable and missing location on the map and direct you to speak with Viznak. They warn you of the dangers brewing on the roads around Mûr Ghala.
Speak with the Steward of Mûr Ghala, Lejâl, at Zajâna

'From the ashes of strife, new hope takes root. Yet renewal is not without trial. Loyalists to the yoke of tyranny still walk among us, servants of the All-seeing Eye, whose hearts remain black with malice. Where they tread, peril follows.
'They raid and burn; they slaughter without mercy, clinging to the vestiges of a crumbling dominion. As the jázga cornered and wounded, they strike with desperate fury, more dangerous now than before.
'Our scouts, though vigilant, report stirrings of wickedness in places where the foulest take shelter, and where unrest secretly brews. This knowledge we pass to those who would stand with our cause, to drive out the last shadows of the long night. And not only in battle, but in the mending of what was broken. We find our strength for hearth and home must be restored if the land is to flourish once more.
'If your heart is willing, reward shall not be withheld, nor honour forgotten. Visit me each day and I will direct your efforts.'
You were directed to speak with a Steward of Mûr Ghala to expand the breadth and impact of your assistance in the land. You should seek the counsel of Lejâl in Zajâna or Calúrmin in Sul Madásh.
Speak with the Steward of Mûr Ghala, Calúrmin, at Sul Madásh

'Mûr Ghala stirs from long slumber, yet the shadows of night do not flee swiftly. Though we speak now of places marred by blight and infested by ancient foes, know that where embers yet smoulder, flame may rise anew.
'Our scouts remain vigilant, but they are few, and the fires of strife may kindle faster than they can be quenched. Speak with a Steward of Mûr Ghala, either Lejâl in Zajâna or Calúrmin in Sul Madásh. They shall guide you in where your strength may best serve the land and her people.'

Speak with Dabâr in Ahâba
Speak with Dabâr at Ahâba
Speak with Dabâr to hear the remainder of his story

'We come to a tale of folly - a tale of ambition unbridled. The story of a king, whose hunger for greatness far outstripped his wisdom.
'A king whose pride cost his people a generation of artisans and labourers.'
He weaves the tale of a king who dreamed beyond measure - a dream of a citadel to surpass the grandeur of Emax Dûl itself. His vision was to carve a bastion from the very bones of the mountains themselves - mountains that even the Temámir dared not tread.
Dabâr's voice darkens, painting a grim picture as he recounts the folly of that decision: the king's heedless command to pierce the mountains, to cut into the stone where nature herself forbade it.
The workers, labouring under the king's ambition, soon began to fall ill, struck by a mysterious wasting disease that sapped their strength and life.
Dabâr speaks of bodies carried back to the hall of the king—pale and shrunken, their faces etched with a terrible sheen.
He recounts, with vivid detail, the horrors of those fifteen long years—of men and women toiling under the weight of a king's dream, even as their bodies withered and their lives dwindled.
He stops for a brief moment.

'The king's folly was not his ambition; that was a fire that could have led to glory.
'No, his folly was in his refusal to listen - to heed the counsel of advisors, or to listen to those who laboured beneath his command.'
Dabâr bows his head, and you begin to ponder the sorrow, wasted lives, and lost opportunity beneath the triumph of the people. Then he breaks the silence.
'Thank you for hearing me. Heed well this tale.'

There is a shift in his voice, 'The people, at last, rose against their oppressor.
'The cries of revolt thundered through the streets, demanding the cessation of the cursed construction and the sealing of the mountain's heart!
'The crowd roared in approval, a shared recognition of the power of the people's will to defy tyranny.
'Thus it was that the surviving workers, their strength spent, withdrew from the mountain.
'They sealed the entrance and put an end to the blight that had threatened them all.'

'You have come from Phardâli? Great is the debt I owe, and little in my keeping can repay such valour. I have naught of worth but a tale - and even that lies heavy upon the heart.
'It is not as gracious as the weave of Vilgêra, nor the bold song of glory spoken by Malgâras. Nay, mine is a darker telling - a warning drawn from the dust of sorrow and ruin.
'Yet such as it is, I offer it as recompense, for it is all I have, and you have saved my life.
'Will you stay a while, and hear it spoken?'
Celebration of Life - Folly

Dabâr paused. You should ask him to continue his tale.
You can find him near the bridge on the northern side of Ahâba.
Dabâr warns that his tale is one of caution and offers it as reward for rescuing him, and the other from the jail. Speak with him near the bridge in the north of Ahâba.

Dabâr paused again, conscious of the eyes upon him. He beckoned you closer to finish his tale.
You should speak with him near the bridge on the north side of Ahâba.
Phardâli bid you find Dabâr in Ahâba. Like others freed from Esh Mekag, he wishes to reward you with a tale that kept the prisoners alive while trapped in the jail.
Speak with Malgâras

'If the stories of the Eternal One be true, then surely his return is at hand!'
He pauses, and offers a wry smile.
'A wave of cheers erupted - some voices loud, others hesitant, but all drawn in by the power of the tale. Yet, amidst the joyous roar, a few remain silent, their eyes darkened with doubt.
'For, not all hearts believe in the legend, and the tale, perhaps, has spun too far beyond the threads of truth to grasp. Yet, it remains a great tale of glory these lands once knew.
'Thank you, for listening, traveller. I hope this tale is reward enough for your rescue.'
Malgâras bids you stay and listen to him. Speak with him beneath the canopy east of the stable-master in Ahâba.
Speak with Malgâras at Ahâba

'Glad am I to see your face, though strange in these lands, it is welcome. You delivered us from a shadow long endured, and for that, no thanks shall suffice.
'Phardâli wisely guided you to me, though I possess little to properly reward your deeds, I wonder, will an old tale - whispered in the gloaming of my youth, recalled again in the gloom of the prison, suffice?
'Perhaps the glory it echoes will inspire you, as it did us, though the lore is strange to those in the North, and may you remember the name as one of a doom-bringer, or harbinger.
'Will you grant me patience awhile, and hear the tale?'

'Hearken, my people, hearken well. Hear now the tale of glory - of the Menundâri, Izighûz the Worthy, the Eternal, who led our folk from the shadow of oppression. He who raised the mighty walls of Emax Dûl. He, who watches over us still, as the Dawn-warden. He, who shall return!
'A great cheer rose from the crowd, swelling with fervour, I raised my hands, bidding them to stillness. The clamor ebbing, I continued weaving the tale of the the rise of Izighûz in glorious tapestry: a rebel leader, who struck against the North, casting down their yoke and reclaiming the land for his people; his wisdom, his strength, and his boundless life extolled with reverence.
'I invoked the statue of the Dawn-warden, shining bright as the sun's first light, and the citadel of Emax Dûl, standing firm against the ages, praising both in fervent voice.
'And - as my tale of the Eternal One reaches its zenith...'
He motions for you to step back.
Celebration of Life - Glory
Malgâras appears finished, a smile spreading on his face. Speak with him again beneath the canopy near the stable-master in Ahâba.
Phardâli bid you find Malgâras in Ahâba. Like others freed from Esh Mekag, he wishes to reward you with a tale that kept the prisoners alive while trapped in the jail.
Speak with Vilgêras in Ahâba

'Now, Zajâna stands as a beacon of liberty and wisdom, a citadel for reason, its halls hallowed by the pursuit of truth.
'The City of Keys remains steadfast, the enduring home of scholars and keepers of lore.'
His voice softens in reverence.
'And though battered and broken, Zajâna shall endure. It shall safe-guard the wisdom, the history, and the truths of our land and our people, tended in reverence by those who seek knowledge in the City of Keys.'
He bows his head, in solemn grace.
'Thank you for listening.'
Vilgêra wishes to share a tale as a reward for helping to release him. Speak with him beneath the canopy near the sheep pen in Ahâba.
Speak with Vilgêra at Ahâba

'I know your face, but not your name. I saw the courage in your eyes, and your well-forged strength - the kind fostered not from pride nor the lure of gold, but from a steadfast heart for a cause both just and unknown. Phardâli said he would suggest you come, and I am glad you have.
'I offer a gift - not of silver nor of blade, but of memory: a tale long kept in the halls of the wise, of our people and of the city that stands at the jewel of Kighân. Grace dwells there, and always has, and always will.
'Will you hear it?'

'It is the tale of how the pride of Kighân - The City of Keys - Zajâna, came into being.'
He weaves a tale of ancient wealth and boundless riches, of travellers wise and seasoned, who, long ago, carved a waystop between Shagâna and the distant lands of desert and jungle to the south.
From this humble beginning, the city blossomed, its streets laden with the promise of knowledge and the riches of the world.
The story unfurls, recounting the many triumphs of the City of Keys—its foundations built on wisdom and the exchange of lore.
Its gates opened to scholars, its halls shone with learning. From these fertile grounds, wealth and knowledge poured in, like waters flowing from an unbroken stream.
But the tale darkens then, shifting with the winds of time. A great sorrow befell the city.
Vilgera shakes his head, to ask for a moment while he mourns.
Celebration of Life - Grace
Vilgêras stops, his voice growing hoarse. He asked you to step closer to hear the remainder of the tale. He awaits you near the sheep pen in Ahâba.
Phardâli bid you find Vilgêra in Ahâba. Like others freed from Esh Mekag, he wishes to reward you with a tale that kept the prisoners alive while trapped in the jail.
Return to Elder Jurmêna in Sormedân
Speak with Lurâkha in Sormedân
Speak with Khaljûn in Sormedân

'You have spoken with each of them? That is welcome news indeed.
'See that the villagers' needs are met, and I will tell you what I know of Khâbakh's whereabouts.'
'You want to help? My cattle are ailing, and my list of chores long. I will take whatever aid you are willing to give, outsider.'

'Jurmêna sent you to do the rounds, did she? I do have something I've been complaining to her about, come to think of it.
'I cannot sleep. A terrible racket keeps puncturing my restless dreams.'

As you stand by the blighted pods that were once mushrooms but have now succumbed to the Lâg Dávrit, the Pale Blight, you hear the high-pitched, warbling sound of the insects called zizani.
Is it your imagination that the pods of the blight respond to the sound of their call, shivering and shaking in time to the notes of the insect chorus? You decide to cull any of the zizani you encounter, quieting the song of the harbingers.

Through your efforts, the song of the zizani has been quieted for a time. It will be back, but for now you have achieved a measure of peace in a forest of unrest. As you look around you see some of the pods touched by the Lâg Dávrit no longer respond to the insect chorus, and you know your efforts were worthwhile.

'Thank you for speaking with them.

'There is much to do in Sen Chatâk. We have been beset by raids recently, attacks from both the west and the east.
'I can scarcely catch my breath, there has been so much to do, to organize and defend our village. But our people have other needs as well.
'If you wish to be of service, speak with Ahâto, Kôrzan, and Jûshal. Each have concerns that I wish to address, but with these attacks I simply cannot.
'Will you aid Sen Chatâk?'
'There is one goblin in particular that threatens Sen Chatâk. If he does not die, Sen Chatâk will never know peace.'

Complete Mission: Vestiges of Lâkindar

'Before the coming of Men to An Shêru, Lâkindar was wealthy and prosperous. Even those dwarves who were alive before the Din of Stone never saw Lâkindar at the height of its glory.
'I understand that it is a dangerous place to explore, but I cannot help but wonder if there is anything left of Lâkindar's happier past that can be found and brought to Jiret-menêsh? Even something as minor as slag would bring joy to the Temámir whose forefathers hailed from that mine.'

'It gladdens me to see that you have safely returned to us! I hope to never set foot in that accursed place myself. Did you find anything?
'Oh, look at that. These are shards of obsidian glass. It cannot be found on the surface of An Shêru. They may have come from trade, but it is more likely that it is from Lâkindar's mines. Though fragile, obsidian blades can be made to have a sharper edge than any steel is capable of. Some crafters also use it as you might use a jewel to decorate jewellery or weapons.
'Thank you for bringing these to us! I will see that families to whom it would mean the most receive these shards. We are honoured to have someone such as yourself helping us.'
'Your mission is to go to the Quelling-house and look for any vestiges of Lâkindar's happier past that can be brought to Jiret-menêsh.'

Standing outside the entrance to Starkhaven, your eye is drawn by the great light-house across the bridge to the east. Climbing the steps in front of the light could lead to a good vantage point from which you could observe the mighty fleet and the ship-yard at which it was constructed.

Engéru gazes out over the vast fleet before speaking again.
'Look for Isamó among the buildings with the chimneys to the east and south of here, friend. Please go.'
The woman watches you carefully.

The man has a furtive air as he looks you up and down.
'This is not your place, stranger. I have lived here for all the years of my life, as did my father before me. I am Engéru. Mine is a family of ship-builders; we have known nothing else. But you have climbed to this height with ruin in your eye. You wish to see the Song destroyed.
'No, do not deny it! I said I was a ship-builder, and that is true. But I am not a soldier. For decades we worked here in Starkhaven, and every new ship that was added to the fleet seemed a trophy for my family. I did not believe they would ever sail, but now a man of Umbar has come to Sûg Nidar, and he commands hundreds of Corsairs. The woman Nakási orders that new weapons be mounted upon the ships, weapons that breathe terrible blue fire. The Orcs have always been here, but they used to keep to themselves across the lake; now we are expected to work alongside them?
'My wife Isamó and I decided to leave Starkhaven, but I am being watched. I will be pressed into service upon one of the war galleys once I descend from this light. Will you meet with my wife and tell her I cannot join her? She must carry out our plan without me. I have eyes only for Isamó; my heart goes with her, even as we must part.
'See you the chimneys to the east and south of here? That is where we intended to meet. Go now and guide my wife from this place, I beg of you. I will decide how to descend from this light: swiftly, on my own terms, or slowly, pressed into service aboard the weapons I helped create. Either way, I want to know my Isamó was given a chance to escape. Thank you, my friend.'

The woman watches you silently, but when you give her Engéru's message she cries out.
'We must return and save him from the soldiers! He will not try to fight them, but you can!'
You shake your head and tell Isamó that it was her husband's only wish that she escape Starkhaven, and that she is to carry out the plan they devised. There will be little time before the soldiers find her, unless she leaves now.
'I cannot do this by myself,' she says, and you cannot tell if she refers to the escape plan or to the unknown days ahead, without Engéru.

She wipes her eyes.
'There is a sloping path that leads to a gate in the south-west reaches of Starkhaven. The gate is usually closed, but Engéru arranged that it would be left open for us on this day.
'Go ahead of me, to this south-western gate, and clear the way of enemies. If you will be my eyes, I will do the best I can to carry out my husband's wishes, though it pains me.'

Isamó stares at the open gate as if part of her wished it remained closed.
'My feet are heavy, stranger, but for Engéru I will let them carry me from Starkhaven. I thank you for showing me the way safely here, and I have only one thing more to ask of you.
'Think not ill of me or of my husband. Each of us were born into our families' work, and the construction of the fleet was all we ever knew. Of course ships are made for war! But when such a fleet sits idle for so many years, is it so strange to believe it might always remain unused? So it was for our families, and for Engéru, and for myself.
'Farewell, stranger. If you might somehow prevail against the Song, know that Engéru and Isamó celebrate with you.'

Isamó has resolved to be courageous, but her eyes are still full of tears.
'Go ahead of me, to this south-western gate, and clear the way of enemies. If you will be my eyes, I will do the best I can to carry out my husband's wishes, though it pains me.'

You have saved the residents of Adagím from the devastation that could have been caused by the opening of the Weirway Gate, at least for now. You will need to find some way to oppose the Song without endangering the peaceful Kintai of Sul Madásh, or any others who live in the lands through which Sûg Nidar would flood at Ghómbok Bóro's command.

Parchments spread upon a table outside the central keep of Starkhaven paint a disturbing picture:
\qYou tell Khâtiph I am not one to be intimidated. I know the one he follows is just one man, and Heirs of Castamir have been slain before; who is to say the son of Balakhôr could escape that fate? If they think to oppose me, remind them of this: I possess the authority to open the Weirway Gate.
'You may be too young to remember the last time it was opened. Count yourself fortunate! It stands behind the central keep of Starkhaven, and is accessed by a wooden walkway. The Weirway Gate holds back the flood, and when it is opened it allows water from Sûg Nidar to spill through the channel, flooding all of forested Adagím to the south. My predecessor used it to control the water level of the lake when the season of the rains seemed to have no end.
'If they move against me, I will open the gate. I have already given the command to one of my trusted men who lives by the plaza of the lion. If anything happens to me he will deliver the parchment with that command, and the Weirway Gate will open. None will shut it ever again, and Sûg Nidar will move to the south, leaving their ships stranded and the Kintai forest underwater!
'Know these are the words of Ghómbok Bóro, and he means every one!'

Judging from the location of the Weirway Gate, you determine that the words of Ghómbok Bóro are no bluff: Adagím lies to the south, and if the gate is opened the waters of Sûg Nidar will flow through the channel into the forest in a dangerous torrent. It seems clear to you that it was the previous opening of the Weirway Gate that caused so much of Adagím to become the treacherous swamp-land it is today.
Ghómbok Bóro entrusted a parchment containing the command to open the Weirway Gate to a trusted man living at \qthe plaza of the lion.\q He must live somewhere nearby, perhaps to the south-east. It is time to knock on some doors!
As you knock on the door, the man you seek returns home!

Still the ships of the Song remain where they are; still the fleet fails to approach your position. Your mind wanders, and you contemplate the island at the end of the bridge.
Once this land was covered with short grasses and small shrubs, and herdsmen drove their flocks of grazing animals beside the steep hill on which was built the citadel of Kasukhín. But that all changed with the coming of Ordâkh and the Din of Stone. The drowning of the plains caused the vast lake of Sûg Nidar, the Fearwater, to form, and the hilltop became an island.
Years later, the Ordâkhai constructed this bridge high above the old floor of the plains to provide access to the ruins. You wonder if they ever think of what the land must have been before their arrival, and decide they likely do not.
You should continue onward and <rgb=#00FF00>listen</rgb> for anything out of the ordinary once you have reached the end of the bridge.

'The trees here are covered in this rot. I can watch as they twist to the infection inside them.
'The foul fungus that grows on them is spreading quickly.
'It seems almost unbelievable how fast they are consumed by the blight. But that is why I know in my heart that Amûma herself is succumbing to it.'

'Look out over this land, ${PLAYER}.
'The ground is covered in a blanket of poison and fungus. Our waters turned murky and vile.'
Irsinith pauses a moment as tears form in her eyes.
'My duty... to this land.. and to Amûma. Is to protect them and hear their words. I have failed.
'This blight has taken so much from me and I feel myself sickly as a result. I feel powerless as I watch my lands wither and die.
'I am sorry. Give me but a moment to compose myself.'

'Well met, friend! The springtime flowers are so lovely, are they not? I'm a gardener by trade, and the happy blooms of spring fill my heart with so much joy. It's my misfortune, though, that as a gardener, I am often too busy in this season to truly enjoy it!
'I've heard of a place to the south that has a yearly celebration of the blooming of daffodils! That sounds like a reason for celebration if I have ever heard of one! But alas, there is too much work here to be done, and I cannot travel to see it myself. It's in a place called Clegur, away to the south, and east of old Cardolan.
'In fact, I have a map showing the way. You may have it if you think you might like to go. Someone should, it sounds wonderful!'

'Hullo traveller! I've also come from a far away place, I have. All the way from Maur Tulhau! Ye may be thinkin', \qShe must really love daffodils, hey?\q and while I do appreciate a nice flower, my true passion is pie!
'I make more pie than even a hobbit can eat herself, I do. So I've come to Clegur to sell some of my pie while there's a celebration on. It's not a business, mind ye, I'm just tryin' to fund more ingredients!
'But ach, it isn't goin' well. The folk here don't know who I am, and are proper suspicious of me, they are. I made these fliers to advertise my pie, but I can't leave my pie here to fend for itself while I hand them out.
'I'll make ye an offer, though. Hand out these fliers to visiting hobbits around the village, and when you're done, I'll give ye a slice for free.'
<rgb=#FF0000>NOTE: This quest will be removed from your quest log when the current festival ends.</rgb>
'Sales have picked up already, they have! Thank ye so much for the help. Here is the pie I promised ye, plus a little coin for yer pocket.'

Talk to Welduth Lhush

'Ach, another stranger tryin' to get their grubby hands on my bulbs? As I told the other one, I'm not in the business of sellin'.'
You ask her if there is anything she would trade. She sighs and thinks about it for a moment before answering.
'Well, to tell ya truly, yes. I've always envied Gloron's carrots. Proper carrots, they are! Large, but not woody, and they roast so sweet...'
She gazes off into the distance for a moment, thinking about carrots.
'Yes, if ye can get Gloron's secret to growin' such fine carrots, I'll give ye some of my daffodil bulbs. But good luck to ye! He holds his secrets close, he does. Ye'll likely have better luck pryin' a coney out of a wolf's jaws.'
'Another banner? Ach, here, take it. I never wanted the things in the first place.'

'Welduth covets my carrot secrets, does she?'
Gloron laughs.
'Why, she's never bothered to ask! If she did, she would find that I would tell her freely, I would. But since ye're doin' tradin', I'll make ye' a trade as well.
'I seen those tidy daffodil banners stuck about the village, and I find myself wonderin' why I didn't get one. It's not really fair, is it? I'm only sayin'.
'If ye get me one of those banners and stick it in over by the barn, I'll give ye the 'secret'.'
'Bless me, you got them! I'm as surprised as I am grateful! It's nothing personal, but I didn't expect you to succeed. Thank you!'

'There's lovely! That's a good banner, it is!
'Well, ye kept up yer end of the bargain, so here's my 'secret'. Everyone knows ye must have loose soil for 'em to get big, but most folks give 'em too much fertilizer. If ye fertilize 'em, yer carrot gets big and leafy up top, but the root stays small. Don't fertilize 'em at all, I say.
'I don't know about flowers, but most vegetables need to struggle a bit. It's the struggle that gives 'em proper character. A lot like people, eh?'

'The secret is to not fertilize them? Are ye pullin' my leg? That Gloron is a shrewd one, he is. Probably havin' a laugh, takin' me for a fool.
'Still, I believe ye that that's what he said, so ye did yer part. Ye can have the pot of bulbs to my left. Take it, and be gone with ye.'
Prized daffodil bulbs collected!
Naffa has asked you to talk to Welduth Lhush, a Stoor reputed to have the best daffodils and the festival, and ask her if you can trade for some bulbs.
Welduth agreed to trade some daffodil bulbs in exchange for Gloron Magimrud's secret to growing carrots. You should talk to Gloron Magimrud in the farming fields of Clegur.

'It's good to see a fellow traveller. I came here from Mossward, to the west of here. A travelling trader told me that this is where I should come to get the finest daffodil bulbs in Eriador. They are indeed quite beautiful, but these Stoors say they aren't for sale!
'Gardening is only a hobby for me, but I don't want to have come here for nothing. Welduth Lhush over there is said to have the finest daffodils, but I think I may have already earned her ire. Would you mind talking to her, and asking if she would sell or trade for some of her prized bulbs?'

For over a hundred years, the Kintai Elves have battled a mysterious blight, seemingly brought on by the Din of Stone. It has already consumed once-beautiful Adagím, and now threatens the rest of the Elven glades. An investigation by the Rangers Faeron and Rhadrog has tracked the source of the blight to The Folly of Nagakhêdi, but what dangers lurk inside the ancient and abandoned wonder?

Meet Faeron outside the Folly of Nagakhêdi

'We have won the day, ${PLAYER}! The Lady of Blight flees, and her 'grand prize' lies slain! Without the aid of you and your fellows, we would surely have met our ends in this pit. We owe you our lives, and the world owes you a debt of gratitude, yet again.
'Take this time to rest and celebrate, and leave tracking Lhaereth to us. She will surely seek out the source of the blight, but not until after she licks her wounds and schemes in secret. We will seek you out when she makes her next move.
'Until then, thank you again, ${PLAYER}.'

'Rhadrog and I have prepared, and are ready to investigate the ancient citadel. We know not what awaits us inside, but caution merits we enter with the strength to defeat the powerful foe we fear may be lurking inside.
'Gather your fellows and travel to the Folly of Nagakhêdi in Adagím. We will inform the Kintai of our intentions and meet you there.'

'This is it. A grand entrance to what was supposed to be a grand work of Men. We will see how near it came to completion in its interior. I am surprised Viznak did not want to accompany us, but then again, I believe he would rather avoid crossing paths with the Lady of Blight a third time....
'The Kintai were alarmed to hear we intended to enter, and made sure one of their own was among our number. The warden Irsinith volunteered to accompany us. I am glad for their expertise in fighting this particular corruption.
'When you and your fellows are ready, we will enter. Let us hope our search for the source of the blight is nearly at its end.'
