'Khemozêl will not be angry if we use this cave for only short time. Prêkh will speak with them if they return.
'If cave belongs to Stôr-weni-Kûl, maybe Kâl-maka-Hôi speak instead. That one listen... to her.'
Prêkh gurgles with laughter, but he is the only one.

'Why should we not avail ourselves of the comforts of this dwelling, at least until its master returns? The Têtikir we rescued are not yet strong enough to make the journey back to Kol Sákla, after all.
'Thrymm Red-beard would never complain about aching muscles and tired bones; he thinks only of others. You understand me, ${PLAYER}?'
Prêkh looks around the cave curiously but says nothing.
'Very good! We will light the fire and rest here for the night in relative comfort, and with as much safety as we might hope for in this fell vale.'
'Intruders are not welcome at home of Ghôl-buri-Prân!'

'You bring branches and meat for Ghôl? Good.
'But this is only beginning. If you want to know what Ghôl know, and to face evils only he can face, you need to earn his friendship... and you are not his friend yet.'

'It is clear to me the ways of the Khemozêl are not the ways of Rohan.
'For the crime of murder, Ghôl-buri-Prân would have paid with his life, and not become an exile. But he did not break the term of his banishment. We intruded upon his home, where he remains the master. If he opposes the evil powers within Nan Ogol, he is an ally, if not a friend. Is he not?'

'We need knowledge more than anything else, ${PLAYER}. If Ghôl-buri-Prân has lived within Nan Ogol for so many years, he may have learned much that might be of use to us.
'It is not our place to judge him for his crimes. His people have done that, and as far as I can see he has not broken the terms of his exile, despite the anger of Prêkh-weni-Pâsh.'

'All in Dhol Têg know story of Ghôl-buri-Prân, who slew his friend. Sad story, but elders spared his life and gave him exile. If he were to return, he would be slain too... but he never returned. When Kâl was told tale, story-tellers said he died in wilderness long ago.
'But he did not die. Somehow Ghôl-buri-Prân lived many years in fell vale. Maybe he has things to teach?'
Maurán stands protectively in front of Pharídi, carefully watching Ghôl-buri-Prân with distrustful eyes. He says nothing.
'He need prove nothing to you. No. You need prove yourself to him.'

'Ghôl live in fell vale for long time. He not miss those like Prêkh-weni-Pâsh, who think himself better than all others. Heart is not home-sick for Dhol Têg or for those who cast him out, but Ghôl not want Khemozêl slain by Were-wolves or crushed by Thyrsar. Evil doings are afoot in Nan Ogol, and he keeps watch against them. Now he is asker of questions.
'What brings so many strangers so deep into fell vale? What is it strangers hope to find?'
You tell the Khemozêl exile that you have come to the Wolven-lands of Draugardh to learn if forces of evil survived the fall of Sauron and might threaten Gondor and the other kingdoms that stood against the Dark Lord. He rubs his nose while he considers your explanation.
'You seek one called Mûlazar. Dark Lord left him to rule over Were-wolves, but they were not content to be ruled. Mûlazar is probably dead. Now wolves rule wolves, and all are loose in kennel that is Bâr Guruthos!'
Ghôl-buri-Prân gurgles with laughter much like you have heard from Prêkh-weni-Pâsh on your travels.
'You stay here for short time, but price will be steep: many chores to do. Defeat mire-maggots, collect kindling, bring skúthuk meat. That is just for start. Ghôl will let you live, but you must work to prove you are his friend. He will judge your Khem-khai.'

'Koi-mêdh-twar is no place for you.
'Speak now, or die.'

'Companions of Prêkh-weni-Pâsh go where they please! He has no need to explain anything to one such as you!
'Ghôl-buri-Prân was once well-loved. But that changed when he spill blood of Bhêg-buri-Chât. They were rivals in all things: in adventure, in skill, in love. But such contest ended with death of Bhêg-buri-Chât by treacherous hands of Ghôl-buri-Prân!
'He was exiled from Dhol Têg and told never to return. But now, even years later, he still wear dread-sheen necklace soaked with hatred for all to see!'
'Speak now, or die.'

'Ghôl was exiled from Dhol Têg, and he did not argue against it. But he did not come to Dhol Têg on this day. You came to Koi-mêdh-twar, Ghôl's own home among his troubles, with insult and with attack. If he turns you away and leaves you to Were-wolves, that would be justice. That would be fair. Why should he not do that?
'You did not come to fell vale of Nan Ogol without reason. You oppose Were-wolves? You think to slay Thyrsar? Why would Ghôl welcome you to his home, when you see him and spit upon the ground?
'He need prove nothing to you. No. You need prove yourself to him.'
Prêkh-weni-Pâsh stares at Ghôl-buri-Prân coldly, but says nothing more.

'Stôr is afraid he must insist. No spears for Ghôl-buri-Prân. We need them here.'
The Khemozêl looks as if he wants to say something else, but he holds his tongue.

'Ghôl-buri-Prân was right to speak of Khem-khai. Fell vale is too dangerous to heed objections of Stôr-weni-Kûl, so Kâl steal spears from Kûs Chela. This theft is for good of all, even if Stôr-weni-Kûl cannot see it.'
The young Khemozêl stares at you fiercely, her eyes blazing.
'Kâl will not wed one such as that. Her mind is made up now. She does not wish ill upon Stôr-weni-Kûl... but she will not listen to him either.
'Let us bring spears back to Ghôl-buri-Prân for good of all who live in Nan Ogol.'

'I underestimated you, ${PLAYER}. Kâl-maka-Hôi say Khemozêl of Kûs Chela not give spears, so she take them anyway. She understand need for action in dark times. She truly understand Khem-khai, after all.'
Ghôl-buri-Prân shuffles his feet and gazes out through the cave entrance.
'I have made decision. I will tell you secret.'
'Let us bring spears back to Ghôl-buri-Prân for good of all who live in Nan Ogol.'

'New friend returns with Kâl! Maybe she has answer now for Stôr?'
Deftly avoiding the question of marriage, you steer the conversation toward Ghôl-buri-Prân's request for spears from Kûs Chela to aid him in his efforts to keep watch on the movement of the Thyrsar titans. Stôr-weni-Kûl's face falls.
'Ghôl-buri-Prân is no friend of Kûs Chela. It is better to leave him alone. It is not safe to deal with such as him. Let him make his own spears! We need our own to fight enemies out of Bâr Guruthos. They are much nearer to Kûs Chela. Ghôl-buri-Prân live in cave far away! He not fear Gaurhoth or Draugrim like we do!
'Kâl must understand. She has apology from Stôr... but no spears for Ghôl-buri-Prân. That is impossible.'

'Ghôl-buri-Prân is no friend of Kûs Chela. It is better to leave him alone. It is not safe to deal with such as him. Let him make his own spears! We need our own to fight enemies out of Bâr Guruthos. They are much nearer to Kûs Chela. Ghôl-buri-Prân live in cave far away! He not fear Gaurhoth or Draugrim like we do!
'Kâl must understand. She has apology from Stôr... but no spears for Ghôl-buri-Prân. That is impossible.'
'Kâl will meet you outside Kûs Chela, ${PLAYER}. It will take time for her to find peace again!'

'Kâl does NOT understand!
'Ghôl-buri-Prân uses spears to track movements of Thyrsar! That is help to all who live in fell vale, including Khemozêl of Kûs Chela! He does not ask only for himself! He asks for all!
'Stôr-weni-Kûl not listen, just like before! Kâl ask him not to go to Nan Ogol, but he go anyway! He leave Kâl behind, and only stay if they wed! Why she not want that? She think maybe it is lack of courage, and seeks out dread-sheen to help, but it is not problem with Kâl. It is problem with Stôr-weni-Kûl!'
The young Khemozêl is more angry than you have ever seen her.
'Kâl meet you outside Kûs Chela, ${PLAYER}. It will take time for her to find peace again!'

'You travel with Khemozêl all the way from Dhol Têg and still not know Khem-khai? Prêkh-weni-Pâsh has not changed at all.
'Khem-khai means \qbend-trust.\q It means today you trust much, tomorrow you trust little. Day after maybe you trust more again. Fell vale is too dangerous to be one or the other all the time. Ghôl not like Khemozêl of Kûs Chela, and they not like him. But each works to help the other, and that is Khem-khai.
'It is Ghôl's habit to leave spears stuck in ground outside lairs of Thyrsar. Then if spears are broken, he learns movements of each Thyrs and can make plan. 'Ghôl hunting in forest not long after last and mightiest shaking from Mountain of Fire. He find blood spattering leaves, trail of droplets leading into thicket. He follow signs, and find Mûlazar dying.
'Ghôl knew him at once. What Khemozêl would not? But it seemed to Ghôl that cruel master of Draugardh tried to flee from Were-wolves he used to rule; now they rule, and savage him with teeth and claws as he escape. Not quick enough, and not for good! Now Ghôl-buri-Prân is his jailor. Ghôl-buri-Prân decide what to do with him.'

'These lands were given to ME, not to those ungrateful pups! I earned their hatred over many years, it is true, but is that not always how it lies with the governed? How many examples of disobedience and failure from them must my Master have stomached? For me once only would have sufficed, but chance after chance my Master gave to them!
'The wolves waited for their moment. That much is clear to me now. When I returned to Bâr Guruthos on that day of confusion when my Master fell, they attacked without warning. I fought them off with sword and spell, but Thothrach seized me in his jaws and shook me, trying to break my back. It was his one chance to slay me, but he failed as he faileth at all things! He will carry the scar I gave him until he dies.
'I managed to reach Nîlugru and he took to the air, but he was wounded as I was, and I fell from his back somewhere over the vale. I knew nothing else until I awoke a prisoner, not of the wolves but of this cursed jailor. He will pay for this as will Thothrach.'

'Mûlazar was once ruler of Draugardh, but no more. When Gaurhoth turn upon him, he flee from fortress of Bâr Guruthos and almost escape being rended by their jaws. Almost. He make it into woods, but he not unwounded. Venom already working upon him.

'None remain to oppose us, my warriors! Search the tower!'

'That one was a young Gaurhoth warrior named Narchraw, a firebrand from the days of his youth in the pits of Mordath under Barad-dûr. He spoke out against me and the other Gúrzyul, against the nine Nazgûl, and against Sauron the Master of all. Before long he had acquired a following large enough to challenge Iurithil, the Lord of Beasts who ruled the Gaurhoth at that time.
'Iurithil lost his throat and his life in the battle that followed, and Narchraw gained the jewelled torc of the Lord of Beasts. He was now Skárashakh and ruled from Bâr Guruthos, a mighty keep in Nan Ogol. He continued to speak, and the wolves continued to listen.'

'Narchraw argued there was no better time to rise up and search Barad-dûr for the secrets that would restore the lost greatness of the Gaurhoth. The Ringwraiths ruled in Mordor, but their strength was abated in the absence of Sauron, and even the powerful Gúrzyul lacked His darkness to fire them. Narchraw believed they might seize the Nine Rings... possibly even the One! And then they would be free of the dominion of Sauron.
'He was a fool. Even then I knew of it. Long had I suspected treachery, and I commanded a host of Orcs and Men to meet the Were-wolves in battle. This would come to be known as the Were-wolves' War, the Wolf-strife, and it would have lasting effect upon the land of Mordor and the domain of Sauron.
'Accompanied by one of the Nazgûl, my host of Orcs and Men engaged the wolves in battle upon the fields of Parth Rhavas.'

'It was Borangos the Horror who betrayed us on that day. Leading a host of dark spirits from his caverns in Nargroth, he fell upon my host with terrible fire, leaving us open to attack from Narchraw's wolves. Orcs and Men scattered before that terrible onslaught, and even the mighty Nazgûl perished. Without my Master to restore him, the wraith languished, powerless to return; nine became eight, and the wolves saw the path to their victory.
'With most of my soldiers slain, I was forced to flee before the combined might of Borangos and Narchraw.'

'The forging of the Rings of Power in Eregion heralded the end of Sauron's reliance upon the Were-wolves. They were among the few in Mordor to whom He revealed that design in those early days, and they greatly desired the rings for their own. It was never His intention to bestow the rings upon the Gaurhoth, but He allowed them to believe it while it suited His purposes. So 'twas that He went alone into Orodruin, toiling for days to shape the One Ring, a master ring to rule all the others.
'When at last He emerged from the mountain, the Gaurhoth sensed the terrible power that had been harnessed, and they coveted it.'

'Sauron commanded His servants to seek an alloy with which He might forge mighty weapons, the better to channel the power of the One Ring. The Gaurhoth found early success with the green crystal delothlín, mined from the forested vale where they dwelt, but it proved harmful even to those who bore it; many wolves perished attempting to refine it. Their incompetence threatened to undermine my Master's plans, and they were punished for this failure and others. But at last Sauron achieved His desire, for the metal-workers of Udûn devised a mix of materials that gave rise to Morgul-steel.
'With the use of the Morgul-steel, Sauron could now fashion stronger and more loyal servants than the Were-wolves had ever proved. He called us to Him, and gave to us a mighty gift he gave to few others.'

'The Gaurhoth were so low in my Master's esteem at this time they knew nothing of His plans. When they learned He had been captured by the King of Númenor and brought to that island kingdom in chains, they despaired, for their power and their very lives depended upon the spirits on which they fed, and it was only His power that provided them.
'They knew not that Sauron's surrender was only the first step in His scheme to see that nation destroyed. He hid the One Ring in some secret place unknown even to His loyal Gúrzyul, and left the Nine Nazgûl to rule Mordor during His absence.'

'What power of thine armies was it brought my Master low? What weapon wielded the upstart king against the Mountain of Fire? A mighty troll-host marched at my command toward the Black Gate when, with terrible noise and tumult, the southern slope of Orodruin sundered itself. My Olog-hai were swallowed in the creation of that lake of flame; I took to wing only just in time.'
You tell Mûlazar that it was no weapon of Gondor that undid Sauron's realm; rather it was the return of his greatest weapon to the fire where it was made, and its destruction brought about the final defeat of the Dark Lord and his plans. Mûlazar shifts his weight, adjusting the set of his chains while he considers what you have told him.
'So the Ruling Ring is gone, and the Nazgûl with it? 'Tis no surprise the Gaurhoth fell upon me at my return to Bâr Guruthos; always have they despised their betters, and waited only for such a chance.'

'I will answer now a question of thine. What dost thou desire to know?'
You ask Mûlazar to tell you why the Were-wolves of Draugardh did not join in Sauron's war, and for what purpose they were held in reserve. He sneers.
'Thy question wilt require a longer answer than the one thou hast given me, for the record of the Were-wolves' disobedience is long and their punishment deserved. Attend thou then to me!'

'My Master's pleasure at the destruction of Númenor turned to anger when he saw what Narchraw had done to his realm. Having recovered the Ruling Ring from its hiding-place, he dominated the minds of the Gaurhoth and exiled them back to Draugardh, starving them of the spirits they craved and permanently diminishing their might.
'Narchraw himself was not permitted to leave the tower. With foul magic he was made into a wraith-like being and imprisoned, kept on the very border of life and death, driven mad by the tortures of Sauron and the memory of what might have been. So broken was the mind of Narchraw that my Master saw fit to loose him at times upon his enemies, but on every occasion the former Skárashakh slinked back to his cell, a pitiful shadow of his former self. 'Twas a suitable punishment.
'Despite aiding the wolves in their rebellion, the return of Borangos to my Master's service caused him to be spared for his part in the Strife. The Dark Lord permitted him to return to Nargroth, but he was banned from ever leaving it save at my Master's command.'
Without warning, Mûlazar shudders as a spasm wracks his body. When he has recovered, you point out that he has not spoken of his own role following the Wolf-strife. He bares his teeth at you in a grim smile.
'Master of Wolves was I named, ${PLAYER}, and every Skárashakh of the Gaurhoth since that day hath been subservient to me. Draugardh is my land, and once I have been restored to my station I will remind them who is their Lord.'

'\qWe should not let them report back to Bâr Guruthos,\q Thrymm whispered to us. \qI am certain they beheld the cave mouth. They will return in greater numbers, and discover Mûlazar within!\q
'\qI wish we could wait for ${PLAYER} to join us,\q I told him, but in that I now see my error.
'\qIs the Hero of Wildermore held in such little regard that he cannot stand against such a small band of Wolven-kin without the aid of another?\q Thrymm answered me, and he rushed away in the direction they had gone. Harthalín and I pursued him, but we learned all too late the small hunting-party had splintered off a larger force. Thrymm had become snared between the smaller force and the larger, and even then he might have won out against them... but for the arrival of a creature out of nightmare.
'It was a terrible misshapen thing, with jointed legs like a spider but grown to tremendous size. It emerged from among the trees and bowled into Thrymm, knocking him senseless to the ground and keeping us from getting near. By the time we could at last approach, some of the Wolven-kin had been slain by the creature and she dined upon their bodies; the others had lifted Thrymm's insensate body and carried him beyond our reach.'

'The terrible misshapen creature was a Thyrs, it can have been nothing else. While we sought to circle around its disgusting banquet and approach Thrymm without being seen, I heard the Draugrim repeating one word, over and over. \qYáranissë! Yáranissë!\q they exulted. That must have been the creature's name.
'But we cannot concern ourselves with Yáranissë now. We must find some way of recovering our lost companion, ${PLAYER}. If they have not already brought him behind the walls of Bâr Guruthos... by tonight they will.'

'Much has happened since then, has it not?
'But let us not delay. Our friends should be waiting for us ahead. Let us join them!'

'I speak in jest, ${PLAYER}. I know it is not fair to say such a thing!
'To learn of an enemy's presence is of value to us, for only then can we adequately prepare to oppose him. But better still is to make the acquaintance of a new friend!
'I am pleased to have met these Khemozêl! I understand they drew some attention outside, for people of the city have not seen visitors such as Prêkh-weni-Pâsh and Kâl-maka-Hôi before now. I know they will be made welcome.'

'I cannot remember anything that transpired in the dungeons below Bâr Guruthos, ${PLAYER}... it is only through the reporting of Orthonn that I know of these events, and they feel as if they happened to someone else. But there is something else that troubles me, beside even this.
'It is bad enough to think I was overcome by a fleeting madness, and the words I spoke there were untrue. But it is worse by far in this case: what if my crazed words in the dungeons were words of truth? What is it that lies beneath Guruthos? What are the verses of victory?
'And why do they fill me with a sensation of fear beyond any I have ever felt in all of my days?'

'Thank you again for your aid and for your friendship, ${PLAYER}. No matter the evils we must face, I believe we possess the strength to overcome them if we stand together.'

'Bodhoi mulom, stranger. You are welcome in our lands so long as you make no disturbance and harm no herd.
'Kol Sákla is a difficult land, but she is ours, at least for now. These are not our ancestral homelands, but they are open, and our herds find enough for sustenance. That is all we require.
'We do not have much, but what we do have we share with those we find worthy. You should speak with Niyoz to learn more.'

'Bodhoi mulom. May your herd find their way home.
'Kol Sákla is where we have made our home, though for many our hearts lie elsewhere. But those lands are closed to us now, and we, like our cattle, have to press on to new pastures.
'If you help the Têtikir within Parth Rhavas, we will see it, and reward you for it. We are not a trusting people, ${PLAYER}. We have seen too much bloodshed to trust easily. But for those who earn it, we are fiercely loyal. Prove to us you bring goodwill and loyalty to the Têtikir, and we will reward you handsomely for it.'

'We are happy to have you in Kol Sákla, as long as your aims are peaceful and your weapons stay sheathed.
'We Têtikir trust what we see, and the actions you take. Prove loyal to the Têtikir, and you will scarcely find a more welcome place than Kol Sákla. Prove yourself an enemy to the Têtikir, and you will find something else entirely.'

'Mae govannen, mellon-in-edhil. A star shines upon the hour of our meeting, ${PLAYER}. I would offer you food and drink, but our food is plain and our drink is but water. A guest of your reputation deserves much better fare than my company and I can offer.
'I am Haereldir, and I am pleased our paths have crossed. On this day I serve Queen Arwen Undómiel, who spoke to me of you. I have heard of your many deeds, and was told should we meet, I must do my best to enlist your aid.
'My company and I are on a quest to survey this land called Heledhris and determine if there are evils here that could threaten the current relative peace. It had been separated from Gorgoroth by the Mithram Spur, but the recent blast of Amon Amarth, ignited by Sauron's defeat, has now opened a rift that allows passage. But that you must already know, as you surely passed though Imrad Angos to get here!
'Alas, we have already encountered a savage folk in this land. Wild with rage, they seem to blindly attack anything that lives, like beasts with a mind-sickness. If you were to travel west of our camp, you will find a horde of them occupying what looks like an abandoned pit-mine.
'If you have the opportunity to spy upon them, I should quite like to know what they are doing, and if they serve anything other than their thirst for blood.'

'Have we met? You have a familiar look about you. Were you by any chance in Osgiliath?'
The Ranger shakes head and sighs.
'It matters not. This land of Draugardh fills me with an unease I cannot disregard. It is said to be the home of Were-wolves, skin-changers possessed by fell spirits. Tales told to keep children from wandering the forests alone, I always thought. I'm beginning to have my doubts. Those Khûrz-hai are mad, but could they be the source of such tales? It seems unlikely. Alas, all we can do is prepare and remain wary.
'It would make me feel better about resting in this place if someone were to patrol the perimeter. We have guards posted in the ravine, but something inside me fears that we are surrounded by wolves. If you are the accomplished warrior that Haereldir says you are, would you mind stepping outside the camp and defeating any wolves you find lurking there?'

'From the sounds of battle coming from around the camp, it would seem that your reputation is well-earned. Thank you for safe-guarding the camp. I would be glad for our ever-cautious Ranger to soon sleep.'

'How fares Mindaug? Worry not, we will have him on his feet soon, with the help of the tulus-bark tea.'

'I spotted a tree I am familiar with, tulus, across the river. I think Mindaug might improve with tulus-bark tea that would reduce his pain and swelling. Were you to collect some tulus-bark, I would be able to make a tea that might speed his recovery.'

'So this is my saviour, eh?
'Aye, you look quite the hero. Thank you, friend, for pulling me out of that rat-infested hole.
'I am called Mindaug the Seeker, and were it not for you, I would be Mindaug the Dead! I am a prospector and I foolishly came from Gorgoroth to Heledhris on my own, following old tales of great gems to be found here. They were said to be the source of a great power. I thought that were I able to lead my king, Váskmun Greytooth, to such a thing, we could use this power to reforge our new kingdom.
'But did you see them? The gems are real, all right, but their power... it is one you want. I do not wish to speak of it, but if you come across a green gem of Heledhris, delothlín, it is called, do not touch it!'
The Stout-axe looks disturbed and shakes his head.
'They are wicked things, and will be of no help to anyone aside from the servants of evil. Leave them be.'
Mindaug looks pained, so you leave him to rest.

'I overheard your conversation with Bhôd-buri-Mêj. I am quite familiar with the Were-wolves, though I hoped them to be creatures lost to time, as I have not heard tidings of them in what has surely been thousands of years now.
'I first recall battling these servants of Morgoth in Doriath. Later, when we first formed the Glánnothrim in Lindon, Lord Celeborn led us on a great hunt that lasted many years, striving to wipe clean Morgoth's filth from Middle-earth, Gaurhoth among their number.
'These Draugrim do not sound like the Gaurhoth of old, though. They were more akin to Wargs, but stronger, larger, and more cunning.
'Given its name, we knew it was possible that Draugardh yet harboured some remaining number of the wolven-kin, but how many are there, and do they pose a threat to the Free Folk? These are the questions we came to answer.'

The guard takes some time to think before he answers your question about what his greatest fears are.
'Starvation, fire, falling rock, angry mountains... all big dangers. Fear? You know fear when you know Kwôhu.
'Kwôhu hunt us like rabbits. Kills many.'
The stocky man looks more sad than fearful for a moment, before continuing.
'You are a warrior? Can you kill Kwôhu? They live not far to the east, in Daerhabar. The less Kwôhu, the better.'
'Kwôhu? I have never heard of such a thing. Is this an individual, a people, or a sort of beast? Ask Bhôd-buri-Mêj, surely he can explain.'

'Kwôhu, the cur-folk. They are... both a people and a beast. The Elves called them Draugrim.
'In the time before my grandfather, we Khemozêl were secret, hidden. Evil Men and Orcs come and go, build things, fight each other... never knowing we were here. Then comes the Eye. Mountains stream forth liquid fire, ash rains down from the sky, and rocks are torn open. Many things die. Plants, animals, and Khemozêl.
'The rocks torn open held green gems that the evil ones like. Then great wolf-men, the Kwôhu come here, looking for them. They find them, and also find the Khemozêl.'
He casts his eyes to the ground momentarily, instead of looking at you.
'They hunt us like prey. Sometimes... to eat. Other times, for no reason at all. Even after all this, Khemozêl people were finding strength again. Then in the springtime, the mountains awoke once more. The Eye is gone, but we struggle to keep living.
'The more Draugrim that die, the more Khemozêl can live. Go to Daerhabar and defeat Draugrim, and you will have the thanks of all Khemozêl.'

'So the tales are true, Were-wolves do stalk these lands. But they are not skin changers?
'It heartens me to hear that you defeated some of them. They are a servant of evil like any other, and can be destroyed like any other.
'You should tell Haereldir of your findings.'

'${PLAYER}, I am glad to see you again! What do you think of these Khemozêl? I appreciate the spirit of their hospitality, but the reality of it is awful. Their meat has no flavour, they drink naught but water, and there is not a proper bed in sight. Perhaps in the last few months I have become too accustomed to comfort, but even in Barad-dûr we were given beds.
'I feel ashamed to do so, but I must ask another favour of you. I began my journey into Draugardh with a pack of supplies and personal effects that I had with me when I ventured into Balthlún, the mine you rescued me from.
'Though the items in my pack have no value to anyone other than myself, I badly want them back. Without my gear, I feel helpless, having to rely on others for all things. Only I cannot muster the courage to return to that place.
'You have been there before, and clearly fared better than I. Would you return and search for my pack?'

'Reunited at last! I am relieved to see that it is in one piece. I was worried those foul beasts would have torn it up and scattered its contents.
'I haven't decided what I should do next, but having my things gives me more options than I had without it. I cannot thank you enough, ${PLAYER}.'

'Thank you for providing Mindaug with what he needed. When you have spent most of your life as a prisoner and have finally found your freedom, it is understandable that the need for self-determination would be potent.
'I will speak to him what he would like to do next, and will make it clear that the decision is his, and his alone, to make.'

'${PLAYER}, it is good to see you! I knew with the widening of the Shard-rift you would once again find your way to Mordor.'
'Follow the valley path in Heledhris east and down the slopes to the plains of Parth Rhavas. There you will find Thurindol and his encampment.'

'Upon my journey from Minas Tirith, my companions and I passed through the Morgul Vale. There we were met by Rangers of Ithilien and heroes of Gondor alike. As we exchanged tales, a small party of allies gathered, to both guide us and explore the unknown reaches of Draugardh. Through the valley of Lhingris we climbed, and across the ash-choked plains of Talath Úrui we marched. The path to the Shard-rift was finally made known to us when we reached the mountains of Agarnaith.
'This group of allies is known to you, ${PLAYER}. Their leader, Thurindol of the Rangers of Ithilien, spoke many times of your bravery! This small band of allies has scouted ahead of us. Thurindol assured me they would set up an encampment, not far from here, on the western edge of the Lothfold. You should seek out Thurindol and tell him what we have learned from our time in Heledhris.
'You have been a most helpful company through the Shard-rift of Heledhris. For a moment, we must part ways, as I await my orders.'

'I shall provide you with information that will prevent the village of Kol Sákla from being raided. There are three watch-towers that dot the eastern cliffs of Parth Rhavas. One of the towers hides a Khashkhilar raiding party. Defeat the raiding party and save the village. It is that simple.'

'Have we reached an agreement? The Summer Crow will tolerate our pact.
'Seek out the Khûrz-hai and free my people. Seek out the Draugrim and sow the seeds of discord. Seek out Tupanyel Bêk, within the audience hall, deep inside the ruins of Rhuvendír, and halt the fool's plans. This I ask of you.'

'A moment of your time is all I require. You must listen well.
'I both admire you and despise you. Yet, fine allies we would make. I am Yazluk-garga, the Summer Crow.
'I have seen you from afar, destroying my people. For that, we are enemies. I have seen your strength, unmatched. For that you will assist these brittle bones and a sharp mind of the Summer Crow. I have seen many leaders of the Khashkhilar rise and fall. All have followed the Wolf-way, as they should. All that is, but Tupanyel Bêk. He leads the Khashkhilar astray, to a certain death that he does not see. The Summer Crow sees it all too well. Tupanyel Bêk seeks power. To obtain that power, he is sacrificing more of us to the Draugrim, to be shaped into Khûrz-hai. If he is not stopped, the Khashkhilar will soon be no more.
'I will give you the information you need to defeat Tupanyel Bêk. He meets with the Draugrim in Rhuvendír as we speak. In return, all I ask is that you spare those who truly follow the Wolf-way. The Summer Crow has spoken.'

'This Tupanyel Bêk is sacrificing his own to be shaped into Khûrz-hai? Zapharo has told me of the Khûrz-hai.
'They are those purposely afflicted with Wolf-sickness from the venom of the Gaurhoth. They are heedless, ferocious trackers and fighters used like hounds by the Were-wolves with no regard for their lives.'

'The Draugrim have occupied Rhuvendír? Zapharo has told me of the Draugrim.
'These lesser Were-wolves do not have the strength of the Gaurhoth. They have lost that strength by adding the blood of Men to their lines. The Gaurhoth rule over them with disdain.'

'Could it be possible the Gaurhoth oversee the Draugrim in Rhuvendír? Zapharo has told me of the Gaurhoth.
'They are Were-wolves of old, bred through dark sorcery. It is said they have lived in Mordor since the First Age, and can bend the will of most any beast.'
'It is as Yazluk-garga said it would be. I hear many voices arguing on the other side of this door.'

'I am certain that Yazluk-garga cannot be trusted. However, there are times when enemies find a common goal. Perhaps this is one of those times. I have no hatred of the Khashkhilar. I only wish for them to leave the Têtikir be. Yazluk-garga also wishes for the bloodshed to be over. I believe we should accept the Summer Crow's offer, ${PLAYER}. We will need to investigate Rhuvendír either way.
'If the Draugrim and Khashkhilar work together in Rhuvendír, we must stop them from gathering strength in Parth Rhavas. I see no other way, if I am to protect the Têtikir in these lands.'

'Do you see the old woman on the bridge as well, or are my eyes playing tricks? You see her too. That is good! She seems to be beckoning you to meet with her.'

'When you have finished here in Parth Rhavas, I will meet you at Urotar in Nan Ogol.'

'While you have earned my trust, you have not earned the trust of my clan, the Yokhut-oba. They will be suspicious of you. That I am certain. However, there is one who will believe us. My plans in Parth Rhavas were her idea, after all.
'I have spoken to my sister, Tasila. I have told her of your bravery and trials in Parth Rhavas. She will trust you, for our bond is strong. She will speak with you now.'
'You are the cunning warrior of which Arzheki speaks so highly? Your skills will be put to the test soon enough. Tell me, what do you really know about the Gaurhoth?'

'I must return to my family at once. They are in dire need of assistance. There are no allies in Nan Ogol, only ghastly horrors!
'The land of Nan Ogol is our home. We must try to halt the horror there, for no one else will. We will not flee. We have our reasons and those reasons will be shown to you in time.
'I went to Parth Rhavas on a mission to search for assistance. When you passed my test, I knew you would be able to assist the efforts of my family.
'With your aid, as well as our Têtikir and Sûhalar allies, my family might survive.'

'Have you returned with meat for the journey? We will need it.
'I hope my family will welcome you, for you have helped me greatly with my tasks. The joy of returning will be short, however. You, and all of Parth Rhavas, are ill prepared for what horrors lie ahead.'

'You have done much to lift our spirits, ${PLAYER}. When we first settled upon Parth Rhavas, I thought this was the end of the Sûhalar. The pain, the death, the endless wars, had all taken its toll. We could not return home, so we came to Draugardh to slowly fade away.
'Now I see a new beginning. The Têtikir prove to be a strong ally! They have even offered us shelter at Obalang, once the village is rebuilt. In return, I will work to bring the rest of the Sûhalar under my banner. It may be a fool's errand, but I must try. They are my brethren, after all!'

'Are you prepared to complete your task, wanderer? I would very much like to see my family and report to them what has transpired in Parth Rhavas.
'You must understand that they are my blood. My family and I have denounced the Khashkhilar way for our own way. There are no allies for my family in Nan Ogol, yet we must stay there. We have been marked for our decision.'

'You are to guide Arzheki back to her family? I am glad that you are making good on your word, ${PLAYER}. Sumbula of Kol Sákla will be pleased. We know not of Arzheki and her family, but I hope this splinter group of Khashkhilar will be an important ally of the Têtikir. I thank you again for your efforts in helping my people.'

'This is where we must part ways, ${PLAYER}. My orders are to keep the road through Parth Rhavas clear. You alone must guide Arzheki to her destination.
'I assure you there will be enough adventure for both of us. My companions and I feel it is important that we investigate the fog below the southern cliffs. I find the clouds beneath Bôk Jekir and Gáyadali unsettling. It reminds me of Thuringwath. I may call upon you again, my friend. Fare well on your travels.'

'Bhôd-buri-Mêj's anger is righteous, though his desire for revenge will likely not do him any favours. We will continue to help the Khemozêl as we are able. Celondor remains at Dhol Têg to help them defend the village. His knowledge and experience as a guardian of Minas Tirith may prove valuable to the people there.
'Speaking of defences, this camp is well positioned, but we must remain wary. Meldir has noted that across the river to the south lurks some terrible kind of disfigured Orcs. They have been transformed by long exposure to delothlín crystals, according to Bhôd-buri-Mêj.
'These you should probably see for yourself. It is an uncomfortably short distance to them, in a place called Ukhroz. Does the crystal give them more power, or does it just make them more unpleasant to look at? You should travel there and defeat some, so you may compare notes with Meldir regarding their nature.'

'What took you so long to get here? That is a joke. We only just arrived.
'${PLAYER}, what do think of the Draugrim?'
The small but burly man looks more tired than you remember seeing him before.
'I am not sure the Khemozêl will survive many more years. Many of us are now gone. My father and my sister were both taken by Draugrim. I can still hear their screams of pain when I close my eyes. It is not a good way to die.'
You can see a subtle shift in his eyes as his pain turns into anger.
'If I had great size and strength, I would hunt them. They would all fear to close their eyes, lest Bhôd-buri-Mêj come with his great spear, wet with the blood of wolves. We would see how they like wondering how long their people will continue to exist.'
Bhôd's anger continues to smolder, but he will say no more.

'Tell me, ${PLAYER}, what did you make of the Orcs at Ukhroz?'
You tell Meldir that they died just like any Orc, and the Ranger laughs.
'Outstanding. That is what matters most, eh? Well done, my friend.'

'Khel Wêro was a stone fortress built by Draugrim, I think? It was deserted long ago, and now Khemozêl watch the valley from here. Below is the Greywall Gate. It goes to Parth Rhavas, where there are both beasts and Men. We watch for new dangers coming in, that we may hide from them.'
'${PLAYER}, you have good timing, my friend. I believe a messenger of some kind just returned. We should quietly observe, and if we are lucky, we may learn something.'
'Let us settle in and quietly keep watch on them. I don't think the wait will be long.'

'Welcome to Khel Wêro, ${PLAYER}. I expected more of a village here, or perhaps something fortified, but this appears to be merely a look-out post.
'Meldir spoke of what you overheard at Mal Rakhúrz. It surprises me that the Wargs are not allies with the Were-wolves, as they are kin, but perhaps it should not. From what I have seen thus far, these Draugrim are tame lap-hounds compared to the great foes we faced in the First Age, while the Wargs are only slightly diminished. As the power of the Were-wolves decreases, it only makes sense that their influence in Mordor would as well.
'We have yet to assess the perils that we may face at Khel Wêro. Bhôd-buri-Mêj appears to be very familiar with this place, though. Perhaps you should speak to him about how the Khemozêl fare here.'

'You are a friend of the Elf? He says his friends will help Khemozêl. I like him. You may stay at Khel Wêro as long as you like, if you help.
'Many things nearby want to kill Khemozêl. Wargs, wolves, grims, ormings, and giant Olog-hai.'
You ask him what ormings are, and the stout warrior shrugs.
'They fly.'
That appears to be all he has to say about that.

'I have not heard of these 'ormings' before either, though I do have a theory on their origin. They seem to be clustered in an area just to the south of here. If you went there and collected some samples from their corpses, I may be able to weigh the soundness of my suspicion.'

'Ah. Yes, all right, let's take a look at these.'
Haereldir closely examines the gory collection of body parts you have presented to him.
'I cannot say for certain, but I find nothing that would prove my theory incorrect. It was said that the fell beasts began as some kind of corrupted drake, and were moulded by evil hands into the form that would become the flying steeds of the Nine.
'I believe it to be quite possible, maybe even likely, that Min-rangenel, where you collected these, is the rookery where the fell beasts were bred. From what we have seen with the Dread-orcs, delothlín has the power to mutate the body, as well as the mind.
'The green crystal was present on the surface of that mountain, was it not? In all other places we have seen in Heledhris, the dread-sheen has been heavily mined. In this singular place it was left alone. There would need to be a well-founded reason to leave a material so desired by our enemies untouched.'
Haereldir sniffs the skin of one of your samples, and the noble, ageless Elf, witness to the Two Trees, hero of the First Age, looks like he is trying not to cast his lunch upon the ground.
'I will... dispose of these. You have done quite enough in collecting them. I thank you for the pains you took. This was very informative.'

'Tell me, ${PLAYER}, do you have children? The joy of parenthood also brings the unending fear of them getting hurt.
'My daughter, Pêk-dhug-Bhôd, has gone to Nan Ogol, taking other Khemozêl with her. It is my great shame that she is not doing what Mêj-dhug-Mêj says we should do. The Clan-mother says we need to remain hidden as much as we can, to survive. It is the Khemozêl way, and it has always worked. When there is a foe you cannot defeat, you run. You hide. That is how you live.
'Pêk is brave. And foolhardy. When the Eye went away, and the mountains awoke, Pêk says Nan Ogol was our land once, and should be again. She says the evil is now weak, and we must take back the green lands of Nan Ogol while we can.
'I wish in my heart that she was right. A part of me wanted to join her. Yes, it would be a better life. But, ${PLAYER}, I fear she will die there.'
The normally stoic man begins to tear up.
'She may be dead already. There is no way to know.
'${PLAYER}, if you one day find yourself in Nan Ogol, please find Pêk-dhug-Bhôd. I would go, but I have a duty. I am to be Clan-father after Mêj-dhug-Mêj, who is very old. I will not leave the Khemozêl without a leader, even if Pêk leaves me without a daughter.'

'Thank you, ${PLAYER}, for the aid you have given to the Khemozêl, in addition to all you have done for myself and the other scouts.
'Navaer, mellon nín. Until our next meeting.'
Quests completed for the Khemozêl (${CURRENT}/${MAX})
Haereldir urged you to talk to Bhôd-buri-Mêj about the plight of the Khemozêl before you leave Khel Wêro for Parth Rhavas.

'I've sent a messenger back to Minas Tirith outlining what we have learned about Draugardh thus far. My company and I will remain here at Khel Wêro while we await a response, though I did recommend that we should continue to investigate the Were-wolves. We don't know who, or what, the Skárashakh is, the sender of the message to the Draugrim.
'Skárashakh is a title, meaning 'beast-lord' in the Black Speech. A fitting title for one commanding Were-wolves, but who are they, and what is their goal? I think it would be unwise to leave these questions unanswered.
'We will stay here awhile, but do not let our expedition delay your own journey. I would ask, though, before you venture forth into Parth Rhavas, that you do what you can to help the Khemozêl, if you have not already done so. They have done well for a people unused to adapting to change, but the presence of the Draugrim may be one change they cannot endure without aid.

Shêi-dhug-Phîn happily takes the dripping honeycomb from you and pops it into her mouth. As she chews, you begin to worry that maybe she tricked you into bringing her a treat.
She gestures for you to hold out your hand, and when you do, she spits a lump of wax directly into it. Surprised by this turn of events, you reflexively pull your hand back, the wax falling to the ground.
You ask the carver for a block of wood. At first, the Khemozêl woman seems to not understand you but then hands you a block of wood that hasn't dried out.

'Ah yes, this is perfect, thank you.
'I'm quite embarrassed to ask you to go back, but I realized that I will also need some beeswax. It is the only other thing I need, I swear it.'

You ask the carver if she has any beeswax you could use. The Khemozêl woman shakes her head and shows you an empty clay jar. Seeing your disappointment, she makes a buzzing sound and points to the west.

You hand the wax to Celonor and decide not to elaborate on its origins.
'Wonderful! I hope it wasn't too much trouble. You have perfect timing, my friend, I just finished carving this fine spoon!
'I spent many long nights as a guard on the walls. I needed something to keep me occupied to not be tempted by sleep, so I took up spoon carving. I think all the men in my company got a spoon from me at some point. I certainly don't need all these spoons!'
He rubs the wax into the carved spoon, causing the grain pattern of the wood to become more visible and giving it a lustrous shine.
'That is a very good wax!' he says, setting the spoon down and looking at it.
'You don't think it's foolish, do you? It is. I won't give it to him. A hero deserves something better than a silly spoon. I don't wish to talk to him anyway. Do with the spoon what you will.'

'What is this? Oh, a lovely carved spoon! This is quite well-done. Fir can be difficult because the grain often changes direction.'
You tell him Celonor made it for him, in an effort to lift his spirits and Haereldir laughs in a friendly way.
'He did, did he? Well, he is a talented artist, and I daresay it has improved my mood! He has my thanks. I shall take good care of it.'
Celonor has has requested you ask one of the Khemozêl crafters in Dhol Têg for some green wood, suitable for carving.
You have gotten a block of carving wood from a Khemozêl crafter, as Celonor requested. You should bring it to him atop the hill in Dhol Têg.

'${PLAYER}, I am worried that my request for a tale has brought down Haereldir's mood. The stirring of memories seems to have caused him some amount of pain. Had I known my request would have such effect, I would not have made it. Or... asked you to make it, rather.
'You have spent more time in the company of Elves than I have. Is there something I can do to revive his spirit? A gift, perhaps? What do Elves like?'
You tell Celonor that Elves like many of the same things everyone does. Poetry and song, good wine, fine foods, and natural beauty. You tell him that the Noldor in particular are known for an appreciation of quality craftsmanship.
'Well, I am no poet, nor a good cook, but you have given me an idea. Would you ask our hosts for a piece of green wood, suitable for carving?'

'So, ${PLAYER}, how do my fighting skills compare? Am I not the equal of our companions?'
You tell her that she has no reason to doubt herself, and she fought quite well, and is assuredly their peer.
'Oh, that is such a relief! I did think so, but when so many people dismiss you for so long, it is difficult to not start believing in their judgements, baseless though they may be.
'Thank you for your help. I will remain steadfast in my self-pride. If they cannot see my worth, their blindness is their own, and not my concern.'
'I am ready to spar whenever you are, ${PLAYER}. Are you prepared?'
Wynflad has asked you to spar with her, and then with some of the other scouts to see how her skill with the sword compares with theirs. You should talk to Wynflad when you are ready to spar.
You have sparred with Wynflad and many of the scouts in order to see how her fighting skills compare to the rest of the group. You should talk to her about what you have learned.

'Though tending the horses is my given task, it is not why I volunteered for this expedition. Long have I trained for battle, but the men above me make every effort to keep me away from the battlefields.
'I wanted to learn the sword at first just to be able to defend myself. The confidence and feeling of strength that comes from competence with a blade is intoxicating, though, and I continued to train beyond the basics. Though I am no master, I believe I can handle myself in battle as well as any man.
'No woman of Rohan can be called weak, but we are expected to only be strong of heart. I can say that I am strong in arms, and the men discourage me from such things, asking why I have no husband and children yet, as if that is all a woman should ever want. It fills me with anger and makes me question my worthiness.
'Brorda dismissed me when I spoke of the sword, so I challenged him to spar. The churl denied me, saying he did not wish to harm a woman! It is infuriating, and yet there is a lingering part of me that wonders if he is correct, and I am not worthy.
'${PLAYER}, he and the others would not dismiss a hero such yourself. Would you spar with me and then with the other scouts and tell me how I compare to them?'

Wynflad wants to test herself against the Wargs of Mal Rakhúrz, in eastern Heledhris. You will find her there, waiting for you.

'I would like to put myself to a true test, but I am not so foolhardy as to run off into battle alone. I would like to combat an intelligent foe, not just unthinking beasts.
'Bhôd-buri-Mêj spoke of a Warg-lair on a mountainside called Mal Rakhúrz. Would you join me one more time, to fell some Wargs? Take your own path, and I will meet you at Mal Rakhúrz, to the east.'

'${PLAYER}, I am relieved you made it! This place is larger than I expected it to be.
'I wish to test myself, but I know better than to venture into such a place alone. I do think though, that if we split up we can bring about confusion, and they will not know which way to go.
'You should approach them from this path here, and I will slip around and attack them from the west. When we have each had enough of Wargs, meet me back here.'

'I think I've had quite enough of Wargs today. What say you, ${PLAYER}?
'Let us return to Dorngol and talk there. I have some thinking I must do on the journey back.'

'${PLAYER}, thank you for your friendship. I no longer doubt myself, and know for a fact that I can fight as well as any man in this company. I would prefer it if they agreed, but I cannot govern the minds of others. What I do have control over is how I view myself, and I now know that what I believe is not untrue.
'While Brorda and the Men that hail from Gondor may never give me the respect I am due, I think Lord Haereldir is different. Elf-maidens have oft joined the fight against darkness, so to him it is not so an unusual thing.
'But I digress. I just wanted to thank you.'

'Thank you, ${PLAYER}.
'It has always been our tradition to leave the fallen where they fell. It is respectful to not move them from the place of their battle. Their body returns to the earth in that place, feeding the life that goes on around it.

Mên-buri-Drû hangs his head in shame.
'I... I moved Hûdh-pulo-Tûth. May he forgive me for my weakness. I put him in a hole in the ground and covered him with rock and dirt. He is hidden away, where some Kwô whelp cannot find him.'

Talk to Brorda at Khel Wêro
Collect gloom-glass (${NUMBER}/${TOTAL})

'Ah, there you are! While you were away, I spent some time watching Hêg-maka-Chêrd hit her rocks together. This will be easy.'
Brorda takes the gloom-glass and strikes one with a knapping rock, breaking the whole thing in half.
'That one must have had a weakness or crack already in it. Let's try another.'
As he continues, it becomes apparent to Brorda that all of the gloom-glass you collected must have had cracks or other weaknesses in them. Soon, all he is left with is pieces too small to be spear points, and it doesn't seem to occur to him that maybe he lacks skill or knowledge.
'I suppose that is what I get for not collecting them myself. Not that I blame you, ${PLAYER}, you were only trying to help.'

You watch as Hêg-maka-Chêrd hits the gloom-glass with another rock in precise locations, using the perfect amount of force to break off shards. With each shard that is removed, the larger piece takes on the shape of a spear point. After allowing you to watch her for a time, she finally speaks.
'I would like to see Horse-rider hunt with a \qrock on a stick\q. If we are so simple next to the Horse-people, he should be able to do it easily, yes?'

'She thinks I should give it a try, does she?'
Brorda laughs.
'Even a babe can clap two rocks together. I accept her challenge!
'${PLAYER}, I shall need some of this gloom-glass. Would you gather some for me?
'I would like a good amount, as I may need a little practice. I recall seeing a lot of it on the northern slope, just outside Khel Wêro.'
Gloom-glass collected (${NUMBER}/${TOTAL})
Hêg-maka-Chêrd, a Khemozêl hunter, overheard Brorda criticizing their primitive weaponry and didn't seem pleased. You should talk to her.
Offended by Brorda's judgement that Khemozêl weapons are primitive and ineffective, Hêg-maka-Chêrd commented that she would like to see Brorda make his own spear.

'${PLAYER}, it amazes me that these people can survive as well as they do with such primitive weaponry. They fight and hunt with what amounts to simply a rock on a stick! It is a wonder that they can hunt boars with the things. How can they defend themselves from the likes of Were-wolves and Olog-hai without good steel? I cannot imagine that their so-called \qspears\q are very effective.'
You notice a Khemozêl hunter listening to your conversation with an unhappy expression. Perhaps you should talk to her.
Hewn Points
Brorda has asked you to collect some gloom-glass for him, so he may answer Hêg-maka-Chêrd's challenge.

'A carving? What about trade?
'Horse-man says he has many tales. I would like to hear a telling.'

'Well, I think the tale of most interest to a Wild Man is the one I spoke of briefly already....'
Brorda tells a colourful tale of how six thousand Riders of Rohan rode to the aid of a besieged Minas Tirith, and would not have made it were it not for the Khemozêl's kin to the west. He describes in detail the exhaustion of the weeklong march, as well as the glory of riding his steed as they thundered across the quaking fields of the Pelennor.
He spoke of monstrous mûmakil, black wraiths with fell flying steeds, and the chaos of battle. Only when the day was won and the fighting ended, did he realize he was greatly injured, and only lived because he was able to get treatment in the Houses of Healing.
Chêl-buri-Chêl listens to the tale with rapt attention, slack-jawed with amazement.

'Good tale!
'I like the good end. Khemozêl tales mostly have bad ends.
'When far-away mountain burst, ground here shakes, and our mountains burst, too, and bleed fire. Great rocks flying through the air... and the air! So much ash, and hot. Hard to breathe. Many Khemozêl die.
'My brother, he went missing. He was a great warrior, and bore the necklace of our fathers. It passed down for long time from many fathers. Now? No more. He die in the ash.
'Here, carving for you, Horse-man. Brorda. Good tale.'

'It is a beautiful thing that you did, ${PLAYER}. I am proud to have played a part in it, small though it was.
'The tears are those of sadness and not joy, but it will begin the healing of his heart, of that I am sure.'

'${PLAYER}, I find the fate of the Westfold almost pleasant compared to what these people have endured.
'I have a thought. Chêl's brother cannot be returned, but maybe that necklace could be. Let us search for it! Let this man have some sort of joy! There is is little of it here, and I know how it feels to lose everything, and be the one that somehow must live on.
'Ah, but alas, I cannot. I have duties given to me from Lord Haereldir that tether me to Khel Wêro at present.
'But you may come and go as you wish! ${PLAYER}, would you search for this necklace Chêl spoke of?'

'Meldir said to me that the Khemozêl are the same manner of folk as our Woses back home. I have heard tales of the Wild Men of the Woods since boyhood, but never have I seen one in the Westfold.
'I was among the Riders of King Théoden as we rode to the aid of Gondor, and it was rumoured that we were being guided through the secret paths of the forest by Woses. I did not get to see one with my own eyes, though I wished to.
'When I return to the lands of my fathers, I will have so many tales to tell! ${PLAYER}, do you think one of the Khemozêl would allow me to have one of their carvings? It would please me greatly to have a token to remember this adventure.'

'I will lead you to the citadel, Bâr Guruthos, when you are prepared.'

'That did not play out how I had hoped, but nevertheless, the Gaurhoth host is scattered and leaderless. This is a victory for the Free Peoples.
'It does trouble me that Elugor escaped, however. The way his people rallied around him, called him their chosen one, went to war for him? That kind of inflated ego doesn’t just dissipate on its own. We have not seen the last of him, and when he shows his face again, he will be out for revenge.
'I will keep an eye on Bâr Guruthos and call for you if he surfaces. Until then, journey well, my friend.'

'I will gather the Scouts and meet you at Bâr Guruthos. We will stay hidden, and see how this ‘wolf civil war’ plays out.
'Help the Unadorned army defeat Thothrach. We already know he is a danger to the Free Peoples. But what will Elugor do with his new-found power, should he win? I don’t trust whatever it is will be in our best interests.
'I know you have been working with him, and perhaps this is… unsavoury… but if those two wolf armies destroy each other, and we’re in position to end this for good….
'Don’t think about it for now. Go to Bâr Guruthos and help the Unadorned. I will find you when I can.'

'We are gathered. I will now declare my intentions.'

'The Gaurhoth have always seen us as fodder, a stock of strong bodies to be turned to Khurz-hai as they please.
'Elugor is different. He treats us as equals. His strong heart will lead us to a golden age!'
'Rrrr. Elugor want us to fight, we will fight. I care not who. Why so much talking when we could be fighting?'

'We look to Elugor for hope because he is not like us. Broken. Lesser. The first in a long time.
'We hope no more will be born like us. We will follow the Unadorned into a brighter future. He will succeed where Thothrach has failed!'

'Hmmm… In asking for our help to challenge his sire for the throne of Bar Guruthos, he breaks laws which have stood for thousands of years. This is not our way, but… I am swayed by his words.
'Our people have suffered for so long, and perhaps he is right. Is Thothrach too traditional to adapt to this new world? Lord Sauron is gone, and his Gûrzyul lackeys control us no longer.
'If Elugor, the chosen one, can forge a path forward, we Gaurhoth will follow.'
'It is done. We will claim my sire’s throne, for the good of all Gaurhoth.'

'I am sorry I interrupted your rest, ${PLAYER}. Old memories of the times Rikháwi and I spent here began to plague me, so I gave up on sleeping.
'I neglected to fully explain why I wanted set up camp here. I wished to be close to the ocean, but more than that: I wanted to see if I was still afraid of it.
'Of course, any good sailor is afraid of the sea. However, that fear is borne of respect. My fear stems from elsewhere: a paralyzing terror that grips me when I take a single step into the water. I -- I tried to ignore that feeling, as you can see. But...'
She sighs.
'Have you had dreams of the dead before, ${PLAYER}?'

'I have a dream that returns like the tides, time and time again, of standing on a nameless, empty shore. I see Rikháwi standing in the water far from shore, looking at me. I try to reach her, yet I only sink into the depths. Then I wake.'
A dry chuckle escapes from her, but there is no humour to it.
'You do not need to tell me what such dreams mean.
'During one storm, the ship sprang leaks in the lower decks. Heavy cargo pinned down my leg and prevented my escape. Struggling did nothing; the water rose ever higher. But Rikháwi helped free me, gave me my life in exchange for losing hers. What have either of us done to deserve such fates?
'The crew and I were the only ones who mourned her. Like me, she had no one left on land.
'I spent the last year trying to avoid thoughts of her. However, the harder I tried, the more furious these memories became. They would not let me forget.
'Tell me ${PLAYER}: do you think peace is possible for the living?'
You drift off to sleep...

'The sea still scares me. Even while I worked on the ship, I could not ignore it -- that faint dread itching at the back of my mind. To depend so heavily on a force that could easily claim my life... that has claimed the life of one close to me.
'I wonder if such feelings will ever fade. Maybe they will dull, with time. However, tonight, I will remain awake and watch the stars.
'Stay a while, if you wish. The night is lonely and I would not mind your presence.'

As you watch the stars together, the hushed world around you continues its slumber.

The recipe calls for pork and turnips as its main ingredients. While the recipe appears complete at first glance, you realize the instructions only make vague references to seasonings. The ingredients list does not contain any relevant information.

'My grandmother used to cook this for me because it was the only way I'd eat turnips. I've been trying to complete the recipe for years now, but I can't replicate the seasoning mixture. Nor can I accurately describe how it tasted -- all I have to refer to are faint memories.
'If the dwarves are the only clue we've got, then we'll make plans to visit them. We can ask about local seasonings, hopefully get the answers I've been seeking, then leave straightaway.
'Travelling to the closest town may be prudent. I'd rather not travel too far from the Shire if I don't have to.'
'Maybe I'll finally put this mystery to rest.'

A well-worn, faded leather cover binds the pages of this journal together. The pages themselves are in much better condition, displaying dried leaves and flowers that have been carefully pressed onto the paper.
Most are certainly local to the Shire; others originate from elsewhere, particularly the northern region of Ered Luin.

These notes consist of loose, but orderly, pages with information on various plants and their applications in cooking. Everything mentioned appears to be local, but the author meticulously details everything there is to know about each plant. It is as if she were addressing these notes to one who has never stepped foot into the Shire.

Inside this nondescript wooden box, you discover pieces of parchment. Each features a recipe written in small, tidy lettering.
A smattering of splotches and smudges adorn the edges of the recipes, signaling frequent usage in the past. You're doubtful that's the case now.

'Some of those plants in the journal came from up north? As in, where the dwarves live? My grandmother often left the Shire in order to collect and try new cooking ingredients, but that's all I know. Nobody was interested in finding out where she went or what she did. Nor was she willing to tell me anything.
'But why go north? Surely the dwarves have nothing that would warrant travelling so far from home for!
'It's just... I simply cannot imagine anything out there being better than what we already have here. Why, I've already been almost attacked by bandits and a bear -- a bear! And these incidents happened right outside the Shire!'
Haldo pauses to breathe deeply and quell his rising distress.
'Apologies again... how embarrassing. If I'm to solve this mystery, I need to be as brave as my grandmother was.
'Which, speaking of the mystery...'
He rummages through the recipe box before pulling out one in particular.
'This is it, right here.'

'That is not what I am here to tell you, however. There is a small group, they call themselves the Khemozêl, who are located near here. 'I do not believe it to be true. I know the Sûhalar.
'These are just Sûhalar lies. A people does not change overnight. I have known their leaders. They are warmongers, desiring nothing but the glory and blood of battle.
'Ask him about his people and their ways. I believe not that these Sûhalar will not war if given the chance. They have merely been knocked down. They prize the chance to rise once more in martial glory.'

'Much comes down to the leader of a people, but it also comes from the people themselves.
'Each of us makes his or her own choice. I am not my father. I am not my king or chieftain. I am only Rashan. We separated ourselves from the others because we did not feel as though we knew or belonged with them.
'Your friend has nothing to fear from us. He would do well to relax. Stroll through Jorbalukh. The only immediate danger are the clouds of stinging gnats - and possibly Alghila's meat pies.'

'I see. I misjudged them - I may not need my sword this day.
'I feel foolish. I do not wish this to be the way those around here remember me.
'Let us do something to make amends. Please, ask Rashan if there is something we can do to aid his mission at Jorbalukh.'

'I would have words with one of these Sûhalar. Keep on your guard - we may have to fight our way out.
'I will stay here, guarding our exit. Speak with that one, over there in the robe. I would know his intentions within Nan Ogol.'

'Battle? Dor Súha. I am Rashan. I have devoted my life to my studies, not to war.
'There are many Sûhalar who wish to die in glorious battle. We are not those Sûhalar. We have been driven from our ancestral homes, forced to fight to survive in Nan Ogol, beset on all sides by all manners of beasts and creatures that would rather eat us than let us live.
'I know I speak for many in Jorbalukh when I say we merely wish to be left alone. We make no war, nor have means or plans to.'

'Actually, it is quite fortunate you have come this day. There is something you can help me with. Long have I wished to gain access to dark lair of Naethion to the north.

'That is a fine idea. We should turn thoughts to action. I would do what I can to help those within Jorbalukh. It is the least I can do, after I have... somewhat misjudged them.'

'We should scout this settlement - if there is trouble to be had I would know its face first. Will you accompany me to Jorbalukh? I believe we may need to fight our way out, and I could use an experienced warrior by my side.'

'I knew you were the very one for this undertaking.
'You have spared me no small measure of needless vexation. Yet, to speak plainly, my friend, my concern over the goblins grows with each passing day.
'They have ever been a nuisance, it is true, but now their boldness waxes. If they walk openly upon the Greenfields, how long shall it be before they press beyond the bounds and into the Shire itself?'
A heavy silence falls.
'But that is a thought for another day. This day belongs to me—and to you as well, of course, my friend!'

'Quickly now. The sooner you return, the sooner shall my mind be set at ease, knowing that the threat is contained—and, moreover, that I shall not be beset by a bevy of displeased hobbits. Go then, clear out the cavern, and let no goblin escape your mighty vengeance.'
Speak with Paladin Took within the Great Smials at Tuckborough

Post:
Required, adventurous type with weapons and gumption to charge headlong into enemy forces and root them out of The Shire. If compelled by these words, seek me out at the The Great Smials in Tuckborough.
- Paladin Took

'Your coming is most fortunate, friend.
'The Bounders bring word of goblins seen in greater numbers about the Greenfields. I will not suffer such foul folk to creep into the Shire; else the townships shall beset me from dawn till dusk, clamouring that I rid them of the menace.
'Rather than send many Bounders to scour the fields and hedgerows for these goblins, I have looked beyond our borders and sought stout-hearted adventurers, such as yourself, to take up this charge.'
He smiles with no small measure of pride.
'For one such as you, it should prove a simple enough task.'
